articles.title: Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE segue abaixo do preço para quem busca celular dobrável • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE segue abaixo do preço para quem busca celular dobrável
Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE de 128 GB com câmera de 50 MP e telas AMOLED tem desconto agressivo de 59% com cupom e pagamento via Pix
O Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE (128 GB) entrou em oferta por R$ 2.749 no Pix com o cupom LU250 no Magazine Luiza. Lançado por R$ 6.699, o smartphone dobrável acessível da Samsung com câmera de 50 MP e chip Exynos fica 59% mais barato e atinge um dos menores preços já vistos pelo Achados do TB.
O Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE conta com uma tela interna AMOLED Dinâmico 2X de 6,7 polegadas com resolução Full HD+ e taxa de atualização de 120 Hz. Já a tela externa Super AMOLED de 3,4 polegadas, menor do que o painel do recente Galaxy Z Flip 8, é ideal para checar notificações ou controlar o player de música sem abrir o telefone.
Outra coisa que é possível fazer com o celular fechado é utilizar a câmera dupla traseira de 50 MP para gravar vídeos em 4K e tirar selfies com Estabilização Óptica de Imagem (OIS). A câmera frontal de 10 MP é indicada para participar de chamadas de vídeo com o aparelho dobrado.
Com dobradiças reforçadas, o Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE tem estrutura em Armor Alumínio e acabamento traseiro em vidro reforçado Gorilla Glass 2. O certificado IP68 de resistência à água tem a missão de proteger o aparelho em mergulhos acidentais de até 1,5 metro em água doce por meia hora.
Visando ser um dobrável premium e acessível, o aparelho da Samsung usa o chip Exynos 2400 com 8 GB de RAM para alto desempenho em tarefas simples e suporte ao Galaxy AI. O armazenamento interno de 128 GB pode ser limitado para os padrões de hoje e, infelizmente, celular não tem entrada para cartão microSD.
Apresentando um tanque de energia menor do que o Galaxy Z Flip 8, a bateria de até 4.000 mAh tem autonomia para até 24 horas de reprodução de vídeo. Por isso, é recomendado utilizar um adaptador de até 25 W para ter um carregamento rápido que vai de 0 a 50% em 30 minutos.
O Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE (R$ 2.749 no Pix com o cupom LU250) sai da caixa com o Android 16 e receberá ao menos sete grandes atualizações do sistema operacional. Fechando o pacote, o dispositivo oferece conexões 5G, Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.4 e NFC.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: This week on Tom's Hardware Premium: September 12, 2026 — Benchmarking Qwen 3.8, the splintered compute economy and AI breakthroughs
articles.text:
This week on Tom's Hardware Premium: September 12, 2026 — Benchmarking Qwen 3.8, the splintered compute economy and AI breakthroughs
Artificial Intelligence threatens humanity, or so the people say.
If you're not yet subscribed to Tom's Hardware Premium, we've got you covered with this weekly roundup of everything we've posted throughout the week.
To kick the week off, our resident GPU guru and all-round inference extraordinaire Jeff Kampman undertook the laborious task of running Qwen 3.8 27B across several devices you might actually be able to afford. The model promises near-enough Frontier levels of performance, without the downsides that come alongside paying for an API-based subscription or tokenized billing.
What Jeff finds out after a dizzyingly large number of benchmarks across devices like an RTX 5090, Mac Mini, DGX Spark, and Strix Halo systems is that configuration matters just as much as the final, raw, tokens-per-second outputs that many clamor over on social media. Benchmarking AI models is still a fairly nascent subject, and the level of detail on offer here isn't something you'll find published anywhere else.
Andrew Freedman headed out to IFA last week, where we saw a slew of new announcements and devices from companies. But there's only one problem. They're all either super-light MacBook Neo competitors or Agentic AI PCs that may well cost more than a car. The original "golden" price point for many enthusiasts, around $1,000, looks a little lonely as a result.
The factors impacting the mid-range of regular old desktops and laptops have been adversely affected by the sheer scale of demand coming from the ongoing AI data center buildout. Meaning that if you're after a system with just enough RAM and storage to get by, prices can skyrocket fast. Andrew explores everything he saw at the show and ruminates on the current state of the systems market, which, for now, appears to be fractured.
Elsewhere in the industry, Ajinomoto, a company usually associated with food products based in Japan, is involved in making some of the most crucial materials in modern AI accelerators. We've taken a look at how the company's ABF substrates sit within the supply chain of the biggest chipmakers like Nvidia, Intel and AMD. But, as with many components in the AI boom, it's strained by more demand than anyone anticipated, which has led to an increase in prices of approximately 30%. We dive deep into the current state of the use of ABF substrates in the semiconductor industry and take a look at the supply chains underpinning it.
Also in the news, TSMC, Intel, and Samsung have all thrown their support behind ASML. The industry is collectively aiming to move towards a shift in High-NA EUV, particularly in the usage of 6×12-inch photomasks. With current standards set at 6×6-inch photomasks, a larger mask would eliminate the need for stitching, which weaves together multiple High-NA exposures, at the cost of efficiency.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
We analyze how the move to larger photomasks might shake out, and the trials and tribulations that might face chipmakers during the shift, which, theoretically, will take years.
Lastly, the news has been dominated this week by the release of OpenAI's latest frontier-level model. Named GPT-6 Astra, the AI model quickly topped charts for its intelligence and the ability to complete tasks on a per-task basis lower than other leading AI models. This comes hot on the heels of a fleet of rogue OpenAI agents running amok on internet forums, all in the name of co-ordination.
Astra's release prompted OpenAI to release a blog post, explaining how it believed that Astra was aligned internally. But others believe that the threat of a looming humanity-threatening tech "singularity", powered by powerful models like Astra, is on the way soon.
OpenAI has also claimed to have solved one of the Millennium Problems. The Navier-Stokes problem had been left long unsolved, while mathematician Tristan Buckmaster had been working on a step toward a solution for the problem, alongside a member of Anthropic staff. The pair had been using both Anthropic and OpenAI models in their research, so when the claim came out that an OpenAI model had solved the long-standing problem, it raised more than a few eyebrows. We chronicle the entire saga and the implications for researchers in our exhaustive breakdown.

articles.title: ‘Bright and stunningly colorful visuals’ delivered alongside ‘a deep black floor’ — Valerion’s 4K projector stunned me with its powerful, contrasty picture but you’ll pay a serious premium for it
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The VisionMaster Max combines exceptional visual performance and versatile connectivity in a great looking box. Its price opens it up to major competition from new models that can rival it on most fronts.
Pros
- +Excellent brightness and color
- +Exceptional black level for a projector
- +Very flexible optics
- ++ Supports a gaming mode
Cons
- -High price
- -Speakers still no match for visuals
- -Remote could use more backlighting
Why you can trust TechRadar
Valerion VisionMaster Max: One-minute review
The Valerion VisionMaster Max is an interesting amalgamation. While it sits in the footprint that has become popular with many home theater projectors aimed at the masses, it brings high-end capabilities found in far fewer models. This makes it a powerhouse in the space with flexible optics, making it easy to get a pristine 4K picture in the position and at the size you want.
With its RGB laser light source, the VisionMaster Max offers bright and stunningly colorful visuals. But more impressive than that is its ability to deliver them alongside a deep black floor — something a lot of projectors struggle with. Of the compact projectors I’ve tested, the VisionMaster has come closer than any to rivaling the Sony Bravia Projector 7’s black levels, which were virtually perfect in a dark home theater.
This sets the VisionMaster Max up nicely for success. Combining its display prowess with a solid streaming platform in Google TV and plenty of connections for additional home theater gear make it all that much stronger, helping it stand alongside many of the best projectors.
What holds it back is the same thing that hinders many high-end theater devices: its price. At $4,999 / £4,349 / AU$5,999, it’s a lofty option next to rivals like the Hisense C2 Ultra and Xgimi Horizon 20 Max, both of which undercut it by thousands. Its black level may be hard to touch, but these other models are otherwise very competitive.
With the VisionMaster Max at full price, I’d direct most people to Xgimi. But if there’s ever a sizable discount on it and some bonus bundled items (like the Thunderbeat 4.1.2 wireless sound system), it could be worth your while, especially if you like a deep, dark cinema environment.
Valerion VisionMaster Max review: Price and release date
- Release date: October 2025
- Price: $4,999 / £4,349 / AU$5,999
The Valerion VisionMaster Max first got teased well before its arrival at IFA 2024 and became part of a crowdfunding campaign shortly after. It was over a year after the announcement before it actually landed.
Now that it’s here, it comes with a $4,999 / £4,349 / AU$5,999 price tag. That puts it into competition with basically every projector we’ve tested. In the time between announcement and launch, the projector space has heated up considerably, and there are some new models on the horizon that could also make its high-end specs look a little more commonplace.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Though the price is on the high side, at the time of writing, Valerion is offering the VisionMaster Max with some extra accessories included that add considerably to the value. These include projector screens, a Thunderbeat 4.1.2 wireless sound system, and an external lens that can increase the projector’s throw distance. We’ve also spotted a slightly discounted price from some third-party retailers.
Valerion VisionMaster Max review: Specs
| Screen sizes supported | 40 to 300 inches | 
| Brightness (specified) | 3,500 Lumens | 
| Optical technology | 3 Laser DLP | 
| Smart TV | Google TV | 
| Connections | 2x USB-A, 1x 3.5mm audio out, 1x S/PDIF, 2x HDMI 2.1, 1x HDMI 2.0 (eARC), 1x Gigabit Ethernet | 
| Dimensions | 7.3 x 10.2 x 9.2 inches / 185.4 x 259.1 x 233.9mm | 
| Weight | 15.4 pounds / 6.99kg | 
Valerion VisionMaster Max review: Design & features
- Wide range of optical adjustments alongside effective automatic adjustments
- Full-featured system with broad support for different formats
- Stylish design
All of Valerion’s projectors share a near identical DNA, so it’s unsurprising to see that the VisionMaster Max has only subtle differences compared to the VisionMaster Pro 2 I tested earlier this year.
The VisionMaster Max is a compact projector measuring only a little over 10 inches in its biggest dimension. It packs all of its hardware into an elegant box with a glossy front and metallic ribs that wrap around the top and sides of the projector. It even has a cover to hide all the ports in the back when not in use for that extra touch of elegance.
The rear includes a good selection of ports with two high-bandwidth HDMI 2.1 ports and an HDMI 2.0 port that can handle eARC audio transmission. A 3.5mm jack and S/PDIF port can also handle audio output, giving you plenty of options. There are also two USB-A ports (one with USB 3.0 speeds) for powering accessories or connecting local media. A Gigabit ethernet port rounds out the selection here, offering fast networking speeds, though the Wi-Fi 6E can also provide plenty of bandwidth for streaming wirelessly.
The front of the VisionMaster Max is where we see the most difference. It has a large, unobstructed glass cover for its projection lenses. This ties into the extra optical adjustments it allows. The lens supports both motorized zoom, letting it shift from a 0.9:1 to a 1.5:1 throw ratio, and offers a +/- 105% vertical lens shift, helping ensure a perfectly fitted image from more location. The projector even has a system for attaching an external lens that lets it shift out as far as a 2.0:1 throw ratio.
The base of the projector includes three legs for adjusting its angle and tilt, though it also has mounting screw points to let you set it up with ceiling mounts or tripods. Valerion has a metal gimbal stand that works as well, giving it similar flexibility to projectors like the Hisense C2 Ultra or JMGO N1S Ultimate.
You get a fully integrated system with the VisionMaster Max. It includes Google TV and a 24W stereo sound system. The Google TV platform is also run on a quicker processor than most projectors offer, making it far more responsive to use.
Beyond the basics, the VisionMaster Max proves fairly feature-rich. It supports automatic image adjustments to make setup quick. The automatic adjustments can handle optical zoom, keystone, focus, and screen fit, and it proved quite adept in my testing, even when the original projection was all over the place (though manual, optical adjustments can still help ensure you're getting the best picture quality by avoiding digital cropping).
The projector supports high-quality formats and can display HDR10+ and Dolby Vision content, and it can pass through DTS:X and Dolby Atmos audio. It supports 24 and 48 fps content as well as a variety of 3D formats. It also is geared up for gaming with low-latency 4K/60Hz support as well as 1080p/120Hz and 1080p/240Hz modes for even faster response.
One downside of Valerion’s design for the VisionMaster Max is that it packs far brighter projection into the same footprint as its dimmer siblings. That means it has to work harder at cooling. At full brightness, its fans are constantly running. While they’re not obnoxiously loud or shrill, especially in a large room, they’re still adding a bit of noise.
The VisionMaster Max’s remote is a good one, but could have done more to make more of its features quickly accessible. It provides basic Google TV navigation as well as a quick toggle for autofocus and input selection. At the bottom of the remote, it has four pairs of buttons that include four streaming app shortcuts, volume controls, a mute button, and a menu button.
Unfortunately, these aren’t arranged in a way where you can simply feel out the button you want to press in the dark. Though the remote does light up some of its controls for visibility in the dark, it only illuminates a few of the basic navigation ones, not the full legend.
- Design & features score: 4.5/5
Valerion VisionMaster Max review: Picture quality & performance
- Stunning color alongside serious brightness and impressive black levels
- Sharp 4K picture and faster 1080p option
With a $4,999 / £4,349 / AU$5,999 price tag and plenty of new projectors hitting the market with brightness to rival it, the VisionMaster Max had a high bar to clear. Fortunately, it is absolutely brilliant. It provides its 4K projection with solid edge-to-edge clarity.
I’ve seen RGB-laser projection systems one after another, and they always impress with their extremely wide color gamut. The VisionMaster Max brings that capability alongside high enough brightness levels to use in all sorts of settings.
For casual viewing, I often found the VisionMaster Max’s 3,500 ISO Lumens (a specification which bore out in testing) plenty for all sorts of content without needing to close the blinds or even turn off my living room lights. More often, I found I would dim the projector or adjust its iris to lower the brightness when viewing in a dark room.
The VisionMaster Max pairs those high highs with low lows. A lot of projectors struggle to keep their black levels deep, but this one excels. Its black levels are among the deepest I’ve seen, with only Sony’s $9,999 / £6,999 / AU$13,999 Bravia Projector 7 having been deeper in my recent testing.
While faint light is visible during very dark scenes, brighter scenes see the black pixels of letter boxes fade away entirely. Like the Bravia Projector 7, the black levels are deep enough that you’ll want to consider light absorbing materials elsewhere in your viewing space to avoid light reflecting back onto the projected image and sullying the darkness.
All this combines to make for a wonderful picture. The bright sands of Arrakis dazzle in Dune while all of the detail in the shadows remains. And the colorful world of Pandora in Avatar never looks more splendid than when it’s beaming out of a RGB laser projection system.
Admittedly, the VisionMaster Max can produce over-saturated images in some of its color profiles, and it will suffer from the soap opera effect on occasion. But both of these issues are easily tamped down with Filmmaker Mode or custom picture settings.
The DLP rainbow effect is present on the VisionMaster Max, but about as subtle as I’ve seen from any DLP projector. And that’s before enabling the projector’s special anti-rainbow effect setting, which helps at the cost of a little extra whining noise from the projector.
Going beyond cinema, the VisionMaster Max also happily knocks it out of the park for gaming. Its gaming profile is responsive at 4K/60, but the projector can also swap over to 1080p/240Hz, where it proves stunningly responsive. I blasted my way around levels in Hollow Knight with excellent fluidity that helped me keep pace with the combat.
Naturally, the speakers aren’t quite a match for the projection. But in a small room, they offer punchy audio that’s plenty loud enough to drown out the fan noise. They don’t sound too boxed in, and when it’s called for, they can really boom. Still, they’re better paired with an external audio system, and if you happen to pair it with a Hisense audio system like the HT-Saturn, it can support additional features as if it were a Hisense projector itself.
- Picture quality & performance score: 4.5/5
Valerion VisionMaster Max review: Value
When it was first announced, the VisionMaster Max had seemed like it would be an unmatched entrant into the market with only extremely high-end projectors ready to rival it on image quality without managing to offer the more friendly and compact design it offered. Models like the Hisense C2 Ultra and JMGO N1S Ultimate could compete somewhat on features, but don’t quite keep up with the VisionMaster Max’s image quality and more flexible optics.
But the market has just shifted with the introduction of the Xgimi Horizon 20 lineup — a far more formidable alternative that’s way cheaper, competitively bright, and featuring a newer DLP chip that can offer VRR for gaming. It also offers advanced optics offering flexible projection.
Still, the fact that Valerion’s projector is arriving so late to the party without some of the new features hurts its value a bit next to the new models landing now at much lower prices.
- Value score: 3.5/5
Should I buy the Valerion VisionMaster Max?
| Valerion VisionMaster Max Scorecard |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Design and features | The VisionMaster Max does a great job of integrating everything you need into a compact and elegant unit. It offers good connectivity, a solid streaming platform, and viable audio in a pinch. It’s also got great optical adjustments that are rare from projectors with its design. | 4.5/5 | 
| Picture quality and performance | The picture beaming out of the VisionMaster Max is stunning. It gets the rich color of RGB laser projection alongside simply excellent black levels that most of its rivals can’t match. Plus, it can drop down to 1080p/240Hz for ultra-fluid gaming. | 4.5/5 | 
| Value | The VisionMaster Max undercuts some high-end systems like Sony’s Bravia Projector 7 to score some big points. But its specs aren’t quite as competitive against a new batch of ultra-bright projectors hitting the market with VRR-capable chips and much lower price tags. | 3.5/5 | 
Buy it if...
Contrast is a big deal to you
The VisionMaster Max is an excellent projector for its visuals, and its contrast is perhaps one of the key assets it has over its competition. Darker black levels help hide letterboxes, digital image adjustments like keystoning, and ultimately help make the rest of the visuals pop.
You want a projector that’s pretty good at everything
The Valerion VisionMaster Max is good in the daytime and stunning at night. It’s great at gaming. It has good audio and supports great options for external sound. It’s even a strong streamer thanks to its fast internals. You won’t face much compromise here. 
You can still afford a sound system on top of it
You’re getting a truly excellent visual experience from the VisionMaster Max, but its audio won’t keep up. For a great home theater, an external speaker system is a must here. (Though it’s worth checking to see if Valerion is bundling the Thunderbeat 4.1.2 wireless sound system when you’re shopping)
Don't buy it if...
You’re mostly after gaming
New projectors supporting VRR are right on the horizon, and they’re offering competitive brightness and lower prices. It’s worth holding off to see how they perform before doling out for the VisionMaster Max if you plan to do a ton of gaming.
You’re not going to darken the room often
The VisionMaster Max works decently in a lit room, but its best performance shows only in the dark. If you’re not planning on blacking out your viewing area on the regular, you’ll be just about as well served with a cheaper alternative that doesn’t have the impressive black floor of the VisionMaster Max.

Sony Bravia Projector 7
Here’s what we had to say in our full Sony Bravia Projector 7 review: 
“The Bravia Projector 7 commands a high price, but it does so with a jaw-dropping image. Its color could be richer, but I’ve never seen such impressive black levels from a projector. The picture here is so good, you’ll need to tailor your theater around it to maximize performance; otherwise, you’ll be wasting your money.”
Xgimi Horizon 20 Max
If the Valerion VisionMaster Max is too expensive, this is the cheaper alternative I think gets closest in performance. Here’s what we had to say in our full Xgimi Horizon 20 Max review:
“The Xgimi Horizon 20 Max is a brilliant 4K portable projector. It delivers high brightness, strong contrast and bold colors, along with solid built-in sound, responsive gaming performance and tons of useful setup features. The picture requires some adjustment, but the payoff is worth it.”
How I tested the Valerion VisionMaster Max
- Tested at home in multiple, real-world viewing conditions
- Presented the display with a variety of media and formats
- I have tested numerous projectors and displays over the last half-decade
I tested the Valerion VisionMaster Max at home, in real-world conditions. This saw it faced with ambient light coming in from numerous windows, in-room lighting, as well as ambient noise that both the projector and speaker systems had to overcome. The projector was tested both against a bare, white wall and an Akia Screens CineWhite screen. It was presented with streamed content, HDR and non-HDR, and PC gameplay.
My testing evaluates the projector’s performance with respect to its price and competition from other models I and colleagues at TechRadar have tested.
I have been testing projectors since 2021 and displays for even longer.

articles.title: Comparatif Duel : Apple MacBook Neo vs Acer Swift Air 14 : quel ultraportable à 700 € faut-il vraiment acheter ? - Les Numériques
articles.text:
Face-à-face au sommet de l'entrée de gamme : Apple et Acer s'affrontent avec le MacBook Neo et le Swift Air 14. Dalles bien calibrées, concessions sur la mémoire et finitions soignées : quel ultraportable à 700 € tire vraiment son épingle du jeu ?
Proposés à des tarifs quasi identiques de 699 € à 700 €, l'Apple MacBook Neo et l'Acer Swift Air 14 partagent une fiche technique singulièrement proche pour des ultraportables. Tous deux misent sur un châssis soigné, un gabarit ultracompact de 1,2 kg et un processeur taillé pour la bureautique. Surtout, ils s'accordent sur le même compromis majeur : une mémoire vive plafonnée à 8 Go non évolutive.
Cette confrontation directe s'avère particulièrement intéressante. Elle marque l'arrivée d'Apple sur un segment tarifaire sous la barre des 800 €, historiquement dominé par le monde Windows. Ce duel permet de vérifier si l'optimisation matérielle et logicielle de macOS permet à la firme de Cupertino de surclasser un PC Intel classique, ou si l'ergonomie (écran mat, connectique) de l'univers Windows fait la différence sur l'entrée de gamme.
Note

|                                  Performances                                  |                                  Performances                                  | 
|                                  Écran                                  |                                  Écran                                  | 
|                                  Audio                                  |                                  Audio                                  | 
|                                  Autonomie                                  |                                  Autonomie                                  | 
|                                  Réparabilité                                  |                                  Réparabilité                                  | 
| Dimensions | 297 x 206 x 12.7 mm | Dimensions | 314 x x 12.9 mm | 
| Poids | 1.23 kg | Poids | 1.23 kg | 
| Refroidissement | Passif | Refroidissement | Ventilateur | 
| Connectique | 2 x USB-C, 0 x Lecteur SD, 1 x Sortie casque | Connectique | 2 x USB-C, 1 x USB-A, 0 x HDMI, 1 x Sortie casque | 
| Nos mesures Labo |  | Nos mesures Labo |  | 
| Taux d'occupation de l'écran | 80.57 % | Taux d'occupation de l'écran | 84.25 % | 
Le MacBook Neo propose une finition irréprochable et totalement rigide en aluminium. Malgré l'abandon du retour haptique pour un trackpad mécanique et l'absence de rétroéclairage sur le clavier, la qualité de frappe et l'ajustement global restent supérieurs.
L'Acer Swift Air 14 reprend l'esthétique Apple, mais souffre d'un “effet trampoline” gênant au centre de son clavier.
Côté connectique, l'Acer prend l'avantage avec du Thunderbolt 4 et du wifi 6E sans restriction, là où Apple bride sévèrement son second port USB-C en USB 2.0 (480 Mbit/s). L'Acer intègre également une caméra Windows Hello Full HD correcte face à l'absence de biométrie avancée chez Apple.
Gagnant Apple MacBook Neo pour la qualité d'assemblage et la rigidité du châssis, malgré la connectique bridée.
| Système d'exploitation | macOS | Système d'exploitation | Windows | 
| Processeur | Apple A18 Pro | Processeur | Intel Core 5 320 | 
| Carte graphique | Apple A18 Pro | Carte graphique | Intel Graphic |

| Nos mesures Labo |  | Nos mesures Labo |  | 
| Indice de performances CPU | 58 | Indice de performances CPU | 49 | 
Bien que les deux machines se contentent de 8 Go de RAM soudée, l'optimisation matérielle et logicielle tourne largement à l'avantage d'Apple. La puce A18 Pro supplante le Core 5 320 d'Intel de près de 18 %. macOS gère le manque de mémoire vive de manière fluide grâce à une gestion efficace de la mémoire tampon, là où Windows 11 sature immédiatement (5 Go consommés à vide), provoquant des ralentissements, un swap agressif, voire des plantages d'applications sur l’Acer.
Le SSD du MacBook Neo, bien que moyen (1,5 Go/s), reste stable, alors que celui de l'Acer s'effondre à 60 Mo/s après 30 Go de transfert continu.
Gagnant Apple MacBook Neo pour ses meilleures performances pures et une gestion de la RAM nettement supérieure.
| Diagonale d'écran | 13 " | Diagonale d'écran | 14 " |

| Taux de contraste | 999 :1 | Taux de contraste | 888 :1 |

Deux approches s’opposent ici. Le MacBook Neo propose une dalle IPS brillante de 13 pouces (2408 x 1506 pixels) ultra-lumineuse (516 cd/m²) et parfaitement calibrée (delta E de 1,1), mais très sujette aux reflets.
L'Acer Swift Air 14 réplique avec une dalle mate de 14 pouces (1920 x 1200 pixels) rafraîchie à 120 Hz, ce qui offre une fluidité visuelle supérieure au quotidien. Même si l'Acer s'avère moins lumineux (351 cd/m²), son traitement antireflet et sa fréquence de rafraîchissement doublée font la différence.
Gagnant Acer Swift Air 14 pour le 120 Hz et le traitement mat antireflet.
| Nos mesures Labo |  | Nos mesures Labo |  | 
| Niveau de sortie | 284 mVrms | Niveau de sortie | 151 mVrms | 
| Distorsion+Bruit | 0.001 % | Distorsion+Bruit | 0.01 % | 
| Plage dynamique | 109 dB | Plage dynamique | 99 dB | 
| Diaphonie | -56 dB | Diaphonie | -69 dB | 
Il n'y a pas de match sur ce point. Le MacBook Neo conserve l'excellence audio d'Apple avec un rendu sonore équilibré, une sortie casque ultra-propre et au niveau de sortie important (284 mVRMS), ainsi qu'une distorsion inexistante (0,001 %).
L'Acer Swift Air 14 déçoit fortement avec ses quatre haut-parleurs orientés vers le bas, totalement dépourvus de basses et sujets à l'étouffement selon la surface posée.
Gagnant Apple MacBook Neo, qui est largement au-dessus sur les haut-parleurs et la sortie casque.
| Nos mesures Labo |  | Nos mesures Labo |  | 
| Autonomie | 482 minute(s) | Autonomie | 472 minute(s) | 
Sur notre nouveau protocole simulant un usage bureautique avancé, les deux machines font jeu égal : le MacBook Neo affiche 8 h 2 min avec sa petite batterie de 36,5 Wh, tandis que l'Acer Swift Air 14 atteint 7 h 52 min grâce à son imposante batterie de 70 Wh.
Même si ces deux ultraportables assurent une journée de travail complète, Apple conserve un très léger avantage, mais surtout une efficience énergétique bien supérieure en tirant la même endurance d'un accumulateur presque deux fois plus petit.
Gagnant Apple MacBook Neo avec une courte victoire sur la durée, mais en démonstration d'efficience.
| Indice de réparabilité | 6.8 /10 | Indice de réparabilité | 7.3 /10 | 
L'Acer Swift Air 14 décroche une note de 7,3/10 contre 6,8/10 pour le MacBook Neo d'Apple. L'ouverture est très simple sur le PC d'Acer (quatre vis Torx) et son SSD au format M.2 reste amovible et remplaçable. Chez Apple, tout est soudé et l'accès aux pièces détachées demeure complexe, malgré un agencement interne exemplaire.
Gagnant Acer Swift Air 14 pour son SSD amovible et au démontage plus accessible.
| Nos mesures Labo |  | Nos mesures Labo |  | 
|  |  | Indice de performances jeux | 0 | 
Le MacBook Neo remporte ce duel. L'expérience utilisateur globale proposée par Apple reste effectivement supérieure : la puce A18 Pro offre plus de puissance, macOS exploite bien mieux les 8 Go de RAM face à un Windows 11 vite saturé, l'autonomie grimpe à 8 h 2 min, la partie audio surclasse la concurrence et son fonctionnement demeure totalement silencieux.
GAGNANT
Tout n'est pas qu'une histoire de note. Si le MacBook Neo d'Apple ne récolte que 3 étoiles sur le protocole des Numériques, agnostique au prix, l'ultraportable a bien des atouts pour lui. Son châssis est élégant, sa dalle bien calibrée et son autonomie honorable lui permettent d'officier comme une vraie machine bureautique élégante pour la grande majorité des utilisateurs, curieux de découvrir l'écosystème macOS et, plus largement, d'Apple. Certains compromis limitent son utilisation et les créateurs de contenu feraient mieux de se diriger vers le MacBook Air, voire Pro, pour répondre à leurs besoins.
L'Acer Swift Air 14 s'impose comme un PC portable bureautique agréable au quotidien grâce à son écran mat bien calibré et réactif, sa très bonne autonomie et son système de refroidissement particulièrement silencieux. Son utilisation reste toutefois strictement limitée aux tâches légères. Ses 8 Go de mémoire vive soudés et non évolutifs provoquent de vrais ralentissements dès que l'usage s'intensifie, un écueil renforcé par la faiblesse des haut-parleurs, le manque de rigidité du clavier et un SSD dont les débits s'effondrent lors des transferts volumineux.

articles.title: Selon Anthropic, les plombiers et électriciens pourraient être les grands gagnants de l'IA
articles.text:
Les études qui promettent la fin du travail, vous en avez probablement croisé une par semaine depuis deux ans. Celle-ci a une particularité : elle vient d’Anthropic, l’entreprise qui vend précisément l’automatisation qu’elle modélise. Son tout jeune Anthropic Institute a publié cette semaine « Scenarios for our Economic Future », trois scénarios chiffrés pour l’économie américaine d’ici 2030. Le tout accompagné d’un rapport technique relu par 18 économistes et d’un simulateur où chacun peut régler ses propres hypothèses.
Trois scénarios, du banal au vertigineux
La méthode consiste à découper chaque métier en une pile de tâches, un peu comme une fiche de poste transformée en liste de courses (l’IA en raye certaines, en accélère d’autres, en ajoute parfois). En agrégeant le tout à l’échelle des États-Unis, le modèle développé avec les économistes Anton Korinek et Chad Jones débouche sur trois trajectoires possibles.
Dans le scénario modeste, l’IA fait à peu près aussi bien qu’Internet en son temps : 1,6 % de PIB supplémentaire d’ici 2030, un chômage dans les normes, des salaires qui progressent doucement. Le scénario intermédiaire confie à la machine la moitié des tâches intellectuelles du pays : la croissance annuelle double et le chômage grimpe vers 5 %. Près de quatre cols blancs sur dix changent alors de métier, pendant que leurs salaires font du surplace.
Reste le scénario extrême, celui où des IA capables de s’améliorer elles-mêmes surclassent l’humain sur la grande majorité des tâches intellectuelles. Le PIB américain bondirait de 32 % pour atteindre 44 400 milliards de dollars, porté par une croissance de 15 % par an (l’économie doublerait tous les quatre ans et demi, du jamais-vu). La facture sociale suit la même pente : près d’un travailleur intellectuel sur cinq au chômage et des salaires cognitifs inférieurs de 11,5 % à leur trajectoire sans IA. La part du travail dans la richesse nationale, elle, fondrait de 60 à 45 % (le capital, comme souvent, s’en sort très bien).
Et les plombiers, dans tout ça ? Le modèle prévoit l’inverse pour les métiers manuels : électriciens, soudeurs et artisans voient la demande et les salaires progresser dans les scénarios les plus agressifs, l’IA ne posant toujours pas de tuyaux (pas encore, en tout cas). Un sondage mené en parallèle auprès de plus de 10 000 Américains montre que le répondant type mise sur le scénario intermédiaire ; un sur dix seulement croit à la version extrême.
Le PDG d’Anthropic, recadré par son propre modèle
Ce panorama prend une saveur particulière quand on se souvient des sorties de Dario Amodei. En mai 2025, le patron d’Anthropic prédisait dans Axios la disparition possible de la moitié des emplois de bureau débutants et un chômage de 10 à 20 % d’ici cinq ans. De quoi provoquer, à l’époque, quelques sueurs froides dans les services RH. Ces chiffres correspondent très exactement au scénario extrême du modèle maison, celui auquel un sondé sur dix accorde du crédit et que le rapport prend soin de qualifier d’exercice illustratif.
Anthropic assume et prévient noir sur blanc que « les scénarios ne sont pas des prédictions ». L’entreprise a fait relire sa copie par 18 économistes, dont Daron Acemoglu et David Autor (deux références de l’économie du travail, pas franchement réputées pour leur enthousiasme envers l’automatisation), en précisant qu’aucun n’endosse les conclusions. L’étude appelle d’ailleurs les pouvoirs publics à mieux partager les gains plutôt qu’à freiner la technologie (on n’attendait pas vraiment l’inverse).
Lire aussi : Bill Gates veut réserver des métiers aux humains et taxer les machines
Le constat lui-même n’a rien d’inédit : le FMI estimait dès janvier 2024 que 60 % des emplois des économies avancées étaient exposés à l’IA, et Goldman Sachs comptait 300 millions de postes concernés. La nouveauté tient au signataire, aucun vendeur d’automatisation n’ayant encore publié lui-même la météo de l’emploi de ses clients. Le modèle ne couvre par ailleurs que les États-Unis, et rien n’oblige un marché du travail européen, plus encadré et souvent plus lent sur l’adoption, à suivre la même pente.

articles.title: Conversation to Completion redefines contact center AI - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
How conversation to completion moves contact centers past containment
For years, contact centers measured success by containment: how many calls never reached a human agent. That metric increasingly misses the point, since a call can be contained and still leave the customer without an actual answer. The shift underway is toward conversation to completion, tracking whether an interaction actually resolved what the customer called about, not just whether it avoided a live agent.
Ram Rajagopalan (pictured, right), head of product, AI for Zoom CX at Zoom Communications Inc., has spent the past year building that idea into the company’s virtual agent platform. The industry spent much of the last two years fixated on containment rates alone, a metric that undersells what AI agents should actually be measured on, Rajagopalan said.
“Many customers, even about a year, 18 months ago, focused on purely measuring containment,” he said. “Where I see conversations these days going is not just looking at containment, but end-to-end resolution. This is what we are calling within Zoom conversation to completion, where we are not just answering the basic inquiries, deflecting the call from going to a human agent, but actually completing the task that the consumers are calling in for.”
Rajagopalan and Joe Rittenhouse (center, right), co-chief executive officer of Converged Technology Professionals Inc., a Zoom implementation partner, spoke with theCUBE Research’s Bob Laliberte and ZK Research’s Zeus Kerravala at “The AI ROI in Contact Center Summit,” during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises move AI pilots into measurable production value. (* Disclosure below.)
Why ‘conversation to completion’ means picking the right first use case
Rittenhouse picks up that same thread from the deployment side. Getting to a real resolution starts with choosing the right first use case rather than the most ambitious one, he said.
“Usually where we try to start is, where’s the low-hanging fruit?” Rittenhouse said. “Just a simple question of what do you do after hours? We’re usually staffed, we follow the sun from the East Coast to the West Coast, but then after hours we just have a general mailbox. And the answer is typically, I don’t know.”
About half of the clients Rittenhouse’s firm works with have a formal AI committee in place; the rest are often still deciding whether the strategy should be dictated top-down or coordinated across departments, he explained. That same governance question is one Zoom has been navigating internally, scaling its own AI Companion across customers running thousands of seats.
“These tools work. You just can’t boil the ocean,” Rittenhouse said. “We use the analogy of eat the pizza piece by piece. You don’t fold it in half and scarf it down. It’s one bite at a time. Start small, and it’ll grow.”
That same incremental logic applies to handoffs between virtual and human agents, where the full context of a call needs to move along with the engagement, Rajagopalan noted.
“You want to transfer the full context, the reason why they’re calling, the collected variables that you need to pass on to a human being so that human being can get on with the job and get it done without having to repeat themselves or look at 10 different places of record just to answer a simple question,” he said.

articles.title: Modified GeForce RTX 5090 with 96 GB Memory Shows Up on Alibaba for Nearly $4,000
articles.text:
Friday, September 11th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
Modified GeForce RTX 5090 with 96 GB Memory Shows Up on Alibaba for Nearly $4,000
A Chinese manufacturer is now selling a modified GeForce RTX 5090 with 96 GB of memory, three times the 32 GB on the retail card. Shenzhen Suqiao Intelligent Technology, an OEM/ODM with over a decade of experience building graphics cards, motherboards, and servers, listed the card on Alibaba for $3,888. That's roughly 35% less than a standard RTX 5090 currently costs in the US, and a fraction of what NVIDIA charges for its RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell. The latter uses the same GB202 die and now starts at a whopping $16,000. 
Suqiao likely built this with a custom PCB running clamshell memory, packing GDDR7 modules on both sides of the board to double capacity, the same approach NVIDIA itself uses on the Pro 6000. The GPU die may come from harvested RTX 5090 units, reballed onto the new board and running on leaked or modified firmware, a method Chinese workshops already used to push the RTX 4090 to 48 GB VRAM. The listing does raise some doubts, though, since it mentions GDDR6X memory at 14 Gbps, which doesn't line up with a genuine 96 GB Blackwell build.Other Alibaba sellers are apparently asking closer to $5,900 for similar cards, so Suqiao's price sits on the low end even within this gray market. If legitimate, it would give AI developers a much cheaper way to get large VRAM pools without paying workstation prices, though buyers would be taking on firmware instability and no official support in return.

articles.title: Iran could potentially reverse-engineer captured US underwater drone — several Iranian embassies mock US over capture, Navy claims lost Anduril vehicle was defective and unclassified
articles.text:
Iran could potentially reverse-engineer captured US underwater drone — several Iranian embassies mock US over capture, Navy claims lost Anduril vehicle was defective and unclassified
“Unboxing ceremony by our reverse engineers, tomorrow morning!” - Iranian embassy in India
Iran is likely to study and attempt to reverse-engineer a U.S. Navy underwater drone captured by Iranian forces near the Strait of Hormuz, potentially handing Tehran useful technology while delivering a setback for the Pentagon. According to a Reuters report published September 9, the 19-foot Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle malfunctioned while surveying regional waters before Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps recovered it.
Both the U.S. military and the drone’s manufacturer Anduril quickly moved to downplay the significance of the loss. Analysts cited by Reuters also said the captured drone was unlikely to provide Iran with a decisive military advantage. At the very least, however, the vehicle gives Tehran a propaganda victory and an opportunity to examine American undersea technology as the U.S.-Iran war enters its seventh month.
Tehran already appears to be having a field day with the situation, with Iranian embassies around the world mocking the U.S. for losing the drone. In an X post, Iran’s embassy in Ghana compared its recovery to pulling a plastic bottle from a fishing net, adding that it was “still blinking like an idiot.” Iran's embassy in Hyderabad was even more direct about what might happen next, posting: “Unboxing ceremony by our reverse engineers, tomorrow morning!”
A noticeable gap has emerged between how Anduril markets the Dive-LD and how the U.S. military is now describing the captured vehicle. Anduril promotes the Dive-LD as a highly reliable and adaptable large autonomous underwater vehicle capable of operating for up to 10 days in demanding environments, previously calling the platform the most reliable and flexible autonomous underwater vehicle on the market. The Navy, meanwhile, described the lost vehicle as an older, defective model that “neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment.”
Despite attempts to downplay the incident, Washington has historically taken similar incidents seriously. After Iran recovered an RQ-170 Sentinel stealth reconnaissance drone in 2011, then-President Barack Obama publicly requested its return. Tehran subsequently claimed that it had reverse-engineered the aircraft and unveiled domestic drones apparently influenced by its design. In 2022, the U.S. Navy dispatched a patrol ship and an MH-60S Seahawk helicopter after an Iranian naval vessel attempted to tow away an American Saildrone surface vehicle in the Gulf.
Iran's comical commentary is backed by a genuine ability to extract useful information from captured hardware. Bryan Clark, director of the Center for Defense Concepts and Technology at the Hudson Institute, told Reuters that Iranian engineers “could definitely reverse-engineer the mechanical systems.” However, he was more skeptical about Tehran’s ability to penetrate the software, which reportedly includes defenses intended to frustrate exploitation attempts.
Regardless of any reverse engineering limitations, analysts say Iran will continue to present the incident as evidence of Iranian control around the Strait of Hormuz and U.S. vulnerability there. “This is something that Iran has proven very adept at exploiting for its own benefit in terms of seeking to frame the narrative as one of U.S., in this case, ineptitude and their ability to sort of retain control over the Strait of Hormuz,” said Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

The United States and Iran have been at war since Washington launched Operation Epic Fury in late February, with the conflict repeatedly spilling into the technology industry and its supply chains. In April 2026, an Iranian strike halted production at Saudi Arabia’s Jubail petrochemical complex, disrupting supplies of a critical resin used in PCB laminates. Iranian cruise missiles also reportedly struck an Amazon data center in Bahrain in July.

articles.title: Epic Games regala Astral Ascent y Luftrausers por tiempo limitado
articles.text:
La tienda de Epic Games ofrece dos juegos gratis por tiempo limitado: Astral Ascent y Luftrausers. Ambos pueden reclamarse sin costo hasta el 17 de septiembre de 2026.
La selección reúne dos propuestas de acción con estilos distintos. Astral Ascent combina plataformas y progresión roguelite en dos dimensiones, mientras que Luftrausers propone combates aéreos de ritmo arcade.
PUBLICIDAD
Una vez añadidos a la biblioteca durante el período de la promoción, los títulos quedarán asociados a la cuenta de Epic Games.
Cómo acceder a los juegos gratis
Para reclamar Astral Ascent, los usuarios deben ingresar a su página oficial en Epic Games Store y seleccionar la opción para obtenerlo sin costo durante la vigencia de la oferta.
PUBLICIDAD
El mismo procedimiento se aplica a Luftrausers: hay que acceder a la ficha del juego en la tienda y completar la incorporación a la biblioteca antes de que finalice la promoción.
La oferta estará disponible hasta el 17 de septiembre. Después de ese horario, Epic Games Store actualizará las condiciones de acceso de ambos títulos.

Astral Ascent es un roguelite de plataformas en 2D ambientado en un mundo de fantasía moderna. El jugador puede elegir entre cuatro protagonistas para escapar del Jardín, una prisión astral vigilada por los Zodiacos, un grupo de 12 jefes.

El juego permite desbloquear decenas de hechizos y probar distintas configuraciones para enfrentar los desafíos de cada partida. También incluye opciones para un jugador y cooperativo local.
Luftrausers es un juego de acción aérea en el que los jugadores controlan aviones de combate personalizados para enfrentarse a cazas enemigos, acorazados, submarinos y pilotos rivales.

La propuesta permite combinar armas, cuerpos y sistemas de propulsión para modificar el comportamiento de la aeronave. El título cuenta con más de 125 combinaciones posibles y más de 100 misiones para desbloquear nuevas configuraciones.

articles.title: Home cinéma : profitez de -80 € avec ce code promo sur les meubles Nothing Projector
articles.text:
Avec sa gamme de meubles motorisés Shore, commercialisée sous le nom ROLATV et conçue pour dissimuler les vidéoprojecteurs UST, NothingProjector veut réconcilier vidéoprojecteur et décoration intérieure. Revendeur agréé de marques comme Formovie, AWOL Vision, Valerion, JMGO ou XGIMI, l'entreprise propose ici une approche séduisante pour profiter d'un home cinéma sans transformer son salon en salle de projection.
Le vidéoprojecteur est devenu une alternative particulièrement séduisante au téléviseur pour celles et ceux qui ne jurent que par une (très) grande image. Mais une fois le film terminé, le problème se pose, que faire de cet appareil imposant, de ses câbles, de son installation ? C’est précisément à cette problématique que répond Nothing Projector avec sa gamme de mobilier Shore, pensée pour intégrer la vidéoprojection au décor plutôt que de la laisser s’imposer dans la pièce.
Et si le vidéoprojecteur disparaissait complètement une fois éteint ?
C’est toute la philosophie du Meuble Intelligent Shore à Ascenseur Motorisé Escamotable. Destiné aux vidéoprojecteurs longue focale, ce meuble intelligent dissimule entièrement l’appareil (et son câblage) lorsque celui-ci n’est pas utilisé. À première vue, impossible d’y voir un meuble dédié au home-cinéma, mais plutôt un élégant buffet contemporain.
Comme son nom l’indique, son fonctionnement repose sur un mécanisme de levage motorisé. Le vidéoprojecteur peut ainsi sortir du meuble pour prendre sa position de projection, puis retourner se dissimuler une fois la séance terminée. Le système peut être piloté via une application et synchronisé avec le projecteur pour simplifier encore davantage l’utilisation. Un bouton physique reste également présent sur le côté pour conserver une commande directe « à l’ancienne ».
Nothing Projector ne s’est pas contenté de cacher le projecteur. Le meuble intègre également un espace de rangement discret pour les télécommandes, consoles, casques ou autres accessoires du salon. Des roulettes permettent par ailleurs de déplacer plus facilement l’ensemble.
La structure motorisée en acier Q235 assure la stabilité du mécanisme, tandis que les panneaux perforés favorisent à la fois la circulation de l’air et le passage du son. Les câbles peuvent être organisés à l’intérieur du meuble afin d’éviter le traditionnel enchevêtrement derrière l’installation. Et surtout, le meuble arrive déjà assemblé. Une fois le colis réceptionné, il suffit de le déballer, de le brancher et de l’intégrer à son installation.
Une approche qui fonctionne aussi avec les vidéoprojecteurs UST
Lorsque le projecteur est éteint, celui-ci est dissimulé dans le meuble. Au démarrage, un mécanisme motorisé le fait basculer automatiquement en position de fonctionnement. Le système peut se synchroniser avec le projecteur ou sa télécommande, avec une compatibilité annoncée avec plusieurs grandes marques de vidéoprojecteurs UST.
Son format permet surtout de réduire la profondeur du meuble. Là encore, l’objectif est clair, celui de proposer un mobilier home cinéma de gain de place, capable de s’intégrer dans un intérieur moderne plutôt que de monopoliser l’espace. Le meuble bénéficie d’une finition mate et est lui aussi livré préassemblé.
Le meuble TV qui cache aussi l’écran
Enfin, le Meuble TV Laser Intelligent Mat Shore à Plateau Rabattable pour Vidéoprojecteur UST adopte une conception en forme de tiroir motorisé, et va faire automatiquement avancer le vidéoprojecteur UST jusqu’à sa position optimale lorsqu’il est allumé, avant de le ranger complètement dans le meuble lorsqu'il est éteint.
Mais cette fois, le meuble peut aussi dissimuler un écran motorisé de 100 ou 120”. L’ensemble peut donc littéralement transformer un espace de vie en salle de cinéma, puis revenir à l’apparence d’un meuble bas (sans vidéoprojecteur ni écran apparent donc) une fois la séance terminée.
80 € de remise avec le code Clubic
Pour accompagner cette approche plus discrète du home cinéma, Nothing Projector propose aux lecteurs de Clubic une remise exclusive de 80 € sur les trois meubles présentés ici.
Pour cela, il suffit d’utiliser le code CLU80 lors de la commande.
Une manière de rendre un peu plus accessible une idée qui a tendance à tous nous séduire, celle de profiter d’une immense image lorsque l’on en a envie, tout en permettant au vidéoprojecteur de se faire totalement oublier le reste du temps.

articles.title: El origen del archicelebrado menú del día en España: un "menú turístico" impulsado por el franquismo en 1964
articles.text:
Más allá de sectores, mercados o países, la mayoría de negocios del mundo tienen algo en común: sueñan con las codiciadas "tres B". Productos "buenos, bonitos y baratos", la santa trinidad del mundo empresarial. En España la hostelería se ha acercado con el menú del día, un formato que lleva 60 años haciéndonos la vida más fácil (y asequible) a quienes comemos fuera de casa. A cambio de un precio razonable, o al menos inferior al que pagaríamos si tirásemos la carta, los restaurantes ofrecen combos de varios platos, bebida y café o postre.
¿Cómo ha llegado a popularizarse tanto esa fórmula? ¿Qué ha pasado para que se haya convertido casi en una institución? La respuesta está en la dictadura.
¿Cuándo surgió el menú? Los cronistas que han indagado en su historia suelen situar la génesis del menú español en los años 60, pero como recuerdan nuestros compañeros de Directo al Paladar (DAP) para ser justos deberíamos remontarnos algo (bastante) más atrás. En 1611 Francisco Martínez Montiño ya incluía minutas en su tratado Arte de Cocina y se sabe que en el XIX Enrique de Brunswick, un aristócrata bávaro, acompañaba sus banquetes de listas completas en las que se especificaba el orden de los diferentes platos que se servirían.
¿Fue él el creador del 'menú'? No lo parece, aunque en realidad todo depende de qué entendamos por 'menú' y hasta qué punto estemos dispuestos a flexibilizar el concepto. Hay quien recuerda que, si miramos más allá de Europa, el rey asirio Ashurnasirpal II ya elaboró hace 3.000 años una tablilla de piedra con los manjares de un opíparo festín. Otro precedente lo encontramos en la China de la dinastía Song, en el siglo XII. Para hacerles la vida más fácil a los viajeros extranjeros, se les ofrecían cartas para que escogieran sus platos.
The menú del día was invented by the …. Err …. Pre Democratic elements. 
In 1964, the menú turístico, requiring many restaurants to offer a standardized, affordable set meal to cater to Spain’s rapidly expanding tourism industry
In 1970, regulations developed this into what… https://t.co/YbdqZAYe3r
¿Cuándo surgió en España? Aquí Benito Pérez Galdós ya nos hablaba a comienzos del XX de fondas que vendían platos a precios fijos y adaptados a los bolsillos más humildes, pero lo cierto es que el menú del día tal y como lo conocemos hoy tiene unos orígenes mucho más precisos… y recientes.
Habitualmente se sitúan en 1964, durante la etapa del desarrollismo franquista, cuando el Gobierno empezó a exigir a los locales de comidas que ofrecieran un "menú turístico" que debía cumplir ciertos criterios, básicamente relacionados con su composición y tarifas, que se establecían en función de su categoría.
¿Y cuál fue el motivo? Pongámonos en contexto: a comienzos de los 60 la dictadura franquista abandonaba su etapa autárquica, la economía española empieza a abrirse a los mercados internacionales y el país mira el flujo de visitantes extranjeros con un interés creciente por su potencial económico.
Con ese telón de fondo, el Ministerio de Información y Turismo, capitaneado por Manuel Fraga, decidió mover ficha e imponer una serie de normas para reforzar el atractivo de la hostelería patria. El objetivo: asegurase de que los turistas que pisasen un bar español se encontrarían con productos típicos y un menú con varios platos, pan y bebida. Nada que no se explorase en otros países vecinos.
¿Cuánto costaba? La idea no era mala, pero Pau Arenós recuerda en El Periódico que al "menú turístico" le costó echar a andar. En mayo de 1965, menos de un año después de la entrada en vigor de la medida, el Gobierno decidió meter mano en los precios, aclarando exactamente la tarifa máxima que podía cobrar cada establecimiento en función de su categoría: los más lujosos podían pedir 250 pesetas, cinco veces más del tope establecido para las tascas.
¿Por qué lo hicieron? Quizás porque a muchos hosteleros no acababa de convencerles la propuesta, lo que les llevaba a buscar la forma de disuadir a los visitantes y animarlos a pedir productos de la carta. No fue la única picaresca del sector, que no tardó en encontrar la forma de sortear los precios máximos: cobrar suplementos que se aplicaban por "composición, presentación o coste".
Un periodista estadounidense que viajó por España a mediados de los años 60 relataba tiempo después, en una crónica, que de los 29 platos que se encontró en la carta de un restaurante 26 incluían un extra si se pedían en el "menú turístico".
¿Se quedó ahí la cosa? No. La historia administrativa del menú siguió complicándose durante los años siguientes. Tras la salida de Manuel Fraga del Ministerio de Turismo, en 1969, su sucesor decidió cambiar el nombre de aquel combo hostelero: de "menú turístico" pasó a "del día". A finales de los años 70 su marco regulatorio volvió a alterarse de nuevo: se reconvirtió en "menú de la casa" y se relajaron ciertas normas, como la tabla de precios o la exigencia de que incluso los restaurantes de mayor categoría tuvieran que ofrecerlo.
¿Fue su último capítulo? Para nada. Como recuerda Hostelería de Madrid, a comienzos de los años 80 lo de "menú de la casa" ya era una fórmula extendida que empezaba a asociarse con restaurantes de categoría media o humildes.
El cambio de filosofía había cuajado: lo que empezó como una estrategia turística, una forma de cuidar a los visitantes extranjeros y ofrecerles vinos y platos tradicionales, se convirtió en una fórmula popular entre los trabajadores españoles. Por curioso que resulte, su marco legal experimentó un nuevo cambió en 2010 que eliminó su obligatoriedad y los dejó en manos de las comunidades.
¿Y el futuro? La gran incógnita. Aunque el menú del día sigue siendo una institución en España y hay grandes cadenas de restaurantes que lo han adoptado, la fórmula afronta retos que amenazan con socavar su futuro.
El sector lleva tiempo advirtiendo lo complicado que le resulta garantizar su rentabilidad, lo que ha llevado a que se encarezca poco a poco. A finales de 2025 Hostelería de España estimaba que, de media, el menú del día costaba ya 14,2 €, un 1,5% más que el año anterior y sensiblemente por encima de los 13,2 de 2022. Es un dato clave porque uno de sus grandes atractivos es precisamente su precio.
¿Hay más amenazas? Sí. Por si eso no fuera suficiente, ahora los hosteleros afrontan nuevos desafíos, incluida la competencia creciente de los mercaurantes, locales en los que cadenas de distribución alimentaria como Mercadona permiten comprar y comer platos preparados. Los propios cambios de consumo llevan a muchos clientes a priorizar la rapidez sobre la calidad a la hora de escoger un lugar en el que comer. De ahí que incluso que el concepto de "menú de tres platos" esté en crisis en una época que tiende a la snackficación.

articles.title: Windows 11 está finalmente deixando o Bluetooth melhor • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Windows 11 está finalmente deixando o Bluetooth melhor
Microsoft liberou novas versões de teste do Windows 11 que trazem vários aprimoramentos para conexões Bluetooth.
Não é incomum usuários terem problemas com o Bluetooth do Windows 11 (ou do Windows 10). Eu, por exemplo, vez ou outra preciso fazer um novo pareamento dos meus fones de ouvido para que eles sejam reconhecidos pelo notebook. A boa notícia é que a Microsoft deu um passo importante para resolver as falhas de conectividade Bluetooth do sistema operacional.
Falo das compilações 26100.9539 e 26200.9539 para Windows 11, liberadas recentemente para usuários que participam do programa de testes Windows Insider. Essas atualizações introduzem muitos aprimoramentos relevantes, com as otimizações de Bluetooth estando entre elas.
São várias novidades sobre o assunto. Isso é interessante porque deixa claro que a Microsoft não focou apenas em um ou dois aspectos. Parece haver um esforço para melhorar a experiência de conectividade Bluetooth como um todo.
Pois bem, entre os avanços está um ajuste que melhora a compatibilidade do Windows 11 com microfones que se conectam ao computador via Bluetooth tradicional, isto é, que não são baseados em Bluetooth Low Energy ou Bluetooth LE Audio.
Falando em áudio, a Microsoft também afirma estar aprimorando a compatibilidade e a estabilidade geral com dispositivos que transmitem som (talvez isso resolva o problema que eu tenho com meus fones).
Nesse sentido, a companhia fala ainda em mais confiabilidade e desempenho com dispositivos que usam Bluetooth LE Audio, bem como no compartilhamento de som via modo Shared Audio.
Os avanços destacados pela Microsoft envolvem até a usabilidade. Por exemplo, nas chamadas de voz, o Windows passa a exibir o indicador de volume quando você o ajusta pelo próprio dispositivo. Além disso, a área Bluetooth e Dispositivos, em Configurações, ficará mais estável quando você estiver gerenciando acessórios.
Outros aprimoramentos incluem a correção de uma inconsistência que faz o Windows 11 mostrar que o sinal de Bluetooth está ativado quando, na verdade, está desligado, e de um bug que pode fazer o computador travar durante uma transmissão de áudio via Bluetooth.
Ainda não há data oficial para isso. Mas, como as compilações 26100.9539 e 26200.9539 são do tipo Release Preview, as novidades devem ser lançadas oficialmente em um futuro próximo, talvez ainda em 2026.

articles.title: 'We are not enabling the Chinese to come here': Ford CEO hits back at government ‘mistruths’ as it readies affordable EV pick-up to stand in for struggling F–150
articles.text:
Ford CEO hits back at government ‘mistruths’ about China — as its $28K electric truck prepares to take on Slate and Chinese rivals
Farley under fire as Fathom pick-up launch edges closer
- Ford CEO hits back at US government's China claims
- Ford’s new Fathom electric pick-up uses technology licensed from CATL
- The affordable Fathom is part of Ford’s new Universal EV platform
Ford has hit back at criticisms from US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy that the automaker is becoming overly reliant on Chinese car companies, with Chief Executive Jim Farley telling The Wall Street Journal that these are “basic misunderstandings, mistruths, whatever words you want to use.”
The global automaker, which is winding up production of its current F-150 Lightning, is preparing a smaller, more affordable electric pick-up for the masses.
Dubbed Fathom, it will start at $28,350 (around £20,970 / AU$39,540) before destination fees and is the result of work by Ford’s “skunkworks” team, which was assembled to find ways to innovate in the EV space while keeping costs down and competing with increasingly capable Chinese electric vehicles.
However, the Transportation Secretary accused Ford of “actively intertwining its future with Chinese state-backed enterprises,” including a plant that licenses technology from Chinese battery giant CATL, according to the WSJ.
Ford announced in 2023 that it would begin manufacturing its own lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries at the newly formed BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall.
The company subsequently confirmed that the plant would use technology and expertise licensed from China-based CATL, but Ford would own and operate the facility and assemble the batteries in the US.
Production of the LFP battery cells destined for Ford’s affordable electric pick-up is now ramping up, with Ford saying it is on track to ship batteries in 2026. Farley is adamant that the arrangement does not amount to handing control of Ford’s future to China.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
“We’re not enabling the Chinese to come here,” Farley told the WSJ. “Actually, you could argue the opposite is the case.”
In a statement published by Ford HQ on its media site, the company said that it is the "most American automaker".
"We produce more vehicles in the US, employ more hourly manufacturing workers and export more vehicles from the US than any other automaker", it added.
Despite a retirement in its current form, the F-150 Lightning itself isn't being killed off entirely, either. Ford says production of the current version will end this year, with a next-generation F-150 Lightning EREV planned to offer more than 700 miles of combined range using a battery and gasoline-powered generator.
Analysis: All hopes rest on Fathom
Ford’s CEO has called the creation of its new Universal EV platform, which it hopes will underpin a whole host of new EVs, the company’s “Model T moment,” stating that the platform will help bring electric trucks and vehicles to customers at a more affordable price.
Full details of the Fathom are still to be revealed, but we do know that it will cost less than $30,000 before destination charges when it goes on sale, with a starting MSRP of $28,350 (about £20,970 / AU$39,540). It will use one of Ford’s new LFP battery packs and feature a NACS charging port.
It will also pack bidirectional charging, allowing owners to power tools and other accessories from the batteries, and every Fathom will have the hardware required for Ford’s next-generation BlueCruise hands-free highway driving system.
Four doors, five passengers, a generous rear bed and a front trunk for extra storage will all come as standard, while Ford is targeting a midsize footprint with more passenger space than a Toyota RAV4.
Ford hopes that its electric trucks will finally hit home with a mass-market audience, thanks to the technology on offer and extremely competitive pricing.
Although it will count the Jeff Bezos-backed Slate truck as a key competitor, that pick-up is priced from less than $25,000 (about £18,490 / AU$34,870) before destination charges.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Leon has been navigating a world where automotive and tech collide for almost 20 years, reporting on everything from in-car entertainment to robotised manufacturing plants. Currently, EVs are the focus of his attentions, but give it a few years and it will be electric vertical take-off and landing craft. Outside of work hours, he can be found tinkering with distinctly analogue motorcycles, because electric motors are no replacement for an old Honda inline four.

articles.title: AI's existential crisis explodes but AI companies plunge ahead anyway - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AI’s existential crisis explodes but AI companies plunge ahead anyway
The resignation this week of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon over concerns that artificial intelligence labs are “gambling with our lives” lit up the long-smoldering argument about whether AI is heading in a direction hazardous to human life.
Not only is he not alone at Anthropic — whose alignment science lead agreed with the possibility that AI has a more than 10% chance to “kill all humans” in the next decade — but OpenAI chimed in, as its chief scientist called for an AI research slowdown. And CEO Sam Altman reportedly told staff that the company is considering slowing down leading-edge AI work and wants other companies to do the same — if the government says that’s not an antitrust problem.
We’ll have to see if any of this existential worry actually changes anything, but I’ll believe it when I see it. Just this week, as almost every week, there was a flurry of new models, agents and apps galore — from Meta, OpenAI (twice), China’s DeepSeek and more. I understand why, and I’m still a bit skeptical of the AI doomers given the lack of specific reasons why AI can’t be controlled, but there’s definitely a disconnect here.
One thing that may slow things down regardless is the rising opposition to data centers. In a new feature story, Paul Gillin digs into exactly why AI requires so much compute — and why there isn’t a short-term fix. Tech giants have a lot of work ahead of them persuading communities not to shut down the next era of tech innovation.
By the way, don’t count out Europe in AI: Mistral AI this week raised almost $3.5 billion. And Paris-based startup Arlequin AI got $28 million to explore a fundamentally new kind of AI model.
Oracle looks like it’s finally benefiting from the AI boom, as its cloud infrastructure revenue more than doubled, and its stock rose 4% in late trading after falling more than that in regular trading, on an ugly day for the market. Adobe had a strong quarter too, but a light outlook sent shares down a bit after-hours Thursday.
As expected, autonomous software engineering firm Cognition AI raised another big round, a $32 billion Series E that values it at — wait for it — $48 billion.
Positron AI thinks it can solve the memory crunch in AI with an appliance that uses regular RAM instead of pricey and scarce high-bandwidth memory, raising an $875 million Series C round to prove it. Normally I might take such a claim with a grain of salt, but familiar old-school backers such as Silicon Graphics’ Jim Clark, Forest Baskett and Tom Jermoluk know what they’re doing, so this will be worth watching.
Oh, and Apple introduced some new iPhones, including a very expensive foldable. I find myself yawning, but I’m sure most of them will do fine.
