articles.title: Zoox is taking on Waymo in San Francisco with free rides and a very different robotaxi
articles.text:
In a nutshell: Zoox is in a difficult position as it tries to enter San Francisco: It must win riders' attention and trust while Waymo already has a much larger presence in the city. So the company is using free rides, local partnerships, and a purpose-built vehicle to establish itself there while it waits for permission to charge passengers in California.
San Francisco has become one of the industry's key test markets, but it has also exposed the risks of deploying autonomous vehicles in dense city traffic. Cruise pulled its vehicles from the road in 2023 after several incidents, including one in which a vehicle ran over and dragged a pedestrian. Waymo has faced its own setbacks, including the death of a bodega cat that was struck by one of its vehicles last year.
Zoox is entering that environment with a smaller fleet and a vehicle that does not resemble a conventional car. The Amazon-owned company is far smaller than Waymo, the dominant robotaxi operator in the city. Zoox has about 100 autonomous vehicles, compared with nearly 4,000 for Waymo. But its vehicles are also markedly different. Zoox built its robotaxis from the ground up without steering wheels, pedals or a driver's seat. Passengers sit facing each other inside a compact, turquoise cabin.
That design is the company's clearest distinction from Waymo, which uses modified conventional vehicles. Waymo cars have become common on San Francisco streets, while Zoox's boxy pods remain unusual enough to attract attention from pedestrians and tourists.
Zoox opened its Rider Lounge in downtown San Francisco in May. The storefront serves as a pickup point for demonstration rides and a place for visitors to look inside the vehicles. The company began offering free rides in the city in November and expanded the program in June, adding trips to eight restaurants and several landmarks, including the Ferry Building, the Painted Ladies, and the Castro.
The service is still not commercial. Zoox can operate free rides in San Francisco, but it needs approvals from the California Department of Motor Vehicles and the California Public Utilities Commission before it can collect fares. The company said it has applied for a DMV deployment permit. The utilities commission's public permit list does not show Zoox as authorized to provide paid service.
"We are trying to get it as quickly as we can, but it is a couple-month process," Carly Wyatt, Zoox's vice president of communications and marketing, told The New York Times. "We own the fact that we're taking these baby steps."
The company has begun charging riders in Las Vegas, its first paid market. Fares there are slightly higher than standard Uber and Lyft trips. In July, federal regulators gave Zoox a temporary exemption from certain vehicle-safety rules, including requirements involving windshield wipers and rearview mirrors. The exemption allows the company to deploy up to 5,000 vehicles over the next two years and collect fares.
Zoox is also working to make its vehicles familiar to people who may not have tried a robotaxi. It has sponsored the Stern Grove Festival, North Beach Festival, and Flower Piano in Golden Gate Park. The company has also partnered with the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and local businesses, including restaurants featured as destinations in its ride program.
Wyatt described the effort as a "community-first approach." Zoox has treated restaurants, events, and tourist sites as ways to introduce people to the service rather than relying solely on app-based ride-hailing.
The approach reflects Zoox's position in a market where Waymo has a major head start. Waymo started as Google's self-driving car project in 2009 and began commercial driverless rides in 2018. It now operates in 15 cities and plans to expand into more than a dozen others. The company recently raised $16 billion.
Zoox says it completes about 10,000 rides a week in the US. Waymo completes more than 500,000 rides a week.
Despite Waymo's lead, autonomous driving remains an emerging business. Companies are not only competing for riders; they are also trying to persuade people that a car without a human driver is a normal way to travel. Jonah Berger, a marketing professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School, said many consumers remain unfamiliar with the category.
"While one brand may be larger in the category and more prominent in the category, many people don't know anything about the category," he said.

iPhone 15 (256 GB) tem maior queda desde o 7.7 com cupom de hoje
iPhone 15 (256 GB) tem chip A16 Bionic e câmera de 48 MP; celular da Apple atinge o menor preço desde o 7.7, com desconto de 46% no Pix com cupom válido somente hoje
O iPhone 15 de 256 GB está saindo por R$ 4.409 no Pix com cupom SUPERDESCONTOS no Mercado Livre. O celular da Apple com chip A16 Bionic e câmera principal de 48 MP alcança o menor preço desde o 7.7, com desconto de 46% sobre o original de R$ 8.099.
Importante: esta promoção é válida apenas nesta sexta-feira (11), enquanto o cupom durar.
O kit de câmeras do iPhone 15 inclui uma wide de 48 MP com OIS e uma ultrawide de 12 MP, que captam belas cenas ao ar livre, e uma frontal de 12 MP que tira ótimas selfies. Todas filmam em 4K a 60 fps.
Seu chip A16 Bionic de 4 nanômetros e os 6 GB de RAM podem não suportar recursos do Apple Intelligence, mas sustentam a execução de apps pesados em multitarefa e games exigentes. Os 256 GB de armazenamento disponibilizam espaço razoável para guardar fotos e vídeos.

O corpo de alumínio do iPhone 15 recebe o vidro Ceramic Shield sobre a tela, que a protege contra pancadas e quedas. Já a certificação IP68 confere proteção em cenários como poeira intensa e mergulhos acidentais.

A compatibilidade com MagSafe e carregamento rápido de 25 W via USB-C oferecem energia suficiente para um dia inteiro de uso, ideal para usuários com agendas corridas e pouco tempo para perder com tomadas.

articles.title: Linux Kernel 7.4 Gets HDMI Upgrade With FreeSync, VRR, and Auto Low-Latency
articles.text:
Friday, September 11th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
Linux Kernel 7.4 Gets HDMI Upgrade With FreeSync, VRR, and Auto Low-Latency
HDMI 2.1 has long been a goalpost for many players in the Linux world, including Valve and AMD, who were both previously working on an open-source implementation of HDMI 2.1 drivers for the Linux kernel, despite roadblocks from the HDMI forum. Now, that appears to be a reality, with the Linux kernel mailing list citing patches that will likely be merged into the upstream kernel driver stack in Linux kernel 7.4
According to the merge request, HDMI 2.1 FRL will be landing in Linux with support for AMD FreeSync, VRR, and Auto Low-Latency Mode, all of which should be very useful for both desktop gamers and for couch gamers on machines like the Valve Steam Machine or its many SteamOS-touting alternatives. Linux kernel 7.4 is slated to land in October 2026, although an exact release date has yet to be determined. Valve also previously declared the work for HDMI 2.1 to be complete for the Steam Machine, although it seemingly has yet to implement the new driver in SteamOS, since the Steam Machine product page still cites HDMI 2.0.

Harry from AMD: lore.kernel.org/amd-gfx/20260501140441.41068-1-harry.wentland@amd.com/
I don't get it.
The wiki article on HDMI didn't tell me much, but "open" is mentioned a few times. It just doesn't make any sense. What legal stuff? If it work in Windows why wouldn't they let anyone do the same for Linux?
NVIDIA's GPUs can run HDMI 2.1 in Linux because their main driver is closed source (binary blobs for both the kernel and user drivers) and the open-source drivers (only the kernel drivers) which have access to the hardware's GSP (which is proprietary and not open-source).
I'm not 100% on the details re: which exact features, but it seems like AMD wanted an open-source driver for Linux support, so that the kernel and its open-source driver could remain open-source, but HDMI 2.1 uses closed-source licenses for some features, so the licensing had to be worked out, I suppose. It's funny, because when AMD announced it'd be working on HDMI support, it sort of seemed like it would be able to throw its weight around to get the HDMI Forum to come around, but it looks like that took more bullying than anticipated.

articles.title: GameStop is reopening recently closed stores despite massive retail cuts — select locations return nationwide starting September 11
articles.text:
GameStop is reopening recently closed stores despite massive retail cuts — select locations return nationwide starting September 11
GameStop hits rewind.
GameStop is bringing some of its recently closed stores back to life. The company announced on social media that “select closed stores” are reopening nationwide starting September 11, although it has not revealed exactly how many locations will return. When asked about the number of stores involved, a GameStop spokesperson reportedly told IGN that the count was “at least one” as of September 11, suggesting that we can expect more details to follow.
The move comes after GameStop reportedly had one of its biggest rounds of store closures listed for January 2026. According to a blog tracking the closures, around 470 locations across the U.S. were listed as either confirmed to close or already closed, as the retailer continued efforts to cut costs and improve profitability. GameStop had already closed hundreds of stores during the previous fiscal year, making the latest shutdowns part of a much larger reduction in its physical retail footprint.
GameStop's decision to reopen select physical stores is notably interesting given the wider shift away from physical game media. Digital downloads have replaced physical discs, while console manufacturers are increasingly offering hardware without disc drives. Recently, Sony took the shift even further after sharing its plans to stop producing new physical PlayStation game discs by January 2028. While that has resulted in a considerable backlash from the gaming community as a whole, Sony did clarify that existing titles can continue to be reordered and disc production will not simply disappear overnight.
It is worth mentioning that GameStop's business has moved beyond physical games. CEO Ryan Cohen said in July that software accounted for less than 12% of the company's business, although GameStop's fiscal 2025 filings put software, including physical games and digital download codes, at 20.1% of sales. Collectibles have become increasingly important, accounting for 29.2% of fiscal 2025 revenue and growing 47.7% year over year. This could explain why GameStop is potentially comfortable reopening selected stores despite the decline of physical games. That being said, it is safe to consider the announcement as a limited reopening rather than a complete reversal of GameStop's broader strategy.

articles.title: This tiny CHUWI workstation can run 300 billion parameter AI models locally
articles.text:
Chuwi UniBox AI495 Pro looks a bit like the old Mac Pro and, with 192GB RAM, matches Apple's new workstation for memory
192GB mini PCs are flooding the market — CHUWI follows Acemagic, GMKtek, and Framework
- CHUWI UniBox AI495 Pro carries up to 192GB of unified memory
- The Ryzen AI MAX+ PRO 495 reaches 5.2 GHz across 16 cores
- CHUWI's new mini workstation can run 300 billion parameter models locally
CHUWI has unveiled the UniBox AI495 Pro at IFA Berlin 2026, combining AMD's new Ryzen AI MAX+ PRO 495 chip with unusually high memory capacity.
The compact machine can carry up to 192GB of LPDDR5x memory, matching the maximum memory offered by Apple's latest workstation.
Its X Frame design also gives the small desktop a shape that may remind users of Apple's older cylindrical Mac Pro design.
A 2.9-litre desktop built for local AI
The UniBox AI495 Pro comes with AMD's Ryzen AI MAX+ PRO 495, with 16 cores, 32 threads, and boost speeds reaching 5.2 GHz.
The chip uses Zen 5 architecture and works with Radeon 8065S graphics containing 40 cores based on AMD's RDNA 3.5 architecture.
The graphics processor can run at up to 3,000 MHz, while the unified memory uses a 256-bit interface with 273 GB/s bandwidth.
Up to 160GB of that memory can be assigned to graphics processing, giving the integrated GPU far more memory than typical desktop graphics solutions.

CHUWI says the system can run large language models locally with as many as 300 billion parameters using 4-bit quantization.
Its complete AI platform can deliver up to 131 TOPS, while the XDNA 2 neural processor contributes as much as 55 TOPS.
This compact workstation measures 209.6 × 209.6 × 67 mm, giving it a stated volume of roughly 2.9 litres despite its hardware capacity.
Storage reaches 2TB through three M.2 2280 PCIe ×4 slots, while networking includes Wi Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4, and two 10Gbps Ethernet ports.
Two USB4 connections can reach 40Gbps, while an OCuLink port adds another option for connecting compatible external hardware to the compact system.
A 240W power adapter supplies the machine, which ships with Windows 11 Pro rather than a specialist operating system for AI work.
CHUWI has not set the price for the 192GB model
CHUWI has not yet disclosed the UniBox AI495 Pro's price, but Acemagic, GMKtek, and Framework have announced mini PCs using the same processor and 192GB RAM.
Those systems are expected to cost more than $2,000, which gives some indication of where CHUWI's machine could sit when it reaches the market.
CHUWI is also preparing the UniBox AI395, which uses AMD's Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 processor with 16 cores and 32 threads.
That model reaches 5.1 GHz and pairs the processor with Radeon 8060S graphics containing 40 RDNA 3.5 graphics cores.
Its graphics frequency reaches 2,900 MHz, while memory capacity tops out at 128GB with bandwidth reaching 256 GB/s across its 256-bit interface.
The AI395 can assign up to 96GB for graphics use and supports local models reaching 235 billion parameters with low-bit model formats.
It also provides up to 126 TOPS across the platform, including as much as 50 TOPS from its neural processing unit.
Both UniBox models share the same compact chassis size, 2TB storage support, 240W power supply, Windows 11 Pro, and dual 10Gbps Ethernet.

articles.title: Blue Origin: New-Glenn-Explosion war stärker als Tschernobyl
articles.text:
New Glenn explodiert: Sprengkraft übertraf erste Tschernobyl-Explosion
Am 29. Mai 2026 war es bei einem Test der Blue-Origin-Rakete New Glenn auf dem Weltraumbahnhof Cape Canaveral in Florida zu einer großen Explosion gekommen. Zum Glück wurde dabei kein Mensch verletzt. Es kam aber zu schweren Schäden an der Startrampe.
Infraschallwellen bis Texas zu vernehmen
Der Knall der durch die Explosion ausgelösten Schockwelle soll laut lokalen Medienberichten bis zu 217 Kilometer weit zu hören gewesen sein. Das sei aber nur die Spitze des Eisbergs, was den dabei produzierten Sound angeht, wie Live Science schreibt.
Einer Studie von Wissenschaftler:innen der militärischen US-Forschungs- und Entwicklungseinrichtung Sandia zufolge haben sich die Infraschallwellen knapp 1.700 Kilometer weit ausgebreitet. Mindestens 36 der über die USA verteilten Sensoren haben entsprechende Töne wahrgenommen, darunter eine im Norden des US-Bundesstaats Texas. Infraschall ist für das menschliche Ohr nicht wahrnehmbar.
Explosion stärker als jene in Tschernobyl
Aufgrund der gemessenen Frequenzen und der Ausbreitung der Schallwellen gehen die Forscher:innen davon aus, dass die Explosion eine Sprengkraft von 0,131 Kilotonnen hatte. Das soll die Sprengkraft der ersten Explosion am Kernreaktor von Tschernobyl im Jahr 1986 sogar noch übertroffen haben.
Darüber hinaus hat das Sandia-Forschungsteam herausgefunden, das bei der ersten Explosion nur zwischen drei und sechs Prozent des vorhandenen Raketentreibstoffs verbraucht wurden. Der Rest dürfte im Feuerball und der Rauchsäule nach und nach verbrannt sein.
Infraschall als Analysetool bei Explosionen
Die Forscher:innen zeigten sich im Rahmen ihrer Studie davon überzeugt, dass Infraschall ein bisher wenig genutztes, aber potenziell vielversprechendes Tool bei der Analyse großer Explosionen wie jener von Raketen sein könne. Die Analyse von Infraschallwellen hatte das Team zuvor schon bei der Verfolgung von Meteoren und Raumfahrzeugen beim Eintritt in die Erdatmosphäre eingesetzt.
Beobachter:innen gehen übrigens davon aus, dass die New-Glenn-Explosion eine der größten Explosionen darstellt, die man bisher im Vorfeld eines Raketenstarts registriert hat. Laut Ars Technica könnte sich allein die Reparatur der dabei zerstörten Startrampe mindestens ein Jahr hinziehen.
Blue Origin: Explosion gefährdet Mondpläne
Das betrifft auch die Nasa-Pläne zur Errichtung einer Mondbasis, die dadurch ins Wanken geraten könnten. Um die entsprechenden Komponenten zum Erdtrabanten zu transportieren, ist die US-Raumfahrtbehörde auf New Glenn angewiesen.

articles.title: Esta herramienta te ayuda a desarrollar apps de Windows en 30 minutos (y es gratis)
articles.text:
Microsoft ha publicado una guía que cambia las reglas del juego para quienes quieren programar aplicaciones nativas de Windows 11. Como parte de su estrategia para mejorar el sistema operativo, la compañía lanzó un documento que explica cómo desarrollar y publicar una app WinUI 3 usando herramientas gratuitas y ayuda de la IA. Según la compañía, todo el proceso puede completarse en menos de una hora y sin invertir un céntimo.
De acuerdo con la web, la propuesta forma parte de un esfuerzo de Microsoft por acercar el desarrollo agéntico a los programadores de cualquier nivel. El flujo de trabajo se apoya en GitHub Copilot y el CLI para aplicaciones de Windows y va desde una simple carpeta vacía hasta llegar a un instalador MSIX listo para desplegarse en la Microsoft Store.
Si bien la idea de facilitar el desarrollo ha estado en la mira de Microsoft casi desde que intentó unificar Windows con Xbox y Windows Phone, ahora es distinto. La llegada de asistentes de programación como Claude Code, Codex o el propio GitHub Copilot ha provocado que personas con pocos o nulos conocimientos sobre desarrollo se aventuren a crear nuevas aplicaciones por medio de "vibe coding".
En el caso de Windows 11, si quieres desarrollar aplicaciones nativas, solo necesitas instalar un conjunto de herramientas gratuitas. La lista incluye Visual Studio Code, el SDK de .NET 10 o superior, el CLI de desarrollo de aplicaciones de Windows (conocido como winapp), las plantillas de WinUI para dotnet new, el CLI de GitHub y el plugin del agente WinUI para GitHub Copilot.
El gigante tecnológico también recomienda conectar el agente de IA a su servidor Learn MCP. Este le permitirá consultar la documentación más reciente de la API de WinUI 3 en tiempo real, en caso de que hubiera algún cambio.
Cómo desarrollar apps nativas de Windows 11 usando IA
Una vez que las instalas, el primer paso es crear una nueva app WinUI desde la línea de comandos a través de dotnet new winui-navview. Esto genera una app básica con una vista de navegación que incluye las páginas de Inicio, Acerca de y Configuración. Después solo tienes que ejecutar dotnet run para comprobar que todo funciona antes de abrir el proyecto en VS Code.
Si te has preguntado a qué hora empieza la IA a hacer su magia, este es el paso. Primero debes abrir GitHub Copilot Chat, cambiarlo al modo Agente y seleccionar el agente winui-dev. Esto evitará que escribas una sola línea de código, ya que solo tienes que describir las funciones que deseas añadir usando lenguaje natural.
Después de eso, el agente se encargará de generar el código necesario, crear los archivos que hagan falta y actualizar la navegación de la app. No está de más mencionar que deberás revisar los cambios y volver a ejecutar la aplicación para confirmar que todo funciona como se espera. La IA ha avanzado mucho en el desarrollo, pero el código no siempre se comporta como esperas y pueden surgir algunos errores.
Con la función ya integrada, es momento de publicar la aplicación en una carpeta y empaquetarla como un instalador MSIX. En este paso, el agente puede generar e instalar un certificado de desarrollo local para pruebas que se instala en la raíz del ordenador. Si tu objetivo es ofrecerlo a través de la Microsoft Store, deberás usar un certificado de Partner Center y enviarla a través del comando winapp store publish desde la línea de comandos.
Aunque el proceso suena muy sencillo, la realidad es que desarrollar apps nativas requiere algo más que dictar las instrucciones a una IA. Saber programar será un aliado para tener idea de cuáles cosas puedes mejorar u optimizar a largo plazo. Esto último requiere una inversión considerable de tiempo, pero funciona a largo plazo.

articles.title: Anthropic CEO outlines plan to ‘pace the frontier’ | TechCrunch
articles.text:
We’ve been seeing increasingly dire warnings from AI researchers about the dangers of artificial intelligence, and even comments from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman that it may be time to “pace” AI development. But what would that actually look like?
In a new blog post, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei not only echoed the call to “pace the frontier,” but also outlined three broad strategies for doing so. And he said Anthropic is “unilaterally committing” to one of them.
The debate over AI safety and alignment intensified this week after researcher Jacob Coxon wrote that he’s resigning from Anthropic over concerns that the leading AI companies are “gambling with our lives” while the people building the technology “earnestly believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” a claim repeated by others at Anthropic.
Amodei’s post doesn’t didn’t explicitly mention Coxon’s resignation or his concerns, but the CEO wrote that two things convinced him it’s time to take a more cautious approach to AI development: the OpenAI-HuggingFace hack, and the fact that “AI has been advancing drastically faster” in recent months, particularly with its “growing ability to build the next generation of AI.”
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”
His proposed first step would involve “embedded evaluators” from third-party organizations like METR — evaluators who can verify that AI companies are actually following their pacing and safety commitments and can also ensure that safety incidents get reported. (OpenAI was recently criticized for not reporting an incident where its AI agents took over a German wiki form.)
Amodei compared these evaluators to regulators who have been embedded with bank employees, and he said that inviting them in is “something Anthropic is unilaterally committing to (and calls on governments to require other frontier companies to match).” That means giving evaluators company badges, desks, and laptops, and providing access “mostly comparable to what internal risk assessment teams have,” with exceptions when required by law or contracts.
Next, Amodei called for the leading AI companies “within democratic countries” to coordinate “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”
Such coordination might seem unlikely, both due to the apparent animosity between Altman and Amodei and also because their companies are reportedly worried that a coordinated pause could lead to antitrust scrutiny. Amodei alluded to that concern in his post, writing that “for antitrust reasons, it’s helpful for the US government to mediate or at least enable these discussions — they don’t need to participate, but do need to issue a narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversations.”
Amodei also acknowledged the spectre of Chinese AI dominance that’s often raised an argument against slowing development. But he said that if the US government and tech companies take steps like refusing to sell powerful chips or semiconductor manufacturing equipment to Chinese companies, as well as cracking down on model distillation, they could “slow China’s progress enough to widen America’s lead significantly over the next 3–5 years.”
Lastly, Amodei called for “global coordination,” where the United States and its allies “attempt to coordinate with authoritarian governments, to the extent this is possible.” Amodei said this would mean “cooperation with China,” and he admitted that there are “stark limits on what can be achieved,” but he still suggested there might be opportunities for agreement, even if it’s just “prohibiting certain narrow and obviously dangerous uses of AI, such as using AI for the production of biological weapons or allowing users to do so.”
With Amodei’s past willingness to acknowledge AI’s potential dangers, and with the company’s relative openness to certain forms of regulation, some AI boosters have already criticized him as a doomer whose comments have fed the current AI backlash. In response, Amodei said he’s tried to offer a “balanced” perspective” and argued that the backlash is “fundamentally a crisis of trust,” as people have become skeptical of tech companies, the tech industry, and the government.
Industry critics have also been skeptical about these apocalyptic AI warnings, suggesting that they’re a distraction from the harm that the technology is already causing.
Journalist Brian Merchant, for example, wrote that he has yet to see “a credible, step-by-step documentation of how exactly AI might move from self-recursively improving AI to killing every single human on the planet”; he also suggested that proposals similar to Amodei’s “would likely only wind up serving Anthropic and OpenAI; it’s what regulatory capture looks like in action.”
In his new post, Amodei wrote that he continues “to believe that AI can enormously improve the quality of human life.”
“My desire to achieve these benefits is undimmed,” he said. “But the benefits will only be achieved if we build the technology in the right way, and — so long as we use the time we gain well — it is worth taking unusually deliberate care to get it right.”

articles.title: Inside Architect Labs’ Two-Week Chip Design - EE Times
articles.text:
Architect Labs is building a platform that lets “anybody” design a custom chip, co-founder Ebrahim Hussain told EE Times in an exclusive interview. Supporting that claim, the startup company has built its prototype Redwood chip on an FPGA in record time.
“Redwood is the first demonstration that is saying this flow works,” Hussain said. “We can actually take something from idea to at least a proof-of-concept. I don’t think you can get any quicker than two weeks.”
That speed includes success on the first batch of test chips from a foundry, known as “A0” silicon. Architect Labs has been using TSMC’s wafer shuttle service that allows multiple chip designs to share a single mask set and production run.
“It’s getting very difficult to build complex A0 silicon on the first shot,” Hussain noted. “We want to help chip companies make it faster but [also] make their development higher quality. The end goal is that A0 goes into full production for our partners.”
Hussain, now 20, skipped high school to study engineering physics at the University of British Columbia before working briefly as a chip designer for Apple and Tesla and joining Stanford University in 2025 as a visiting researcher. He started Architect Labs in July 2025 with co-founder Aaditya Subedi, 19, who today leads a team of 25 people engaged in machine learning, hardware and software engineering, including chip veterans with 20 to 30 years of experience per person.
“I worked for Apple, I worked for Tesla,” Hussain said. “I was on the architecture team and saw how long these cycles really were. It felt like AI would have a big impact on the chip design cycle, but at the same time, it felt like the approach that many people were taking in terms of using AI was not really that potent, it didn’t really feel like it could change much.”
Architect Labs said its technology lets people provide inputs to an AI system that can take over the design and verification of a chip.
“It can test the firmware stack, how the software will interact with the chip,” Hussain said. “It’s very orthogonal to how the traditional verification flow is. Redwood is our first test that is showing this verification technique scales, and we can build complex chips with it.”
The company has built internal blocks and intellectual property for Redwood, which Architect Labs uses as its own training data to recursively improve models.
The company used Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6 as a primary frontier benchmark for the development of Architect Labs’ models.
“We’ll be releasing a future post about how we’ve gotten our models to actually beat whatever the frontier is providing, which is exciting,” Hussain said.
More creators
OpenAI’s Jalapeño and Amazon’s Trainium demonstrate that more people can create a high-performance chip that’s as good as any inference silicon, Steve Jang, founder of Kindred Ventures and an investor in Architect Labs, told EE Times.
“There’s a serious opportunity to open up this market,” Jang added. “Architect Labs has an opportunity to be analogous the way Claude Code is to software.” In Architect Labs’ case, the company is using AI to slash chip design time.
One notion is that even with a reduced design team, lead time, and capital needs, a project can get halfway to a “productionized” chip in a few weeks, Jang said.
“That’s really cool,” he noted. “Because then you’re making go/no-go decisions with capex and time and resources, having something that you’ve at least been able to test on an FPGA and then run something better than simulations. It would take you a year to two, three years to do that before.”
Customers
Hussain didn’t name customers but said Architect Labs is working with partners to design “some of the most complex ASICs in the world, full-reticle networking switches to bulky chiplets, many different things.” He added, “That’s really our sweet spot: the advanced design nodes. Over time, we’ll start to build more complex ASICs that are built for different purposes than just edge inference.”
The company will announce business engagements soon, including startups, Fortune 500 companies and big chip names, according to Hussain.
“The first instances you see are the model labs,” Hussain said. “They’re the first people with the capital and the demand where it makes sense to build their own chips. As AI grows from the data center to the physical world, we’ll have wearables, robotics, humanoids, self-driving vehicles, all applications that will demand custom chips. Those companies building in those spaces are the ones we want to partner with.”
Hussain has met companies that know workloads very deeply and are buying chips but are starting to think about having their own silicon roadmap.
“If I built a custom chip, what would be the performance gains, the power gains, all of these things?” Hussain asked.
Circumventing EDA
Architect Labs aims to accelerate chip design by circumventing much of the EDA process.
“The bottleneck with traditional EDA is let’s say I have 100 agents working on different parts of a chip,” Hussain said. “It’s difficult to pull together 100 commercial EDA licenses. We take a hybrid approach where around 90% of the verification happens without a commercial simulator. We use some of our own tricks, our own simulators, different technologies we’ve built, and then we use traditional EDA for the sign-off, making sure that this is going to pass all the regression tests.”
Regression tests are automated verification checks that run whenever hardware description code, such as Verilog or VHDL, changes.
Architect Labs doesn’t necessarily expect chip design jobs to become obsolete.
“The chip engineers that we do have in the industry are very supply-constrained,” Hussain said. “With the technology we’re building, we believe more engineers will be able to own more complicated blocks. You’ll need fewer engineers per project, but you’ll now have more projects. Silicon roadmaps will become more aggressive.”
Competition
Architect Labs isn’t alone. Competitors include ChipAgents and Ricursive. ChipAgents announced in September that Andes Technology, a supplier of RISC-V processor IP, cut a processor customization task from 8.5 weeks to six weeks. Ricursive founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini are former Google Brain employees who designed AlphaChip, an AI tool that generates a chip layout in hours. EDA tools provider Synopsys last year said it uses AI agents to “tame” the complexity of chip design.
Jang is betting on Architect Labs.
“The most important thing is, EDA companies don’t want you to solve your problems super-fast,” Jang said. “They want you to spend money, they want you to use their consulting services.”

articles.title: How Professional Computer Repair Can Help Australian Businesses Reduce Downtime and Stay Productive - Tech Guide
articles.text:
For most Australian businesses, computers are no longer simply office equipment. They are part of the infrastructure that keeps everyday operations moving.
Employees use them to communicate with customers, prepare documents, access financial systems, manage projects, store important information and work with cloud-based applications. When those systems perform reliably, business can continue without much interruption. When they begin to fail, even a relatively small technical problem can quickly turn into lost time and unnecessary disruption.
Professional Computer Repair can play an important role in helping businesses deal with these problems before they develop into larger disruptions. A computer that repeatedly freezes, takes too long to start or struggles with everyday software might not appear to be a serious business concern at first. Yet when several employees experience similar problems, the effect can become much larger. Work gets delayed, staff have to find temporary solutions and business owners may end up spending valuable time dealing with technology instead of focusing on customers and growth.
The right approach is not simply to fix a machine after it stops working. Businesses also need to understand why problems occur, whether existing equipment remains suitable for its workload and how individual computers fit into the wider IT environment. This broader perspective can help companies maintain more dependable systems while making better decisions about repairs, upgrades, replacements and ongoing support.
Why Small Technology Problems Can Have a Big Business Impact
Technology problems rarely arrive at a convenient time. A computer may suddenly stop working before an important presentation, a storage drive may begin showing signs of failure while an employee is working on a critical project, or a network issue may prevent several people from accessing files and applications.
The direct cost of such an incident is only part of the problem. Employees may be unable to complete their normal responsibilities while the issue is being investigated. Customers may experience delays, appointments can be affected and important internal tasks may be pushed further behind schedule.
This is why businesses should look beyond the question of whether a computer is technically operational. A machine can still turn on while performing poorly enough to affect productivity. Slow storage, insufficient memory, outdated software, overheating and hardware degradation can all reduce the efficiency of an otherwise functional computer.
Identifying these issues early allows businesses to decide whether a device needs maintenance, an upgrade or replacement. In some cases, a relatively straightforward repair may restore a computer to a useful working condition. In others, continued repairs may no longer make financial sense.
Business Computer Work Requires More Than Basic Troubleshooting
The technology requirements of a business are different from those of a typical home user. A business computer may need to connect to shared files, printers, servers, cloud applications, security systems and other workplace devices. Changing one part of that setup without considering the rest can create additional problems.
This is where professional business computer work becomes valuable. Rather than treating each machine as an isolated device, technicians can consider how computers fit into the wider workplace environment.
For example, setting up a new workstation may involve installing required applications, transferring data, configuring email, connecting printers and ensuring the device can access appropriate shared resources. Upgrading an existing computer may also require checking compatibility with current software and network systems.
A structured approach can help businesses maintain more consistent technology across their workplace. It also makes it easier to identify older equipment, plan future upgrades and avoid situations where employees are using significantly different systems for similar tasks.
Preventive Maintenance Can Be Better Than Emergency Repairs
Many businesses only think about IT support after something stops working. While reactive support is important, preventing recurring problems can be even more valuable.
Regular maintenance can reveal warning signs before they develop into complete failures. Storage health, system performance, software updates, backups and security settings can all be reviewed as part of a wider technology maintenance strategy.
This does not mean every business needs an expensive technology overhaul. Often, relatively simple improvements can make a noticeable difference. Replacing failing storage, increasing memory, updating outdated systems or improving backup arrangements may resolve problems that employees have been dealing with for months.
Preventive maintenance can also help businesses plan their spending. Instead of unexpectedly replacing several computers after failures occur, a company can gradually identify which equipment is approaching the end of its useful life and budget for replacements accordingly.
Computer Repair Should Be Part of a Wider IT Strategy
For businesses, fixing a damaged computer is only one part of maintaining a dependable technology environment. The more important question is whether the repair fits into the company’s wider IT requirements.
Computer Repair can address issues such as failing hardware, slow performance, damaged components and software-related problems, but businesses may also need support with networks, backups, security and cloud platforms.
For example, repairing a workstation without addressing an unstable network may solve one problem while leaving another source of downtime untouched. Similarly, replacing a failed computer without reviewing the company’s backup process could create unnecessary data risks in the future.
A broader IT strategy helps connect these individual areas. It allows businesses to consider how devices are maintained, how information is protected and how employees access the systems they need to work effectively.
Managed Services Can Change the Way Businesses Handle IT
As businesses grow, managing technology entirely on an ad hoc basis can become increasingly difficult. More employees mean more devices, more accounts, more software and more potential points of failure.
Managed services provide a more structured way to oversee an organisation’s IT environment. Instead of waiting for every issue to become an emergency, businesses can have ongoing support and monitoring designed around their particular requirements.
For a small business without a full-time internal IT department, this can be especially useful. Routine technical responsibilities can be handled alongside troubleshooting and strategic planning, allowing employees to concentrate on their primary work.
Managed services can also provide a clearer understanding of the business’s technology needs over time. A business may initially require basic support, but as it grows it could need improved networking, stronger security, better backups, Microsoft 365 management or additional cloud resources.
Cloud Services Are Now Part of Everyday Business Operations
Cloud technology has changed the way many businesses store information and access applications. Employees can work with documents, email, collaboration platforms and business software without everything being dependent on a single computer or physical office server.
However, moving services into the cloud does not remove the need for proper IT management. Cloud accounts still need to be configured correctly, access permissions need to be controlled and businesses need to understand how their information is protected and backed up.
Well-managed cloud services can provide flexibility for businesses with employees working across different locations. They can also make it easier for authorised users to access information when working remotely or from another office.
At the same time, businesses should avoid assuming that every cloud service automatically solves their backup and security requirements. A reliable IT strategy should consider how important information is stored, who can access it and what happens if an account is compromised or data is accidentally deleted.
A Reliable Network Supports the Entire Workplace
Computers depend on more than their individual hardware. A reliable network is essential when employees need to share files, access cloud platforms, use printers, communicate internally or connect to business applications.
Network problems can be particularly disruptive because a single issue may affect multiple employees at the same time. A poorly configured wireless network, outdated equipment or unstable connection can create slowdowns that are difficult to diagnose from an individual computer.
Businesses should therefore consider networking as part of their wider IT environment rather than treating it as a separate technical concern. Proper configuration, secure wireless access, appropriate network equipment and regular maintenance can help create a more dependable workplace.
For businesses operating across Western Sydney, having access to local technical expertise can also make a difference when onsite assistance is required. Local support can be particularly useful when an issue involves physical equipment, office networking or a workstation that cannot easily be diagnosed remotely.
Security and Backups Should Be Part of the Same Conversation
A computer that works perfectly but has inadequate security or backup arrangements can still present a serious business risk.
Businesses routinely hold customer information, financial records, internal documents and other valuable data. Hardware failure, accidental deletion, malware or other incidents can make that information unavailable at the worst possible time.
Regular backups provide an additional layer of protection, but businesses should also consider whether backups can actually be restored when needed. A backup that has never been tested may not provide the reassurance a business expects.
Security should similarly be approached as an ongoing process. Software updates, account protection, antivirus solutions, secure passwords and appropriate access controls can all contribute to a safer technology environment.
The goal is not to make a business completely immune to every possible problem. Rather, it is to reduce unnecessary exposure and ensure that the organisation has sensible recovery options when something does go wrong.
The Right Repair Decision Is Not Always Replacement
When a computer develops a problem, replacing it immediately may seem like the easiest solution. However, that is not necessarily the most economical choice.
Some issues can be resolved through relatively simple repairs or upgrades. A failing drive, insufficient memory or damaged component may be replaceable without requiring the business to purchase an entirely new system.
On the other hand, an older computer that has become increasingly unreliable may no longer justify continued repair costs. If it is also incompatible with modern software or lacks the performance required for the employee’s role, replacement may be the better long-term decision.
Professional assessment helps businesses make that distinction. Instead of spending money based purely on assumptions, business owners can consider the age, condition, performance and role of each device before deciding what to do.
How Australian Businesses Can Build More Reliable IT
Technology should support business growth rather than become another source of daily frustration. That requires more than responding whenever a computer fails. Businesses can benefit from looking at their technology as a connected environment in which computers, networks, cloud platforms, security systems and data protection all contribute to productivity.
A practical approach also recognises that every business is different. A small office may have completely different requirements from a multi-location company, while a professional services firm may rely on different systems from a retail or manufacturing business.
Businesses should therefore focus on solutions that match their actual operations. Reliable computer maintenance, sensible upgrades, managed services, secure cloud systems and dependable networking can work together to create an IT environment that is easier to manage and less likely to cause avoidable disruption.
For companies in and around Penrith, Richmond, Windsor and wider Western Sydney, this can be especially important as more everyday business functions become dependent on connected technology. Local businesses can benefit from having support available for both immediate technical problems and longer-term technology planning.
Frequently Asked Questions
How often should a business have its computers checked?
There is no single schedule that suits every company. Businesses with older equipment, heavy workloads or critical systems may benefit from more frequent checks. Regular monitoring and maintenance can help identify performance, storage, security and software problems before they result in significant downtime.
Is repairing a business computer better than replacing it?
It depends on the age, condition and performance of the computer. A relatively modern machine with a replaceable faulty component may be worth repairing, while an older device with repeated problems may be more economical to replace. A professional assessment can help determine which option makes more sense.
Can IT support help prevent computer downtime?
Yes. Regular maintenance, monitoring, software updates, hardware assessments, backups and network management can reduce the likelihood of avoidable failures. The objective is to identify potential issues early rather than waiting until they interrupt normal business operations.
Why are managed services useful for small businesses?
Managed services can give small businesses access to ongoing IT support without necessarily requiring a large internal technology team. They can help with routine maintenance, monitoring, security, cloud systems and troubleshooting while allowing employees to focus on their normal responsibilities.
Do cloud services eliminate the need for local IT support?
No. Cloud platforms can reduce dependence on physical infrastructure, but businesses still need to manage accounts, permissions, security, backups, connectivity and integrations. IT support remains useful for ensuring these systems work together effectively.
What should businesses do if a computer keeps experiencing the same problem?
Repeated failures should not simply be treated as separate incidents. The underlying cause should be investigated. It could be ageing hardware, software compatibility, insufficient resources, overheating, network issues or another recurring problem. Identifying the root cause can help prevent the same disruption from happening again.
Final Thoughts
Reliable technology is one of the foundations of modern business productivity. When computers, networks and cloud systems work as expected, employees can focus on customers and completing their responsibilities instead of spending valuable working hours dealing with technical problems.
Professional support can provide more value when it goes beyond emergency troubleshooting. By combining maintenance, business computer work, managed services, cloud services, networking, security and sensible hardware decisions, businesses can create an IT environment that is more dependable and easier to manage.
For Australian businesses, the goal should not simply be to keep computers running. It should be to build technology systems that support the way the business operates today while remaining flexible enough to accommodate future growth. A practical approach to IT can reduce unnecessary downtime, protect productivity and give business owners greater confidence in the systems they rely on every day.

articles.title: BlizzCon 2026 : comment voir la conférence de Blizzard sur WoW, Diablo, Overwatch et StarCraft ?
articles.text:
La rentrée des jeux vidéo n’est pas terminée. Après le State of Play de Sony et le double Direct de Nintendo, Blizzard Entertainment organise, ce week-end, la BlizzCon 2026. Il s’agit d’un rendez-vous incontournable pour les fans des licences phares de l’entreprise américaine.
Ce retour n’a rien d’anodin : la BlizzCon n’avait plus eu lieu depuis novembre 2023. Blizzard avait renoncé à l’édition 2024, faute d’annonce d’envergure à présenter, avant de faire de nouveau l’impasse en 2025. Après trois ans d’absence, l’éditeur joue gros avec cette édition 2026.
La BlizzCon 2026 est bien évidemment l’occasion idéale de faire des annonces, via une conférence d’ouverture qui sera aussi diffusée en ligne. Notez que Numerama est présent sur place pour couvrir l’événement.
Comment suivre la cérémonie d’ouverture de la BlizzCon 2026 ?
Si l’entrée de la BlizzCon 2026 est payante pour les personnes sur place, ce n’est pas le cas de la conférence d’ouverture. Pas besoin de ticket pour la visionner, et c’est tant mieux. Décalage horaire oblige avec Anaheim, le show démarre en soirée en France.
- Quand ? Ce samedi 12 septembre 2026, à 19h30, heure française (un préshow est prévu dès 18h30),
- Où ? Ici, sur YouTube, sur Twitch ou sur Battle.net,
- Quoi ? La conférence d’ouverture de la BlizzCon 2026.
La cérémonie d’ouverture doit durer environ 1h15. Les utilisatrices et les utilisateurs Twitch et YouTube pourront obtenir des récompenses pour divers jeux en associant leur compte à Battle.net. Plus vous regarderez, plus les récompenses seront nombreuses.
Les annonces, minute par minute
H-2 heures
Une autre photo, proposée par Michael de KGW, montrant le tout début de la file – et les fans les plus motivés !
Il y a vraiment beaucoup de monde
Encore deux heures à attendre, et la file d’attente du public s’est allongée considérablement ; et encore, il y a aussi toute une foule qui se forme aussi sur les côtés.
Olala le monde
Purée de pomme de terre.
Il était très tôt à Anaheim, mais les fans s’amassaient déjà près des portes pour entrer à la BlizzCon. Et ça commençait à lancer des « Pour la Horde » ou « Pour l’Alliance ». L’ambiance monte !
Numerama est sur place
Nous allons pouvoir vous faire vivre la cérémonie d’ouverture en direct, si vous ne la suivez pas déjà de votre côté !
Nous pourrons par ailleurs vous proposer très rapidement des prises en main, impressions et contenus autour des annonces de la BlizzCon 2026. Stay conected !
La BlizzCon arrive
C’est l’évènement que les fans de Blizzard attendent chaque année, et il n’y a désormais plus qu’une poignée d’heures à attendre : dans moins de trois heures, la cérémonie d’ouverture de la BlizzCon 2026 débutera.
Que va annoncer Blizzard lors de la BlizzCon 2026 ?
La BlizzCon est pensée comme une véritable fête qui rend hommage aux différentes sagas de Blizzard Entertainment. Par conséquent, on peut espérer des annonces pour Warcraft, Diablo, Overwatch ou encore StarCraft.
Comme toujours, World of Warcraft sera l’un des sujets les plus discutés, avec un accent sur la troisième extension de l’arc l’Âme-monde (la Worldsoul Saga), lancée en 2024 par The War Within et poursuivie en 2026 par Midnight. Il reste The Last Titan à découvrir. Une grosse mise à jour pour WoW Classic est aussi attendue. Outre la conférence d’ouverture, WoW aura droit à plusieurs panels pour évoquer l’avenir du MMORPG, un premier dès ce samedi 12 à 21h.
Concernant Diablo, il ne faudra pas s’attendre à un gros chamboulement, puisque la licence a déjà eu droit à son événement dédié pour fêter ses 30 ans. Par ailleurs, Diablo 4 a reçu une deuxième extension il y a quelques mois. Au mieux, on aura un teasing pour le futur gros chapitre, entre autres initiatives moins majeures. Il y a quand même un panel « L’avenir de Diablo IV », prévu ce dimanche 13 à 20h.
Il sera en revanche nécessaire de surveiller StarCraft, l’une des grosses attentes de cette BlizzCon 2026. Laissée de côté ces dernières années, la saga de RTS pourrait revenir en fanfare, à en croire des indices laissés par Blizzard Entertainment sur le site officiel.
Pour rappel, d’autres contenus seront proposés tout au long du week-end, certes à des horaires loin d’être favorables, des panels aux compétitions eSport (comme la Coupe du monde d’Overwatch). Il n’y a que les concerts qui ne seront pas retransmis, étant réservés aux visiteurs.

articles.title: NordVPN lance une extension gratuite pour comparer les prix des hôtels
articles.text:
NordVPN lance PriceMice, une extension Chrome gratuite destinée à comparer le prix d’une même chambre d’hôtel selon le pays depuis lequel elle est réservée.
Le prix d’une nuit d’hôtel ne dépend pas toujours uniquement de la chambre et des dates choisies. Selon votre localisation, une plateforme de réservation peut afficher un tarif différent. Avec PriceMice, NordVPN propose désormais de comparer directement ces différences depuis le navigateur, avant d’utiliser éventuellement un VPN pour réserver depuis le pays qui propose le prix le plus intéressant.
- storage9500 serveurs
- language167 pays couverts
- lan10 connexions simultanées
- moodEssai gratuit 30 jours
- thumb_upAvantage : sécurité polyvalente
Changer de pays pour payer moins cher
Disponible sur Chrome, PriceMice fonctionne pour l’instant uniquement avec Booking.com. Une fois l’extension installée, vous effectuez vos recherches comme d’habitude, puis pouvez comparer le prix d’une même chambre depuis plusieurs pays. Si vous trouvez un tarif inférieur dans l’un d’eux, vous pouvez alors vous connecter à un serveur VPN dans le pays concerné avant de finaliser votre réservation sur la plateforme.
PriceMice compare les montants finaux, taxes et frais compris. Les écarts ne dépendent toutefois pas uniquement de votre localisation : taux de change, taxes locales ou tests de prix menés par la plateforme peuvent aussi faire varier la facture.
NordVPN n’est pas le premier fournisseur de VPN à explorer ce terrain. Surfshark s’est déjà associé à RatePunk, une extension qui compare elle aussi les prix des hôtels selon votre localisation. Dans les deux cas, vous pouvez utiliser l’extension indépendamment du VPN du fournisseur concerné. Pour réserver au tarif repéré, vous pouvez ensuite passer par n’importe quel VPN proposant un serveur dans le pays correspondant.

articles.title: Process and precision: Artisera exhibition showcases contemporary Indian printmaking
articles.text:
Process and precision: Artisera exhibition showcases contemporary Indian printmaking
In this photo essay, we showcase artistic highlights from a printmaking exhibition at Bengaluru’s Artisera gallery.
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,015 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.
Art platform Artisera wraps up its exhibition in Bengaluru this week, titled The Mark of the Matrix — Impressions from Contemporary Indian Printmaking. It features the works of eleven Indian contemporary printmakers (see our coverage of its earlier shows here).
Founded in 2025, Artisera is a gallery and online platform promoting contemporary Indian art, traditional art, and collectibles. Located in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, it aims to create an offline-online experience via physical exhibitions as well as a digital touchpoint.
“This exhibition reflects our belief that Bengaluru deserves a stronger platform for printmaking,” Varun Backliwal, Founder and CEO of Artisera tells YourStory.
Printmaking is an artistic process that involves transferring an inked image from a prepared template or matrix onto another surface, like paper or fabric. As compared to drawing directly on a page, printmaking allows an artist to create multiple original copies or editions from a single surface.
As seen in this photo essay, the exhibition celebrates the richness and complexity of printmaking. Featured exhibitors are senior, mid-career and emerging artists from across India.
The artist lineup, some of whose works are featured here, includes Durgadas Garai, Dushyant Patel, Jayasimha Chandrashekar, Leticia Alvares, Nisha Dhinwa, Priyoum Talukdar, Swapnesh Vaigankar, Tsering Negi, Venugopal VG, Vijay Bagodi, and Vishakha Apte.
Walking through the exhibition hall invites viewers into a world of not just imagery but processes as well. Each printmaking technique leaves its own distinct trace, rhythm and character on paper.
Such characteristics include direct marks of woodcuts, delicacy of etching, tonal subtlety of lithography, and graphic immediacy of serigraphy. To experience these techniques together is to become more attentive to the surface of the image.
Features that come to the fore are the pressure of the line, the grain of the paper, the density of ink, the variations in tone, and the edge where one colour meets another. The very act of looking itself seems to become more tactile.
“Every print begins with a matrix – a carved woodblock, an etched copper plate, a lithographic stone, or a silkscreen. The matrix is where the image is conceived, refined, revised and ultimately brought to life,” Backliwal says, describing the concept behind the exhibition.
“The matrix is the invisible origin of every print. It carries within it the marks of labour, experimentation and countless artistic decisions,” he adds.
A range of printmaking techniques is featured in the exhibition. It includes woodcut, etching, aquatint, engraving, drypoint, lithography, serigraphy, and algraphy.
“The exhibition celebrates printmaking not just as a means of reproduction, but as an original artistic practice in which every impression bears the evidence of craft, precision and intent,” Backliwal affirms.
Artisera hopes this exhibition is the first in its annual series dedicated to contemporary Indian printmaking. “While printmaking has a rich history and has played a significant role in the development of modern and contemporary Indian art, it has often remained under-represented within mainstream exhibition programming,” he observes.
Artisera hopes to showcase the innovation as well as collectability of contemporary printmaking. “The gallery brings greater visibility to the artists working within the medium,” he says.
There are interactive features in the gallery as well – visitors can hold some of the tools, matrices and proofs that shape a print before it becomes a finished work. “The exhibition celebrates not only the final impression but also the journey of experimentation that precedes it,” Backliwal says.
“At its heart, this exhibition is an invitation to look beyond the finished image – to recognise the matrix as the true beginning of every print, and to appreciate the dialogue between artist, material and process that gives printmaking its enduring vitality,” he says.
A group exhibition makes this dialogue especially vivid. Techniques begin to converse across the gallery, and differences become discoveries.
There is also delight in the surprises that a printmaking exhibition can deliver. What initially appears to be a quiet, flat image can reveal extraordinary depth when seen up close.
It opens up the chance to encounter art through the intelligence of the hand, the chemistry of materials, and the discipline of process. In an increasingly AI-driven age, printmaking brings the focus of creativity back to the human at the core.
Artisera and the Brigade Group have also launched THRESHOLD, a national artist development programme. It supports six practising Indian visual artists through a financial grant, mentorship, professional development, and three exhibitions across Bengaluru, Chennai and Hyderabad.
This gives the finalists the opportunity to connect their practices with new audiences, collectors and the wider art ecosystem. Artists will also gain access to Artisera’s verified client and collector network, alongside professional visibility and the possibility of continued gallery support.
“Cities such as Delhi, Mumbai, Baroda, and Kolkata have long nurtured important printmaking traditions. But opportunities for artists and audiences to engage deeply with the medium in Bengaluru have remained relatively limited. We hope this exhibition contributes to building a lasting community around printmaking in the city,” Backliwal signs off.
Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?
(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at Artisera.)

articles.title: OpenAI estudia frenar sus sistemas de inteligencia artificial más avanzados tras un incidente de seguridad
articles.text:
OpenAI, la empresa dirigida por SamAltman, estudia ralentizar el desarrollo de los sistemas de inteligencia artificial más avanzados y busca que otras compañías adopten una medida similar para reducir los riesgos de esa tecnología. El consejero delegado comunicó esta posibilidad a toda la plantilla durante una reunión celebrada esta semana, según Bloomberg.
La inquietud aumentó después de que agentes de inteligencia artificial de la compañía colaboraran para eludir medidas de contención y acceder sin autorización a un sitio web de terceros. El episodio intensificó las dudas sobre la capacidad de controlar sistemas que adquieren mayor autonomía.
PUBLICIDAD
La empresa ya moderó algunos desarrollos y suspendió entrenamientos internos por razones de seguridad. En julio de 2026, Altman también dialogó con funcionarios de la Casa Blanca sobre la necesidad de reducir el ritmo de avance de la inteligencia artificial.
La presión interna para limitar los sistemas más avanzados
La discusión no se limita a la dirección ejecutiva. El científico jefe de OpenAI, Jakub Pachocki, publicó un artículo en el que alertó sobre los peligros de la inteligencia artificial y planteó que las empresas deberían coordinarse para frenar el desarrollo cuando las condiciones de seguridad lo exijan.
PUBLICIDAD
Pachocki espera que esas pausas voluntarias se vuelvan habituales hasta que existan límites de seguridad compartidos. La propuesta apunta a evitar que cada laboratorio continúe acelerando por temor a perder terreno frente a sus rivales.
La preocupación se extendió entre trabajadores de las principales compañías del sector. A finales de julio, más de 1.000 empleados firmaron una petición para reclamar un mecanismo que permita moderar el desarrollo de la inteligencia artificial.
PUBLICIDAD
El martes, el investigador Jacob Coxon dejó su puesto tras haber trabajado tanto en Anthropic como en OpenAI. Acusó a ambas empresas de competir para crear una inteligencia artificial superinteligente, capaz incluso de acabar con la humanidad durante esta década.
Coxon, que se desempeñaba en preentrenamiento en Anthropic, sostuvo que ninguna de las dos compañías actuaba con responsabilidad. “Están jugando con nuestras vidas”, afirmó al explicar sus cuestionamientos, informó Financial Times.
PUBLICIDAD
Dos investigadores que habían abandonado recientemente Anthropic y DeepMind, la división de inteligencia artificial de Google, expresaron el jueves preocupaciones similares. Ambos reclamaron mayor transparencia sobre los riesgos de los modelos avanzados y cuestionaron la rapidez de los lanzamientos.
Las salidas que expusieron el debate sobre la seguridad
Las renuncias en OpenAI reflejan una transformación interna que excede las diferencias sobre seguridad. La organización fue fundada en 2015 como un laboratorio sin fines de lucro, pero ahora debe comercializar productos, garantizar infraestructura informática, atender a clientes empresariales y responder a inversores.
PUBLICIDAD
Ilya Sutskever, cofundador y científico jefe de OpenAI, fue una de las figuras centrales de esa etapa inicial. También integró la junta que destituyó temporalmente a Altman en noviembre de 2023, aunque después manifestó que lamentaba haber participado en esa decisión.
Sutskever anunció su salida en mayo de 2024 y posteriormente creó Safe Superintelligence, una empresa enfocada en desarrollar una superinteligencia segura sin priorizar, al menos en un comienzo, productos comerciales. No atribuyó públicamente su renuncia a un conflicto puntual sobre seguridad.
PUBLICIDAD
Mira Murati, exdirectora de tecnología y directora ejecutiva interina durante la crisis de 2023, dejó la compañía en septiembre de 2024. Murati había participado en el desarrollo y lanzamiento de ChatGPT y DALL-E, y dijo que necesitaba tiempo y espacio para emprender sus propias exploraciones.
Su partida coincidió con las renuncias de los líderes de investigación Bob McGrew y Barret Zoph. Las tres decisiones fueron presentadas como independientes, según informó Reuters.
PUBLICIDAD
El caso de Jan Leike expuso uno de los desacuerdos más explícitos. El codirector del equipo de Superalignment, dedicado a investigar cómo alinear sistemas de inteligencia artificial avanzados con objetivos humanos, renunció en mayo de 2024 tras sostener que la seguridad había quedado relegada frente a los “productos brillantes”.
El equipo de Superalignment fue disuelto después de las salidas de Leike y Sutskever, y sus integrantes fueron reasignados a otras áreas. Leike se incorporó después a Anthropic, una empresa fundada por antiguos empleados de OpenAI.
PUBLICIDAD
La reorganización de OpenAI como compañía global
Brad Lightcap contribuyó a construir la estructura financiera, legal, comercial y de alianzas de OpenAI antes de convertirse en director de operaciones. En abril de 2026, dejó ese puesto para concentrarse en proyectos especiales y cuatro meses después anunció que saldría de la empresa para crear una nueva compañía.
Lightcap expresó confianza en OpenAI y la empresa indicó que sus funciones ya se habían alejado de la gestión cotidiana. Su salida fue confirmada por Reuters y no se esperaba que tuviera un efecto inmediato sobre los equipos.
La reorganización se aceleró en abril de 2026, cuando Kevin Weil, Bill Peebles y Srinivas Narayanan dejaron áreas estratégicas en la misma jornada. Weil había dirigido producto y luego OpenAI for Science; Peebles lideraba el equipo de generación de video Sora, mientras Narayanan era director de tecnología para aplicaciones empresariales.
OpenAI integraba sus iniciativas científicas con otras áreas, reducía proyectos que ya no consideraba prioritarios y concentraba recursos en herramientas para empresas. Narayanan explicó que quería pasar tiempo con sus padres antes de definir su próximo paso profesional.
Un recuento publicado en Infobae registró al menos 14 altos cargos que abandonaron sus puestos o redujeron su participación durante 2026. La lista incluyó responsables de operaciones, ingresos, marketing, producto, ventas empresariales, infraestructura, ética y seguridad.
Fidji Simo dejó su cargo de tiempo completo por motivos de salud y pasó a ser asesora. Johannes Heidecke, responsable de sistemas de seguridad, y Chloé Bakalar, líder de ética en inteligencia artificial, también salieron de la compañía durante ese proceso de cambios.
La seguridad fue integrada de forma más estrecha con la investigación, mediante responsables interinos y mayores atribuciones para la vicepresidencia de investigación y seguridad. Ese esquema puede incorporar controles desde el diseño de los modelos, pero también puede reducir la independencia de quienes deben cuestionar el ritmo de desarrollo.
Bakalar había defendido que la ética debía ser una responsabilidad distribuida en toda la organización y no recaer en una sola persona convertida en el “centro moral” de un desarrollador de inteligencia artificial. Su planteamiento no fue presentado públicamente como una acusación directa contra Altman.
Altman reconoció recientemente que la industria, incluida OpenAI, ha hecho un “trabajo terrible” al explicar a la sociedad los beneficios de la inteligencia artificial y la forma de mitigar sus efectos negativos.
PUBLICIDAD
