articles.title: Studie misst nach: Homeoffice schlägt Büro bei der Produktivität
articles.text:
Wo sind Angestellte produktiver – zuhause oder im Büro? Bei dieser Frage scheiden sich die Geister. Während Mitarbeiter:innen das Homeoffice vor allem schätzen, um berufliche und private Verpflichtungen besser zu vereinbaren, bemängeln Arbeitgeber:innen den fehlenden Austausch. Um herauszufinden, in welchem Umfeld die Produktivität messbar höher ist, begleiteten Forscher:innen des Tippie College of Business der University of Iowa 219 hybrid Beschäftigte über eine Arbeitswoche hinweg. Emily Campion, Professorin für Management und Unternehmertum und Mitautorin der Studie, hat mit Phys.org über die Ergebnisse gesprochen – und gibt Arbeitgeber:innen eine klare Empfehlung.
Angestellte sind im Homeoffice produktiver
An den Tagen, an denen die Testpersonen von zuhause arbeiteten, sei jede:r von ihnen produktiver gewesen. Sie hätten größere Fortschritte bei der Erreichung ihrer Arbeitsziele gemacht und arbeiteten schneller als an Bürotagen. Je öfter sie im Homeoffice arbeiteten, desto stärker sei ihre Produktivität angestiegen. Die Forscher:innen baten die Beschäftigten zusätzlich, ihr Energieniveau an denselben fünf Tagen stündlich zu protokollieren. Dabei stellten sie fest, dass das Energieniveau an Tagen, an denen sie von zuhause areiteten, gleichmäßiger war. Die Gründe: Hier seien die Beschäftigten weniger Ablenkungen ausgesetzt und könnten ihren Zeitplan leichter selbst festlegen.
An Tagen im Büro habe das Energieniveau tendenziell stärker geschwankt. „Diese Energieschwankungen bei der Arbeit, die durch mehr und unterschiedliche Reize ausgelöst werden, können es erschweren, sich in eine Aufgabe zu vertiefen und Fortschritte zu erzielen”, so Campion gegenüber Phys.org. Konkret hätten die Mitarbeiter:innen an Homeoffice-Tagen im Vergleich zu Bürotagen etwa 33 Prozent weniger Schwankungen im Energielevel verzeichnet. Jeder Rückgang der Energieschwankungen um einen Prozentpunkt habe zu 26 Prozent mehr Fortschritt bei der Zielerreichung geführt.
Unterbrechungen senken das Energielevel
Laut Campion sei es nicht die Arbeit im Homeoffice selbst, die den Mitarbeiter:innen mehr Energie gebe. Ein gleichmäßigeres Energieniveau führe aber zu höherer Produktivität als die Höhen und Tiefen der Arbeit im Büro. Zuhause könnten Beschäftigte beispielsweise eine E-Mail ignorieren oder Slack-Benachrichtigungen ausschalten, um konzentrierter zu arbeiten. „Stellen Sie sich vor, wie viel Energie es kostet, zu einer neuen Aufgabe zu wechseln, weil jemand in Ihr Büro kommt und Sie um etwas bittet“, erklärte Campion. „Dann müssen Sie Energie aufwenden, um wieder zu der Aufgabe zurückzukehren, die Sie vor dem Auftauchen dieser Person erledigt haben.“
Laut der Studie spiele auch die Art der Unterbrechungen eine Rolle. Ablenkungen am Arbeitsplatz, wie spontane Anfragen von Kolleg:innen, Geräusche aus anderen Büros oder beschwerliche Pendelwege, würden laut den Forscher:innen mehr an der Energie zehren als Ablenkungen zuhause. In der Studie nannten die Forscher:innen hier beispielsweise das häufig kritisierte Wäschewaschen. In einer Zeit, in der immer mehr Unternehmen ihre Mitarbeitenden zurück ins Büro holen, senden diese Ergebnisse ein deutliches Signal. Um die Produktivität zu steigern, sollten Arbeitgeber:innen verstärkt hybride Modelle in Betracht ziehen, so Campion.
Studie sieht Zusammenhang mit Narzissmus
Forscher:innen der Wharton School an der University of Pennsylvania untersuchten in einer Studie, warum Chef:innen ihre Mitarbeiter:innen überhaupt zurück ins Büro holen – und fanden die Ursache in Narzissmus. In einem Gastbeitrag für die New York Times erklären sie, dass je höher Führungskräfte sich selbst einschätzen, desto mehr würden sie nach Macht und Status streben – und desto stärker würden sie die Rückkehr ins Büro befürworten. Die Arbeit im Homeoffice hindere egozentrische Führungskräfte demnach daran, Anerkennung von ihren Mitarbeiter:innen zu erhalten.

articles.title: LG responds to TV spying allegations
articles.text:
Earlier this week, Gamers Nexus, Level1Techs, and independent security researchers detailed some alarming findings about how LG’s TVs are logging and uploading data on its users. Now the company is pushing back against those allegations, saying that “Some recent media coverage may have contributed to misconceptions about how LG smart TVs work.”
LG responds to TV spying allegations
The company claims reports about its capturing and uploading audio are misleading.
LG released a statement in which it claims that its “TVs do not continuously record or transmit users’ conversations,” and that wake-word detection is all processed locally. However, the word “continuously” is doing a lot of heavy lifting here as Gamers Nexus demonstrated an LG TV keeping extensive logs of ambient conversations long after one would assume its AI assistant had stopped listening.
LG also said that its features like “Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), voice recognition, and interest-based advertising are optional,” and “not enabled by default.” The company says that:
ACR uses audio fingerprinting technology using the TV’s internal audio processor (not a speaker) to identify content and does not collect screenshots, screen recordings, video recordings, voice recordings, or other audio recordings from the TV.
The company did not address broader concerns about how much data it collects, who it shares it with, the potential for bad actors to exploit its features, or the misleading way in which its privacy options are presented.

articles.title: The JBL Live 680NC review: these headphones may sound good, but the stamina and litany of features are the star of the show
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The sound quality on the JBL Live 680NC is good for the price, if a little bass heavy. But more impressive are the various features included as well as the amazingly long battery life. Just be aware that the fit does put some pressure on the top of the head and that you’ll have to source your own USB-C cable to charge.
Pros
- +Good, warm sound
- +Full of features like adaptive ANC and personalized EQ
- +Incredible battery life
- +A lot on offer for the money
Cons
- -Headphone weight sits on top of head
- -Occasionally overwhelming low-end
Why you can trust TechRadar
JBL Live 680NC: Two-minute review
The JBL Live 680NC are a strong pair of headphones for the price. They have a lot to offer, such as a whole litany of features including well-implemented active noise cancellation (ANC) and Ambient Aware, a lot of EQ-related options, spatial audio, and Auracast support. They also offer a very, very long battery life.
But they come with some compromises to meet that $160 price point. The sound quality, while good, does have an unruly low-end and a more rolled off high end than I would like. The spatial audio is a bit underwhelming in practice. They don’t come with a charging cable. And they do put a little bit of pressure on the top of the head during long listening sessions.
If you’re trying to stretch your budget, they may be the best wireless headphones for you, but manage your expectations; they’re not going to compete with something like the Sony WH-1000XM6. And if you have the ability to spend an extra hundred bucks (or the equivalent in your regional coin), the slightly more expensive JBL Live 780NC do sound a fair bit better and handle the weight distribution a little better as well. That said, these are tough times for a lot of people, and the price tag on the Live 680NC is reasonable, especially considering everything that they can do.
JBL Live 680NC: Price and release date
- Priced $159.95 / $129.99 / AU$199.95
- Launch date March 12, 2026
With a price tag of $159.95 / £129.99 / AU$199.95, the JBL Live 680NC technically fit into the mid-range tier of headphones while still being a cool $100 cheaper than the JBL Live 780NC that was released concurrently in March 2026.
As you’ll see in this review, there are a few reasons to spend that extra hundred dollars (though you could spend even more for the JBL Tour One M3 Smart Tx). But if you’re okay with a slightly less articulate sound quality or marginally less comfortable fit, you can save that hundred bucks if you’re on more of a budget.
JBL Live 680NC: Specs
| Drivers | 40mm drivers | 
| Active noise cancellation | Adaptive | 
| Battery life | Up to 50 hours with ANC On, 80 without | 
| Weight | 231.16 g | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0 | 
| Frequency range | 10Hz - 40kHz | 
| Waterproofing | N/A | 
| Other features | Multipoint connectivity, App Support, Adaptive Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency Mode, Hi-Res, Spatial Audio, Fast Charging, Auracast, Voice Assistant | 
JBL Live 680NC: Features
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
- Multipoint connectivity and Auracast available
- Very adjustable Active Noise Cancellation and Ambient Aware
- Powerful EQ including personalization options
The JBL Live 680NC are chock full of features. Multipoint connectivity, Auracast (allowing connection to multiple headphones from one source), Bluetooth with LE Audio (unavailable for Apple users), the ability to customize on-ear controls, and on-ear wear detection are just some of what’s on offer. You can also upmix via JBL’s own spatial audio feature.
Adaptive active noise cancellation (ANC), Ambient Aware, and TalkThru modes are available with a good amount of customizations for the first two through the app. And while these modes won’t beat the best of Sony or Bose, they work pretty well. I don’t hear ambient noise with the ANC on at 50% (while something is playing), while I can hear ambient noise clearly with music at around 60%, which is nice when using these headphones for a walk or run.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
There’s plenty more fine tuning available through the app. Of course, there’s plenty in the way of EQ. Not only are there a handful of EQ presets, but there’s a parametric EQ with the ability to boost or cut up to 6 dB anywhere between 32 and 16kHz, which is much more powerful than a lot of EQs available with other headphones.
Plus, JBL’s Personi-Fi 3.0 feature allows for creating a personalized EQ curve based on how you hear. It does so via a test of different frequencies at different volumes for each ear. Not only do I appreciate the personalization aspect of it, but also that it takes the guesswork out of trying to adjust the EQ.
Call-related features are available in the app as well, including allowing you to hear your own voice, as well as some relaxation focused features that, while they feel a little gimmicky, are a nice addition for anyone who wants to hear the sound of rain or birds chirping without pulling up a youtube channel for it.
- Features score: 5 / 5
JBL Live 680NC: Design
- Light, on-ear headphones
- Weight sits a little heavily on top of head though
- Comes without a charging cable
The JBL Live 680NC are fairly sharp looking headphones for around $160. They’re not quite premium, but they’re pretty close with a combination of plastic, metal (particularly the hinges), and leatherette-covered foam. There’s plenty of padding on the headband and ear cups, but since they’re on-ear more than over-ear, their fit is a bit different to the JBL Live 780NC I just reviewed.
They’re not that heavy at around 231 grams, but since they sit on the ear instead of over, more of the weight sits on top of the head. So while there’s plenty of cushion, I feel the headphones pressing on my skull in a way that lingers after wear. It’s not a lot so I didn’t feel discomfort, exactly, but it is something that separates it from its more expensive big brother.
Other than the fit and, relatedly, the ear pads, the JBL Live 680NC are identical to the Live 780NC in terms of design. They’re available in the same five colors (black, blue, green, white, champagne), have the same round ear cups, and have the same one and a half inch height adjustment per side. They’re foldable and have a big L or R on the inside of the non-removable ear pads as well.
Controls and ports are the same as well. The left ear cup houses the volume controls, while the right has the power and bluetooth slider along with the ANC / AmbientAware / TalkThru cycle button, not to mention that you can top on the center of the ear cup in various configurations to play or pause, rewind, or fast forward to the next song. The USB-C charging port is also on the right side.
And just like the JBL Live 780NC, the JBL Live 680NC come with a soft carrying case, a USB-C to Aux cable for analog listening, and come without an actual charging cable, though you can just use whatever you charge your phone with (you don't still have a Lightning iPhone, do you?).
- Design score: 4/5
JBL Live 680NC: Sound
- Low-end is often overwhelming
- Warmer sounding headphones with slight high-end roll off
- Incredible battery life
The JBL Live 680NC is a competent, if not quite inspiring set of headphones to listen to. There’s plenty of volume thankfully, so if you’re trying to fast track hearing loss, you can certainly do that with these headphones.
Just like the more expensive 780NC, the low end on these headphones is almost out of control. I’ve done a lot of my listening with the “studio” EQ preset, which is basically a flat EQ with a slight bass cut, and I still feel like I’m hearing too much bass, regardless of whether I’m listening to Bruno Mars or Nothing. Of course, fans of EDM and Hip Hop will probably love that.
And just like the 780NC, the JBL Live 680NC use 40mm drivers. However, they don’t have quite as much ‘sparkle’ or clarity in the top end so don’t have quite the presence. I would describe the high-end as slightly rolled off. It’s still pleasant to listen to, but just doesn’t sound as Hi-Fi despite also having the 10Hz to 40kHz frequency range, which is considered high resolution.
That roll off does give the JBL Live 680NC a little warmer of a sound, helped along by the fact that the mids are a bit more forward here. Some people may like that. Of course, audio can sound a little bloated with mid-heavy mixes, aka any dense rock-leaning mixes.
This also affects the soundstage as there isn’t quite the separation I’m used to. I am setting the bar a little high as I experienced better separation between instruments and audio elements in the more expensive JBL headphones, but that’s a hundred dollar difference. And these wireless headphones sound good for $150.
Also worth noting, the spatial audio here is not a fully immersive experience but just a virtual upmix of existing stereo audio (the headphones only have one driver per side). It’s an interesting inclusion that adds a little space to any audio I’m listening to, but is fairly nuanced to the point where you might not even realize that it’s on.
On the other hand, the battery life on the JBL Live 680NC is outright impressive. You get 80 hours on a single charge without ANC on, and 50 hours of use with it on. A fast charge of five minutes gives an additional four hours of use.
- Sound performance: 4 / 5
JBL Live 680NC: Value
- Great value proposition
- Comes with similar tradeoffs of other budget / mid-tier headphones
- As fully featured as anything else at this price point
The JBL Live 680NC is a very good value proposition. I do like the JBL Live 780NC more — it sounds better and has a better fit — but its $250 price tag might be a big ask for some. And the JBL Live 680NC still sound good if slightly different, having a warmer sound signature while still have the same battery life and feature set of the more expensive headphones.
Other headphones trying to bridge the gap between budget and mid-tier end up closer in price to the 780NC than the 680NC. The Beyerdynamic Aventho 100, for example, are a pair of headphones that I really enjoyed that also came with a handful of compromises to keep cost down, except that cost is higher at $229.99 / £199 / AU$314. They sound good but not great, have an interesting look, great battery life, and solid implementation of ANC.
- Value: 4.5/5
Should I buy the JBL Live 680NC?
| JBL Live 680NC scorecard |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | ANC, Ambient Aware, a parametric EQ, and spatial audio are just some of what’s on offer. | 5/5 | 
| Design | These headphones are portable, look good, and fit well, though they do put a little pressure on the top of the head. | 4/5 | 
| Performance | The JBL Live 680NC sound good, despite having too much bass and a bit of high-end roll off. The battery life is impressive, though. | 4/5 | 
| Value | You get a lot for the price with these headphones. Despite the compromises, these are a great value. | 4.5/5 | 
Buy them if…
You want it all without spending a lot
The JBL Live 680NC offer a lot from ANC and personalized EQ to spatial audio, while keeping the price pretty affordable.
You want a ridiculously long battery life
Being able to use the headphones for up to 80 hours without a charge is seriously impressive. Being able to get an additional four hours from five minutes of charging even more so. 
Don’t buy them if…
You want audiophile quality sound
These headphones sound good, but, despite the high resolution capabilities, don’t quite have the clarity or sound signature for particular listeners.
You have a sensitive head
My head didn’t hurt from using these headphones for a long listening session, but I did feel the pressure on top of my head. If you’re sensitive, you might want to consider something else, like the Live 780NC.
JBL Live 680NC: Also consider
JBL Live 780NC
The JBL Live 780NC have the same everything-but-the-kitchen-sink feature set and ridiculously long battery life, along with some of the same negatives like that overwhelming low end and lack of charging cable. But they’re a little more comfortable to wear and do sound better. They’re also a hundred bucks more.
Read our full JBL Live 780NC review
Beyerdynamic Aventho 100
The Beyerdynamic Aventho 100 are just a little cheaper while still providing a good looking (and feeling) pair of headphones that travel well and come with an almost as impressive battery life. They’re more limited in features though, and don’t wow in the audio department (they do still sound good).
Read our full Beyerdynamic Aventho 100 review
How I tested the JBL Live 780NC
- Tested over a week period
- Tested with different music as well as video streaming
- Tested the various features
I spent a week using the JBL Live 680NC as my daily headphones. While using them, I listened to all sorts of genres from electronic and hip hop to rock and acoustic music to compare the frequency range and soundstage. I also tested the various settings such as ANC, transparency mode, EQ, and multipoint.
I’ve spent the last few years reviewing audio equipment and have spent even longer using my critical ear as a listener and musician to understand what does and doesn’t sound good.
- First reviewed in April 2026
James Holland loves checking out gadgets of all sorts, whether it's audio equipment, laptops, or vacuums (especially of the robot variety), and does so for a number of Future Publications including TechRadar, Top Ten Reviews, Homes & Gardens, and T3. He's built up an expertise for in-depth reviewing over the last four years. When he's not putting in the work on the latest tech, he loves to travel, play music, and eat questionable food.

articles.title: Windows 11 can now reinstall itself from the cloud — Cloud Rebuild revives dead systems without secondary boot media, wipes broken installation and downloads a fresh copy of the OS
articles.text:
Windows 11 can now reinstall itself from the cloud — Cloud Rebuild revives dead systems without secondary boot media, wipes broken installation and downloads a fresh copy of the OS
Windows recovery gets easier.
Microsoft has finally solved one of the biggest pain points of Windows with the rollout of Cloud Rebuild. The new recovery feature can reinstall Windows 11 even when an existing Windows installation is corrupt or refuses to boot. Available as a beta through the newly released Windows 11 Insider Beta Preview Build 26220.9343, the feature is essentially a hassle-free alternative to creating a Windows installation USB drive when a PC needs to be recovered.
According to Microsoft, Cloud Rebuild is designed to restore a Windows 11 PC to a “clean, known-good state” by downloading a fresh image of Windows along with the required drivers directly through Windows Update. Unlike the existing Reset this PC functionality, it does not depend on the health of your existing Windows installation, nor does it require users to have a USB drive or custom recovery image available.
Available via the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE), users can access it by selecting Troubleshoot > Recovery and uninstall > Cloud rebuild from WinRE. Speaking of which, Microsoft has also improved networking support in WinRE. The recovery environment can now reuse eligible Wi-Fi profiles saved within an existing Windows installation, allowing a PC to connect during recovery without requiring administrators to separately configure Wi-Fi credentials in WinRE. Once the PC is connected, Cloud Rebuild checks Windows Update for the target Windows build and downloads the required files. Users can then confirm the Windows edition, language, and build before starting the reinstall.
The only catch here is that Cloud Rebuild completely wipes the system drive, meaning that the process removes all data stored in your main installation or C: drive, including locally stored files, accounts, applications, and settings, before reinstalling Windows. Thus, it is recommended to back up all your important files either locally or using a cloud-based service before starting the process. Once the installation is complete, the PC boots into the Windows out-of-box experience, similar to a fresh installation of Windows. For admin-managed PCs using Windows Autopilot and Microsoft Intune, the system can automatically reconnect to the organization's management infrastructure and restore assigned applications, policies, and backed-up settings.
Cloud Rebuild could particularly be useful when Windows becomes too corrupted to boot normally. Instead of finding another PC, creating installation media, and manually reinstalling Windows, users can potentially perform the entire recovery process directly from WinRE. The feature is still in preview; however, we can expect a wider release later this year.

articles.title: Munich-based Furo raises €3.44 million to make industrial battery storage economically viable | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Furo (formerly Lumera Energy), a Munich-based energy software company, today announced that it has closed a €3.44 million ($4 million) funding round to further develop its software, expand into additional European markets, and grow its team.
The round was led by US investor TQ Ventures, with participation from Sandberg Bernthal Venture Partners, the fund of Sheryl Sandberg, as well as Neo and CDTM Venture Capital.
“Our customers did not buy a battery in order to own a technology, but in order to lower their electricity bill. In one of the most volatile power markets in the world, that is decided by the software, not by the hardware. That is exactly why we founded Furo,” said Lena Sophia Voß, co-founder of Furo.
Furo was founded in 2025 as Lumera Energy by Voß, Leonie Wagner and Simon Wittner, who met on a joint master’s programme at the Centre for Digital Technology and Management (CDTM) of LMU Munich and the Technical University of Munich.
It is a software company for the control and optimisation of commercial and industrial battery storage. The platform forecasts power prices and weather up to 48 hours ahead, optimises the operation of the storage systems in real time on that basis, and markets unused capacity in energy trading.
According to the company, global energy demand from AI data centres is rising sharply, hitting energy-intensive industrial companies hardest, especially in Germany, where electricity prices are already among the highest in the world.
It notes that battery storage provides the solution here, by storing surplus solar or wind power and releasing it when needed; the problem is that most installations have so far operated on rigid, pre-programmed rules, regardless of how the weather or electricity prices are actually developing.
Furo claims that its software works differently because it forecasts electricity prices and weather up to 48 hours ahead and decides in real time when a storage system charges and when it releases or sells power.
The company states that this enables customers to reduce their electricity costs by up to 40 per cent. It is not sold directly to end customers but rather through installers, project developers, storage manufacturers, and utilities. More than 800 companies use the platform across over 6,000 sites in Germany and Europe. The platform adapts to the respective role, from system sizing through asset operation to the marketing of free capacity in energy trading.
The German startup opines that the European and German power markets, in particular, are among the most volatile in the world, owing to the rapid build-out of wind and solar energy. Furo highlighted that its forecasting module prices in exactly these fluctuations, while static systems have so far remained blind to them.
Inflexible energy demand costs industrial companies an estimated 580 billion US dollars a year worldwide. The cause is not the build-out of renewable energy itself, but price volatility, high grid fees, load peaks and a lack of flexibility in consumption.
“Lena, Leonie and Simon understand the European energy market at an extraordinary level of depth. It’s a remarkable example of team-market fit. Together, they bring exceptional technical depth and operational experience in Europe’s most complex power market. That’s already reflected in the number of projects and the data they’ve built up. Coupled with a global market for storage flexibility set to multiply in the coming years, we see this as one of the greatest opportunities in Europe and beyond,” said Schuster Tanger, co-founding partner at TQ Ventures.
Earlier this month, Furo announced a partnership with Berlin-based LUOX Energy, the end-customer brand of Lumenaza GmbH, to launch a combined solution for optimising commercial and industrial battery storage systems. In May 2026, the company announced its rebrand from Lumera Energy.

articles.title: Microsoft kennt diesen Excel-Bug seit Jahren – eine Behebung wäre fatal
articles.text:
29. Februar 1900: Warum Excel an einem Tag festhält, den es nie gab
In Excel ist seit Jahrzehnten ein falsches Datum enthalten. Das Programm geht nämlich fälschlicherweise davon aus, dass das Jahr 1900 ein Schaltjahr war. Microsoft ist sich dessen bewusst, hat die Ursachen dokumentiert und könnte das Problem prinzipiell beheben. Trotzdem gibt es gute Gründe, warum das voraussichtlich nicht geschehen wird. In einem Beitrag zur Problembehandlung erläutert Microsoft die Ursachen und Folgen dieses scheinbar kleinen Fehlers.
Lotus-1-2-3-Legacy: Warum der 29. Februar 1900 in Excel lebt
Laut Microsoft besteht das Problem bei mehreren Excel-Versionen. Aber wie konnte es dazu kommen? Excel verwendet Seriennummern zur Darstellung von Datumsangaben. Der 1. Januar 1900 trägt die Seriennummer 1, der 2. Januar die 2 und so weiter. Hinter der Formatierung verbergen sich also lediglich einfache Zahlen. Das Problem tritt Ende Februar 1900 auf. Da es sich in jenem Jahr nicht um ein Schaltjahr handelte, hatte der Februar nur 28 Tage. Excel behandelt den 29. Februar aber so, als gäbe es ihn, und weist ihm die Seriennummer 60 zu. Der 1. März trägt daher die Seriennummer 61 und jedes Datum danach erhält eine Seriennummer, die fälschlicherweise eine Stelle zu hoch ist.
Der Fehler geht auf Lotus 1-2-3 zurück, das in den 80er-Jahren zu den führenden Tabellenkalkulationsprogrammen zählte. Hier war der 29. Februar 1900 erstmals irrtümlich enthalten. Microsoft übernahm für Excel dasselbe Datumssystem, um eine bessere Kompatibilität zu gewährleisten. Im Allgemeinen gelten Jahre, die durch vier teilbar sind, als Schaltjahre, mit Ausnahme von Jahrhundertjahren.
Diese müssen zusätzlich durch 400 teilbar sein. Da 1900 nicht durch 400 teilbar ist, hätte der Kalender direkt vom 28. Februar auf den 1. März übergehen müssen. Diese Regel funktionierte für fast alle Jahre – versagte aber bei dieser besonderen Regel für Jahrhundertjahre. Microsoft weist darauf hin, dass Excel alle anderen Schaltjahre richtig behandelt, einschließlich der Jahrhundertjahre. Der Fehler betreffe nur das Jahr 1900.
Abwärtskompatibilität als Risiko: Warum ein Fix Excel zerstören würde
„Obwohl es technisch möglich ist, dieses Verhalten so zu korrigieren, dass die aktuellen Versionen von Microsoft Excel nicht davon ausgehen, dass 1900 ein Schaltjahr ist, überwiegen die Nachteile dieser Vorgehensweise gegenüber den Vorteilen”, heißt es in dem Beitrag weiter. Würde Microsoft den 29. Februar 1900 aus Excel entfernen, hätte das weitreichende Folgen. Der 1. März würde von der Seriennummer 61 auf 60 rutschen – und alle Folgetage hätten plötzlich eine andere Seriennummer.
Wenn der Fehler behoben werden würde, müssten sich also alle Datumsangaben in aktuellen Excel-Arbeitsblättern und anderen Dokumenten um einen Tag verschieben. Die Korrektur würde erhebliche Zeit und Mühe erfordern, insbesondere bei Formeln, die Daten verwenden. Einige Funktionen, etwa die für Wochentage, würden dann unterschiedliche Werte zurückgeben, sodass Formeln in Arbeitsblättern möglicherweise nicht mehr korrekt funktionieren.
Außerdem würde die Korrektur die Seriendatumskompatibilität zwischen Excel und anderen Programmen, die Datumswerte verwenden, unterbrechen. Die Vorteile einer Fehlerbehebung wären dagegen deutlich geringer. Der einzige Gewinn bestünde darin, dass der 29. Februar 1900 nicht mehr angezeigt wird. Da dieses Datum aber kaum verwendet wird, sei das Problem extrem selten.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 04.09.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Noch blöder ist, dass die Funktion =kalenderwoche() eine falsche Woche zeigt, falls der 1. Januar nicht in KW 1 liegt. 2027 beginnt KW 1 am 4. Januar, zumindest in Europa. Es sind sogar schon fehlerhafte gedruckte Kalender im Umlauf. In Excel sollte man =isokalenderwoche() verwenden. Im Prinzip müsste man zum Jahresbeginn einen Kalendervergleich mit allen Lieferanten und Auftraggebern durchführen.

articles.title: Anthropic says Claude thwarted bioweapon research from state-sponsored actors — covert accounts used U.S. proxies to attempt to engineer deadlier viruses, tried to evade identification and regional blocks
articles.text:
Anthropic says Claude thwarted bioweapon research from state-sponsored actors — covert accounts used U.S. proxies to attempt to engineer deadlier viruses, tried to evade identification and regional blocks
Plague Inc. could eventually be more than just a game.
These days, AI companies directly or indirectly announcing how their respective wares are smarter than their competitors has become a genre of elevator music. Even so, some in-depth articles can be quite insightful, like Anthropic's occasional reports on attempted misuse of its wares. The latest one covers activity between November 2025 and September 2026, with an important reveal: five situations where Claude was asked to perform work determined to potentially be used in biological weapons.
Right out of the gate, Anthropic remarks on the difficulty of understanding if a particular line of inquiry pertaining to biology is meant for nefarious purposes, to create defense mechanisms like vaccines, or simply to establish predictions of how a virus spreads. The company says that "out of an abundance of caution [....] launched recent models with stronger safeguards."
Among the tens of case studies presented in the lengthy report, Anthropic discusses five cases that it deemed particularly concerning, three regarding viruses, and two more discussing toxins. The common theme across all of them is that all threat actors used varying degrees of anonymization techniques and did their best to evade Anthropic's own regional blocking. The report doesn't mention specific states, but the firm is known to block access to Claude for China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, among others.
In the first case, a request for assistance in developing a grant application involved finding ways to improve the chikungunya virus. The purported researchers were trying to come up with ways to both add extra abilities to chikungunya (increased mutation) and increase its virulence. The topic itself already raised some concern, but Anthropic's hand was forced after finding that although the grant application seemed to be for civilian researchers, the actual investigation was meant to proceed at a military facility.
The firm also found that the request would have gone through a third-party LLM platform associated with military as well as civilian institutions. The countries involved are geo-blocked by Anthropic, and that platform routed comms traffic through the U.S. to try to evade detection, used gray-market resellers, and specifically catered to customers looking to skirt content restrictions. Anthropic banned the accounts in question and shared the information with government authorities, though the same people repeatedly tried reaching Claude again via zero-data-retention services.
Case #2 pertained to a non-US researched who was looking to dig into how avian flu adapts to mammals, and how it can cause diseases other than in the respiratory tract. The problem is that avian flu has a high fatality rate, and there's little population immunity.
While the virus doesn't easily spread from person to person, therein lies the rub — the research could end up discovering mechanisms to increase transmissibility. The researchers used a random username, a private email service, and accessed Claude through a VPS, leading Anthropic to investigate and ultimately turn its nose up at this strain of thought.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The story with the third case bears a resemblance to the previous two. Once again, an account was trying to prepare a supposed grant application, this time around about orthopoxviruses, the family that houses smallpox and Mpox, among others.
The application discussed containment facilities and live experimentation with the viruses, and focused on understanding their genetics for the purpose of evading immunity. The research didn't initially trigger alarms, but Anthropic came to notice it was created via a reselling service, with a randomly-generated email, tunneled through U.S. infrastructure to reach Claude, and traced back to a banned account farm.
In the last two cases, instead of viruses, the purported researchers were focusing on toxins. In case #4, a person mapped out venom toxin peptides from multiple families of animals and created a program to optimize their toxic characteristics.
Although the stated goal was to create painkillers, antidepressants, and other therapeutic molecules, the data would equally allow the creation of potent harmful compounds. Anthropic also came to learn the content Claude was generating was part of a state-sponsored program in an "unsupported region."
In the fifth and final case, a theoretical scientist was also using Claude to try and redesign a set of toxins, also supposedly for therapeutic purposes, under a national public search program. However, the work touched upon "a bacterial toxin subunit and a protein of the hemorrhagic-fever virus" that happens to be on the World Health Organization's list for particularly nasty, pandemic-inducing diseases.
The scientist tried to obscure the subject of the research, directing Claude to be vague about descriptions. Once again, the story ended with Anthropic cutting off access to Claude from a location that broke its terms of service.

He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Does Apple’s Live Rewind really turn the Apple Watch into a ‘mass surveillance device’? Here’s how the new feature works using NATO-grade privacy tech
articles.text:
Is Apple’s Live Rewind a privacy nightmare? Here’s how the Apple Watch feature really works — and whether it violates your privacy
Get the lowdown on the new feature
- Apple debuted a new Apple Watch feature called Live Rewind
- It lets you play back audio from the last 15 seconds
- Some observers are worried it could violate people’s privacy
When Apple announced its Live Rewind feature at its Surprise and Shine event earlier this week, many observers were concerned that it would allow you to secretly record other people without their consent. After all, the tool just requires you to press a button on your Apple Watch and it plays back any audio that was captured during the last 15 seconds.
Is this feature a privacy nightmare, one that turns every Apple Watch into a “mass surveillance device,” as some people have worried? Or have people misunderstood what is happening, with Apple putting enough safeguards in place to prevent abuse and privacy violations?
Social media users seem to be divided, with some calling it “creepy and antisocial,” while others pointed out how it could be useful for deaf people or those with autism. Let’s take a look at the facts to find out what’s really going on.
How does Live Rewind work?
What is this Live Rewind feature that is causing so much consternation? According to Apple, users of the Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 will be able to double-press the Digital Crown and receive a text transcription of what was said over the last 15 seconds. The company says this is useful if you missed something important, are deaf or hard of hearing, or are trying to recall a tip or recommendation from a friend.
Some people have worried that this would allow you to surreptitiously record other people without their knowledge, then save these recordings to your device for nefarious purposes.
However, Apple explained during the event that the feature never records or stores audio, it doesn’t identify anyone’s voice, and audio cannot be accessed by anyone (including Apple). To clarify matters, Apple has published an Audio Intelligence Privacy Overview that lays out how this feature — and Apple’s other new Audio Intelligence tools, including Siri Recap — works in detail.
When it comes to Live Rewind, any audio is processed in the Apple Watch’s Secure Enclave. This is a separate part of the S11 chip that, in this instance, processes audio. The Secure Enclave is siphoned off from the rest of the device and no part of the operating system can access it or the raw audio it handles. That includes both first- and third-party apps, and not even Apple can get to anything in the Secure Enclave.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Apple’s privacy paper notes that audio is never saved or recorded when you use Live Rewind. Instead, the audio is processed by the Secure Enclave and used to generate a transcript, then permanently deleted from both your device and from iCloud. There’s no way anyone can listen to the audio at a later date or extract it from your device.
Audio flows into the Secure Enclave on a rolling basis, which means that old data is continuously overwritten and deleted when new audio comes in. When activated, Live Rewind tries to send the last 15 seconds of audio to your iPhone. If it can’t — such as if your iPhone is not within wireless range — the audio is immediately discarded. If the process is successful, the audio is converted to text on your iPhone, deleted, then the text is sent back to the Secure Enclave in your Apple Watch.
The saved text stays available on your Watch for 30 seconds after the screen dims, after which it is discarded. You can optionally choose to save it to the Siri app, where it is end-to-end encrypted. This is the only instance where something is saved in the Live Rewind process. As mentioned previously, the text does not contain any speaker attribution.
You can ask Siri about your transcripts, at which point the text is sent to Apple’s secure Private Cloud Compute servers. If you use iCloud with two-factor authentication and have secured your device with a passcode, any transcripts from Live Rewind are synced using end-to-end encryption and not even Apple can decrypt them.
Respecting those around you
What about other people? Will they know that you’re using Live Rewind? Can you use the feature secretly?
Thankfully, you can’t really use Live Rewind without anyone knowing. When you double-press the Digital Crown, your Apple Watch plays an audible chime that occurs even if your device is in silent mode or you are listening via headphones. A full-screen animation also plays on screen and the microphone icon is displayed. Whether visually or through sound, your Apple Watch tries to alert other people about what is happening.
Apple also says that Live Rewind is opt-in rather than opt-out, and you can enable it when setting up a new device. You can also enable or disable the feature in Siri Settings on your Apple Watch or in the Siri Settings section of the Apple Watch app on your iPhone.
Although it would be polite to do so, there’s no way for Apple to force you to ask permission before using Live Rewind. But you might take some solace from the fact that there’s no way for anyone to save or extract the audio that the feature uses, nor can they attribute speakers. All a user gets out of it is a text transcript.
These privacy guardrails go some way to distancing Live Rewind from Meta’s so-called “Pervert Glasses” and their consent-busting data collection.

articles.title: Molybdenum Quasi Phase-Only Masks Improve EUV Imaging (NYCU, TSMC)
articles.text:
Home
                        
       			
					
TECHNICAL PAPERS
		
								September 11th, 2026 - 
								By: Technical Paper Link
								
							
						
Researchers at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University and TSMC published a technical paper titled “High contrast EUV imaging enabled by topological quasi phase-only masks.”
Abstract Excerpt: “Here, we propose a paradigm shift in EUV PSM technology by introducing molybdenum (Mo)-based quasi phase-only masks (quasi-POMs) with high reflectivity and minimal absorption. Through rigorous electromagnetic simulations, we demonstrate that Mo quasi-POMs deliver up to 35% higher image contrast, a fivefold increase in common focus window, and 92% lower peak telecentricity error than conventional tantalum (Ta)-based absorbers, enabling 12.5-nm half-pitch resolution for 0.33 numerical aperture (NA) EUV systems with monopole illumination.”
Find the technical paper here. August 2026.
Po-Hsun Fang, Pokai Chang, Chaowei Huang, Lee-Feng Chen, Yen-Liang Chen, and Peichen Yu, “High contrast EUV imaging enabled by topological quasi phase-only masks,” Opt. Express 34, 30091-30105 (2026)

articles.title: Friday Squid Blogging: Rotting Squid on a Beached California Boat - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
Friday Squid Blogging: Rotting Squid on a Beached California Boat
Smells awful:
But an estimated 30 to 50 tons of dead squid remain inside the boat’s catch tank, where they have been decomposing for days. “That is nasty. I wouldn’t want to do that,” said commercial fisherman Dick Ogg of the Bodega Bay Fishermen’s Marketing Association.
Ogg said anyone familiar with the fishing industry understands what happens when a large catch sits for an extended period.
“If you think about what happens after four or five days, it’s a gooey mess,” he said.
The odor has become a defining feature of the operation, and the beach remains closed to the public while crews work on a removal plan.
According to salvage expert Ernie English of Parker Diving Service, the squid has deteriorated into a thick mass that will be difficult to remove.
“It’s like concrete,” English said when asked about its consistency.
As usual, you can also use this squid post to talk about the security stories in the news that I haven’t covered.

articles.title: Kimi-maker Moonshot AI targets $2B in annual revenue | TechCrunch
articles.text:
One of China’s most prominent AI labs, Moonshot AI, believes it can turn its popular open-weight model into serious sales growth. On Friday, Bloomberg reported that the lab is targeting $2 billion in annualized revenue by the end of the year, double the company’s reported revenue run rate for August. It’s an aggressive goal that reflects the success of the company’s K3 model since its release this summer.
While K3’s usage figures have declined slightly in recent months, OpenRouter data currently shows as many as 300 billion tokens being generated each day by K3 models on the system.
Moonshot’s projected revenue is still dwarfed by that of OpenAI and Anthropic, which recent reports put at $40 billion and $65 billion, respectively. Because Moonshot’s model weights are freely available, the company has far lower margins than its closed-weight competitors. The rising projections show there’s still money to be made from open-weight AI models, even if they’re not as lucrative as closed-weight frontier models.
Still, Moonshot’s model development practices remain controversial — if not downright illegal. Earlier this week, Anthropic accused the company of a long-running model distillation campaign that routed nearly 300,000 requests from Kimi directly to Claude Opus, effectively serving Opus in place of Kimi’s own models. In total, more than 23 million responses were collected from Anthropic models for use in Moonshot’s training, the company alleged.

articles.title: Test de la Suunto Run 2 : notre avis complet — Frandroid
articles.text:
Derrière l’hégémonie de Garmin dans le segment des montres de sport et la forte croissance de Coros, la marque finlandaise Suunto parvient peu à peu à tirer son épingle du jeu. Après s’être essentiellement positionnée sur le marché des montres outdoor, elle s’attaque désormais aux montres de running plus classiques.
    Pour aller plus loin
            Quelles sont les meilleures montres connectées de sport en 2026 ?
            
Avec la Suunto Run 2, le constructeur propose une montre conçue pour l’analyse des performances en course sur route, avec un vrai argument, la cartographie locale au poignet, pour un prix bien plus accessible que la concurrence. Voici le test complet de la Suunto Run 2.
Suunto Run 2Fiche technique
| Modèle | Suunto Run 2 | 
|---|---|
| Dimensions | 46 mm x 46 mm x 11,7 mm | 
| Définition de l’écran | 466 x 466 pixels | 
| Dalle | AMOLED | 
| Mémoire interne | 4, 64 Go | 
| Poids | 35 g | 
| Accéléromètre et boussole électronique | Oui | 
| Analyse du sommeil | Oui | 
| Capteur de lumière ambiante | Oui | 
| Indice de protection | 5ATM | 
|  | Fiche produit | 
La montre de ce test nous a été fournie par le constructeur.
Suunto Run 2Une montre au design à la fois sobre et très marqué
La Suunto Run 2 est la deuxième montre du constructeur à viser le segment de la course sur route, c’est-à-dire du 5 km au marathon. Le premier modèle de la marque, la Suunto Run, est sorti plutôt récemment, en mai 2025, et il paraît donc logique que le constructeur n’ait pas réinventé la roue.
On a droit ici à une montre particulièrement similaire à la première Suunto Run. La Suunto Run 2 reprend donc le même design minimaliste qui fait la signature de la marque finlandaise. On a à nouveau droit à un unique format de 46 mm de diamètre pour une épaisseur de 11,7 mm. Il en va de même du côté des matériaux avec une lunette en acier inoxydable plutôt bienvenue autour de l’écran pour éviter les rayures, ainsi qu’un verre Gorilla Glass.
À l’usage, la Suunto Run 2 se porte plutôt confortablement. Dans mon cas, c’est la première montre Suunto que j’ai eu l’occasion de tester et son format n’est pas sans me rappeler celui de la Coros Pace Pro ou de la Garmin Forerunner 570, notamment par l’utilisation de métal autour de la dalle. Au poignet, la Suunto Run 2 n’est pas trop large et offre un bon compromis entre les montres de trail, bien plus massives, et les montres de running parfois trop petites. De même, le poids de 53 g avec bracelet, est plutôt bien géré et je n’ai jamais eu l’impression que le contact se perdait entre la montre et ma peau lors de mes séances de running.
À titre de comparaison, la Coros Pace Pro affiche quant à elle un poids de 49 grammes avec bracelet, la Coros Pace 4, plus petite, de 40 grammes et la Garmin Forerunner 570 de 50 grammes.
La Suunto Run 2 propose par ailleurs un système de bracelet standard. La montre est fournie par défaut avec un bracelet en silicone, mais on pourra cependant facilement en changer et le remplacer par un bracelet de 22 mm de large avec pompe à relâchement rapide. Le bracelet fourni est d’ailleurs le principal point que je reprocherais à la Run 2, avec son fermoir qui a trop tendance à se détacher et à pendre en l’absence de passant.
Pour le reste, on est sur du très classique, avec une montre dotée de trois boutons positionnés sur la droite du boîtier, dont une couronne rotative au milieu. On notera l’absence de micro et de haut-parleur, sur laquelle on reviendra plus tard, ainsi que les nombreux marquages « Suunto » plus ou moins discrets : sur le bracelet en lui-même, sur le bas du boîtier, en argenté, et même sur le côté gauche, gravé directement dans le boîtier. Ce n’est pas nécessairement des plus discrets, mais, à l’usage, ça ne gêne nullement.
Notons enfin que la Suunto Run 2 est certifiée 5 ATM et qu’elle pourra donc être portée sans crainte sous la douche, en faisant la vaisselle, voire pour de la natation en piscine à condition de rester en surface.
Suunto Run 2Un écran confortable et lumineux
L’une des principales nouveautés de la Suunto Run 2 par rapport au modèle précédent concerne l’affichage. Si le constructeur a conservé un affichage Amoled sur sa montre connectée, comme c’était déjà le cas sur les Suunto Vertical 2 et Race 2, on retrouve cette fois un écran bien plus lumineux.
Concrètement, Suunto indique que sa montre peut désormais monter à un pic de luminosité de 2000 cd/m², contre 600 cd/m² sur la première Suunto Run. À titre de comparaison, c’est la même luminosité maximale que la Garmin Fenix 9, l’Amazfit Balance 2 ou l’Apple Watch Series 11. Pour une montre de sport d’entrée de gamme, c’est particulièrement confortable et on pourra consulter ses données sans peine en entraînement, que ce soit de nuit ou en plein soleil estival.
    Pour aller plus loin
            Écran Amoled ou MIP transflectif : quelle est la meilleure technologie d’affichage pour les montres de sport
            
Notons par ailleurs que la montre est équipée d’un capteur de luminosité automatique et qu’elle pourra donc adapter automatiquement l’éclairage de l’écran à votre environnement.
Pour le reste, la Suunto Run 2 conserve les mêmes caractéristiques d’affichage que la Suunto Run, à savoir un écran de 1,32 pouce de diamètre avec un affichage de 466 x 466 pixels. Concrètement, cela offre une densité de 353 pixels par pouce largement suffisante pour consulter l’écran sans être gêné par des pixels visibles individuellement. À titre de comparaison, les écrans dits « Retina » des Apple Watch sont quant à eux normés à 326 pixels par pouce. Toujours du côté des chiffres, on notera les larges bordures autour de l’écran avec un affichage qui n’occupe que 53 % de la surface du boîtier. C’est peu et on aurait apprécié profiter d’un affichage plus large compte tenu du format tout de même conséquent de la montre.
Suunto propose aussi un mode d’affichage always-on pour garder en permanence certaines données affichées à l’écran. Une fonction non seulement esthétique, mais aussi bien pratique pour consulter discrètement l’heure sans avoir à lever ostensiblement le poignet face à votre interlocuteur.
Il est aussi possible de basculer la montre en mode sommeil sur certaines plages horaires, par exemple de nuit. Dès lors, ce mode va automatiquement désactiver l’affichage always-on ainsi que le paramètre allumant l’écran lorsqu’on lève le bras. Bien pratique pour éviter d’être ébloui durant le sommeil alors qu’on a levé malencontreusement la main trop près de ses yeux.
Du côté des cadrans, la Suunto Run 2 est fournie d’emblée avec un cadran digital dont on pourra modifier la teinte et les complications. Néanmoins, sur son application mobile, Suunto propose de télécharger près d’une cinquantaine de cadrans supplémentaires, tous gratuits. On pourra aussi créer son propre cadran à l’aide d’une photo, du choix de police pour l’heure et des complications que l’on souhaite.
Suunto Run 2Une montre pensée avant tout pour le sport
Comme toutes les montres de Suunto, la Run 2 est compatible à la fois avec les iPhone et avec les smartphones Android. Pour appairer la montre avec votre téléphone, il vous faudra, sans grande surprise, installer l’application Suunto.
Pour la navigation au sein de la montre, la Suunto Run 2 se contrôle à l’aide des trois boutons latéraux, dont la couronne rotative, et de l’écran tactile avec les gestes suivants :
- glissement vers le haut / le bas / rotation de la couronne : accès aux widgets ;
- glissement vers la gauche / appui sur la couronne : accès aux profils d’entraînement sportif ;
- appui sur le bouton supérieur droit : accès à la dernière activité lancée (personnalisable) ;
- appui sur le bouton inférieur droit : retour en arrière.
On pourra en outre ajouter ou modifier les raccourcis sur les boutons supérieur et inférieur, que ce soit pour l’appui court ou l’appui long. Par exemple, la Suunto Run 2 permet d’ouvrir le panneau de configuration, pour les paramètres rapides, via un appui court sur le bouton inférieur lorsqu’on est sur le cadran. On peut aussi lancer une application spécifique, comme le suivi de la fréquence cardiaque, la météo ou le lecteur multimédia à partir de l’appui long sur le bouton supérieur.
Dans l’ensemble, on a ici une interface assez similaire à celle que l’on peut retrouver sur des montres de sport concurrentes comme chez Garmin, Coros ou Suunto, basée sur les widgets de données. La Suunto Run 2 étant la première montre de la marque que j’ai eu l’occasion de porter, je dois cependant avouer avoir eu un peu de mal à m’y retrouver. Pour accéder à l’ensemble des applications, il faut par exemple nécessairement faire défiler la liste des widgets. Dommage, un raccourci pour ouvrir uniquement les applications préinstallées aurait été plus pratique.
En outre, signalons que Suunto ne propose aucune application tierce et qu’il n’est donc pas possible d’étendre les fonctions de la Run 2 en installant davantage d’applications ou de champs de données. C’est d’autant plus dommage que la marque finlandaise propose sa boutique d’applications SuuntoPlus sur des montres plus hautes en gamme. À défaut, on se consolera avec la possibilité de recevoir les notifications venues de son smartphone pour être alerté en cas de message WhatsApp ou d’appel téléphonique. La montre permet aussi de stocker directement de la musique que vous pourrez ensuite écouter sur un casque ou des écouteurs connectés en Bluetooth, avec 4 ou 64 Go de stockage proposé selon le modèle de montre.
Néanmoins, la Suunto Run 2 n’intégrant pas de haut-parleur ni de microphone, elle ne pourra pas servir pour passer ou recevoir des appels téléphoniques. De la même manière, elle n’intègre pas de lampe-torche et ne profite pas non plus de puce NFC pour le paiement sans contact.
Suunto Run 2Une précision redoutable pour les données sportives
La Suunto Run 2 profite de l’attirail classique des montres de sport en matière de capteurs. On retrouve ainsi un capteur optique de fréquence cardiaque, un oxymètre de pouls optique, un gyroscope, un accéléromètre, une boussole, un altimètre barométrique et un suivi GPS autonome. La montre ne propose cependant pas d’électrocardiogramme.
La précision du GPS de la Suunto Run 2
Pour le suivi de géolocalisation durant les entraînements, qui permet de mesurer la distance parcourue, les tracés et la vitesse, Suunto propose ici une puce compatible multi-GNSS (GPS, Galileo, Glonass, Beidou et QZSS) et GPS double-fréquence.
Concrètement, la Suunto Run 2 profite donc de ce qui se fait de mieux sur le marché en termes de suivi GPS, avec des caractéristiques devant assurer, en théorie, un suivi GPS fiable aussi bien sur des routes droites et dégagées qu’en ville malgré les immeubles.
    Pour aller plus loin
            GPS, GNSS, double-fréquence : tout comprendre à la géolocalisation des smartphones et montres connectées
            
Pour évaluer la fiabilité du suivi GPS de la Suunto Run 2, je l’ai portée à mon poignet gauche lors de plusieurs sessions de course à pied, aussi bien dans un parc qu’en ville ou sur piste d’athlétisme – sans activer le mode piste dédié. J’ai ensuite comparé les distances et les tracés à ceux d’une montre outdoor haut de gamme, la Garmin Fenix 8.
| Courses | Garmin Fenix 8 | Suunto Run 2 | Écart | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Course 1 (piste) | 11,956 km | 11,980 km | +0,20 % | 
| Course 2 (parc) | 17,117 km | 17,078 km | -0,23 % | 
| Course 3 (ville) | 7,429 km | 7,367 km | -0,83 % | 
| Course 4 (parc) | 8,665 km | 8,659 km | -0,07 % | 
| Course 5 (ville) | 12,547 km | 12,564 km | +0,14 % | 
| Course 6 (ville) | 9,595 km | 9,501 km | -0,98 % | 
| Course 7 (parc) | 8,818 km | 8,795 km | -0,26 % | 
| Total | 76,127 km | 75,944 km | -0,24 % | 
On le constate déjà sur les distances, la Suunto Run 2 propose un suivi très proche de celui de la Garmin Fenix 8, avec un écart total de moins de 200 m sur plus de 75 km, que l’on considérera comme marginal. Il n’y a finalement que sur quelques séances en ville que l’écart augmente entre les deux montres.
Comme on le voit sur les tracés ci-dessus, les différences ne sont par ailleurs pas nécessairement aux dépens de la Suunto Run 2. Sur le tracé en ville, la montre de Suunto s’en sort même mieux que la Garmin Fenix 8, notamment avec des virages plus serrés et plus proches du tracé réellement effectué.
En outre, l’une des principales nouveautés de la Suunto Run 2 réside dans sa cartographie. Alors que la première Suunto Run en était dépourvue, la Run 2 va vous permettre d’afficher un véritable fond de carte pour vous aider à vous repérer dans votre itinéraire. Une fonction pratique non seulement en trail ou en randonnée, mais aussi en course à pied en ville pour savoir comment rejoindre au mieux un point donné. Sur le segment des montres de sport, à l’exception d’Amazfit, rares sont encore les marques à proposer une telle fonction sur un modèle à moins de 300 euros.
On notera tout de même que Coros a récemment mis à jour sa Coros Pace 4, positionnée sur le même segment de prix et le même créneau de la course sur route, afin qu’elle profite elle aussi de la cartographie en local.
La précision de la fréquence cardiaque de la Suunto Run 2
La Suunto Run 2 inaugure un tout nouveau capteur cardio optique chez la marque finlandaise, avec douze canaux. On a droit ainsi non seulement à un capteur plus avancé que celui de la Suunto Run de première génération, mais aussi différent de celui des dernières Suunto Vertical 2 et Suunto Race 2. D’ailleurs, le positionnement des diodes et des capteurs n’est pas sans rappeler celui du capteur Elevate Gen 5 des montres Garmin.
Afin d’évaluer la précision du capteur cardio de la montre, je l’ai portée à mon poignet durant plusieurs séances de course à pied. D’abord sur un footing à intensité constante, puis sur une séance de seuil avec des intervalles longs et enfin sur une séance de VMA avec de fortes variations d’allures plutôt courtes.
    Pour aller plus loin
            Montre de sport, ceinture cardio, brassard… comment mesurer précisément votre fréquence cardiaque durant le sport
            
J’ai ensuite comparé les données et les courbes de fréquences cardiaque à celles d’une ceinture cardio à électrodes portée en même temps, la Garmin HRM 600, qui me sert ici de référence.
| Mesure FC | Ceinture cardio | Suunto Run 2 | Écart moyen | Écart moyen après 10 min | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FC moyenne | 143 bpm | 143 bpm | -0,12 % | 0,00 % | 
| FC max | 151 bpm | 150 bpm |  |  | 
| Mesure FC | Ceinture cardio | Suunto Run 2 | Écart moyen | Écart moyen après 10 min | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FC moyenne | 156 bpm | 156 bpm | -0,21 % | -0,20 % | 
| FC max | 187 bpm | 185 bpm |  |  | 
| Mesure FC | Ceinture cardio | Suunto Run 2 | Écart moyen | Écart moyen après 10 min | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FC moyenne | 153 bpm | 153 bpm | -0,12 % | -0,06 % | 
| FC max | 186 bpm | 185 bpm |  |  | 
Dans les faits, la Suunto Run 2 propose un suivi particulièrement précis de la fréquence cardiaque en course à pied, et ce quel que soit le type d’exercice, avec un écart minime par rapport à la ceinture basée sur un électrocardiogramme. Il n’y a finalement que sur la séance de seuil que la montre a légèrement décroché au début du deuxième intervalle, mais elle a su rapidement se raccrocher à la fréquence cardiaque réelle.
Rappelons néanmoins que la mesure de la fréquence cardiaque au poignet est soumise à de nombreux aléas entre la taille du poignet, la présence de tatouage ou même la température en extérieur, avec des vaisseaux sanguins qui vont se contracter avec le froid hivernal et rendre l’analyse plus difficile. Heureusement, la montre de Suunto permet de connecter des capteurs tiers, qu’il s’agisse d’une ceinture ou d’un brassard, pour compenser.
Les fonctions de sport et santé de la Suunto Run 2
Alors que les gammes Race et Vertical chez Suunto sont pensées avant tout pour le trail, la gamme Run était jusqu’à présent conçue pour la course sur route. Du moins c’était le cas de la première génération.
Avec sa Suunto Run 2, le constructeur propose désormais des fonctions également orientées vers le trail. On l’a vu, c’est le cas notamment de la cartographie intégrée, mais aussi de la fonction Climb Guidance qui, lorsque vous avez sélectionné un itinéraire, va vous indiquer le profil, le dénivelé et où vous vous situez dans la côte, à la manière de la fonction ClimbPro chez Garmin.
La Suunto Run 2 inaugure aussi une nouvelle fonction « EnergySense » censée analyser votre réserve d’énergie durant une course en fonction de l’intensité que vous y mettez. Cette fonction, censée vous aider à ajuster au mieux votre allure, se rapproche sur le papier de l’indice « Stamina » chez Garmin. Dans les faits, je n’ai cependant pas réussi à la trouver parmi les champs de données de la montre et n’ai donc pas pu la tester.
La Suunto Run 2 intègre par ailleurs un nouveau mode d’entraînement dit « marathon ». Malgré son nom, il s’agit surtout d’un mode dédié au jour de course, que ce soit sur 42,2 km, 21,1 km, 10 km ou 5 km. Concrètement, ce mode intègre une prévision de temps de course en fonction de votre allure pour vous indiquer, à tout moment, le temps sur lequel vous pouvez tabler en fonction de votre allure moyenne durant la course.
En outre, comme toutes les montres de Suunto, la Run 2 profite des différentes analyses de charge d’entraînement avec le TSS pour la charge d’entraînement sur une séance, le CTL pour la charge d’entraînement à long terme sur 42 jours, l’ATL pour la fatigue à court terme et le TSB pour savoir si son état de forme est supérieur à la fatigue engendrée par l’entraînement.
Bien évidemment, la Suunto Run 2 propose aussi une mesure de la SpO2 ainsi qu’un suivi du sommeil et de la VFC durant la nuit. En revanche, comme on l’a vu plus tôt, elle n’intègre pas d’électrocardiogramme.
Suunto Run 2Une autonomie de près de six jours en usage intense
Du côté de l’autonomie, malgré un boîtier de taille identique, Suunto indique avoir intégré une batterie de 380 mAh sur sa Run 2, contre 295 mAh pour le premier modèle, soit une augmentation de la capacité de l’ordre de 29 %.
D’après le constructeur, la montre serait ainsi capable d’atteindre environ dix jours d’autonomie ou 24 heures en suivi GNSS double-fréquence.
De mon côté, comme sur tous les tests de montre connectée sur Frandroid, j’ai poussé la montre dans ses retranchements, en activant tous les paramètres. J’ai ainsi opté pour un affichage always-on de 9h à 23h et un mode sommeil la nuit, activé le suivi du sommeil, de la SpO2 et de la VFC durant la nuit et activé le suivi de la fréquence cardiaque 24 heures sur 24. En outre, pour les entraînements sportifs en extérieur, j’ai paramétré le mode batterie « performance », soit le plus précis, mais le plus énergivore.
Avec tous ces paramètres, j’ai pu porter la montre durant cinq jours et 19 heures avant qu’elle ne passe de 100 à 0 % de batterie. Sur cette période, je l’ai par ailleurs utilisée à trois reprises pour des entraînements de course à pied, soit 3 heures et 28 minutes de suivi multi-GNSS double fréquence.
Pour la recharge, Suunto fournit le même chargeur sur sa Run 2 que sur la Vertical 2 et la Race 2, doté de son propre câble avec embout USB-C. Malheureusement, le câble fourni, de 51 cm, est un peu court. J’aurais aimé un câble plus long ou, à défaut, la possibilité de pouvoir brancher mon propre câble USB-C directement au socle de charge.
Pour une charge complète de 0 à 100 % d’autonomie, il faudra compter sur un peu plus d’une heure et quart.
Suunto Run 2Appel et communication
Comme on l’a vu plus tôt, la Suunto Run 2 n’intègre ni micro, ni haut-parleur. Elle ne peut donc pas être utilisée pour passer ou recevoir des appels téléphoniques.
La montre se connecte au smartphone en passant par une connexion Bluetooth. Elle peut par ailleurs se connecter au réseau Wi-Fi, notamment pour le téléchargement de la cartographie ou des mises à jour logicielles.
En outre, la montre intègre une connectivité multi-GNSS double fréquence pour le suivi de géolocalisation, avec une compatibilité avec les constellations GPS, Galileo, Glonass, Beidou et QZSS.
Enfin, la Suunto Run 2 ne propose aucune puce NFC et ne pourra donc pas être utilisée pour le paiement sans contact. De la même manière, la montre n’embarque pas de puce e-SIM et ne pourra donc pas se connecter au réseau 4G.
Suunto Run 2Prix et date de sortie
La Suunto Run 2 est disponible en France depuis ce mardi 8 septembre 2026. La montre n’est proposée qu’en une seule taille, de 46 mm, mais déclinée en trois coloris : noir avec bracelet noir, noir avec bracelet vert ou doré avec bracelet blanc.
Par ailleurs, la Suunto Run 2 est déclinée en deux modèles selon le stockage pour la musique et la cartographie. La version 4 Go est affichée à 299 euros et la version 64 Go est proposée à 349 euros.

articles.title: Regulatory AI company Ultimarii raises $13-million Series A round | BetaKit
articles.text:
Calgary-based regulatory AI company Ultimarii has raised a Series A worth more than $13 million CAD.
The news: Ultimarii made the announcement on Thursday, saying it had raised the Series A with equity investment support from the Business Development Bank of Canada’s (BDC) Industrial Innovation Venture Fund, Mistral Venture Partners, Staircase Ventures, Alpaca VC, and more than 30 angel investors. The round also included debt financing and non-dilutive funding from the National Research Council of Canada’s Industrial Research Assistance Program.
From the source: “Ultimarii has been built around the premise that North America cannot build infrastructure at the speed and scale required without modernizing the systems used to approve it,” the company, which uses AI to navigate and streamline application and permitting processes, said in a statement.
The context: With more than $18 million CAD in total capital raised to date, and customers across national and provincial governments, oil and gas, mining, energy production, and major utility operators, Ultimarii’s Series A financing will go toward expanding the company’s regulatory intelligence platform across Canada and the United States. Additionally, Ultimarii said it would use the new capital to substantially expand its regulatory infrastructure, with a particular focus on building deeper data sets around US-based regulatory frameworks, including the Environmental Protection Agency, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, and the Texas Railroad Commission.
Final thought: Investment in Ultimarii comes at a moment when Canada is navigating a glut of planned nation-building infrastructure projects, all of which will come with unique regulatory and permitting requirements to be successful. That’s creating an opportunity for Ultimarii to position itself as the behind-the-scenes solution that can speed up and streamline projects at a moment when government and business in Canada are focused on delivering on projects needed to shore up sovereignty and energy security.

articles.title: The Download: biotech’s future and cheaper, cleaner steel
articles.text:
The Download: biotech’s future and cheaper, cleaner steel
Plus: Anthropic says it has blocked potential plots to build biological weapons.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Meet the under-35s shaping the future of biotech
Every year, MIT Technology Review puts together our 35 Innovators Under 35, a list of some of the brightest and best young minds working across science and technology. This year’s honorees include nine people transforming biotech, whose work spans everything from lifesaving innovations to groundbreaking longevity tech.
Their innovations include a “reprogramming” therapy that reverses vision loss, tiny brain electrodes inspired by Japanese art, and a personalized gene-editing treatment for a baby with a rare genetic disorder. There are even efforts to design new viruses with generative AI, which (hopefully) will produce new drugs or soak up pollution.
Get to know the biotech innovators behind these breakthroughs.
—Jessica Hamzelou
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.
Biotechnology is one of four categories in our 35 Innovators Under 35 list for 2026, featuring young people worldwide doing groundbreaking work in science and technology. Meet the rest of them here, or explore the full list across the AI, computing and robotics, biotechnology, and climate and energy categories.
This founder is making cheaper, cleaner steel
The steel industry isn’t exactly known for innovation. Very little has changed about purifying iron ore since the process was invented and commercialized in the 1850s. But Laureen Meroueh, founder of Hertha Metals, has an idea that could change that.
Meroueh may have found a way to clean up steelmaking without driving up the price. Her new furnace turns iron ore into refined liquid steel in a single step and swaps coal for natural gas. Together, those changes slash emissions by at least half, she says, and cut costs by 25% compared with steelmaking as usual.
Here’s how she plans to make steel cleaner without making it more expensive.
—Bridget Reed Morawski
Laureen Meroueh is one of the climate change and energy honorees on our 35 Innovators Under 35 list.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Anthropic says it has blocked potential plots to build biological weapons
The company identified five such cases. (NYT $)
+ And six cases of using AI to build software for conventional weapons (BBC)
+ Governments are also using Claude for surveillance.(Axios)
+ While Russia-linked hackers used it to automate attacks on Ukraine. (Quartz)
+ The threats were revealed in a new Anthropic report. (Guardian)
+ Bill Gates says AI needs new guardrails. (MIT Technology Review)
2 California has banned addictive social media features for under-16s
The law prohibits infinite scroll and autoplay. (Guardian)
+ It also introduces new rules for AI and companion chatbots. (Reuters $)
+ It’s the first law of its kind in the US. (NYT $)
+ Social media encourages the worst AI boosterism. (MIT Technology Review)
3 Two AI researchers have left Anthropic and Google over safety risks
They left a day after Jacob Coxon’s viral departure from Anthropic. (NBC News)
+ Elon Musk called their concerns a “setup” and a “psyop.” (Guardian)
+ AI fears are pushing Congress toward tougher regulation. (WSJ $)
4 Sam Altman is pitching OpenAI’s cyber defenses to power companies
The meetings followed reports of AI attacks on critical systems. (Politico $)
+ Altman also told staff that OpenAI is open to slowing down AI. Bloomberg $)
5 After years of fighting AI, music labels are starting to embrace it
Universal is partnering with ElevenLabs on an AI remix platform.(Gizmodo)
+ AI is complicating definitions of creativity. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Chinese drugmakers are challenging US dominance in weight-loss drugs
They’re developing hundreds of GLP-1 treatments for global markets. (WSJ $)
7 Electric air taxis have begun official test flights in Texas
They’re the first flights under the White House’s new pilot program. (Verge)
8 Chinese drones are helping to rescue survivors of Nepal's floods
They’re delivering food and airlifting bodies from flood-hit areas. (Ars Technica)
9 NASA and IBM have built an AI model to map the moon
It could help locate ice and identify safer landing sites. (Register)
10 One man is on a quest to digitally preserve America’s public restrooms
His Restroom Archive is a museum-style repository of 3D scans. (404 Media)
Quote of the day
“I didn't ask Facebook to build a profile of my family—I posted a video of me singing in the car with my kids.”
—Kalie Roberts, a travel content creator, says in an Instagram reel that Meta AI used years of Facebook posts to piece together her children’s identities and pinpoint where her family lives.
One more thing
Chinese tech workers are starting to train their AI doubles—and pushing back
  In April, a GitHub project called Colleague Skill struck a nerve by claiming to “distill” a worker’s skills and personality—and replicate them with an AI agent. Though the project was a spoof, it prompted a wave of soul-searching among otherwise enthusiastic early adopters.
A number of tech workers told MIT Technology Review that their bosses are already encouraging them to document their workflows for automation via tools like OpenClaw. Many now fear that they are being flattened into code and losing their professional identity.
In response, some are fighting back with tools designed to sabotage the automation process. Read the full story on their battle with clone workers.
—Caiwei Chen
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ Worried about Flock cameras? These guys designed a car to fool them.
+ Webb’s Near-Infrared Camera has captured a galactic merger’s dazzling final phase.
+ An exquisitely preserved 66-million-year-old bird feather was found in a fossilised dinosaur dropping.
