articles.title: Kiteworks Acquires Bonfy.AI to Fill the AI Gap in Data Governance
articles.text:
Kiteworks has announced the acquisition of AI data security company Bonfy.AI, a move aimed at extending real-time policy enforcement over sensitive data exchanged by both human users and AI agents.
Kiteworks delivers a content-sharing platform to safeguard sensitive data as it moves across enterprise networks, external organizations, and internal systems. It includes regulatory compliance, governance, and audit tracking.
Bonfy.ai is an AI‑native content‑security platform protecting sensitive data across human workflows and AI‑agent reasoning. It offers real‑time classification, contextual enforcement, and cross‑SaaS governance.
The cost of the acquisition has not been disclosed but is estimated by CTech at ‘tens of millions of dollars’.
The Bonfy technology will be used to extend Kiteworks’ policy enforcement across agent and human data exchange and usage in real time and inline across email, file sharing, SaaS applications, data repositories, Internet-facing AI assistants, and autonomous agents.
It fills, says Kiteworks, a structural gap in how enterprises protect sensitive data. Enterprises have detailed inventories of their sensitive data, but the inventories do not necessarily control what happens to that sensitive data when it is used or transferred. Bonfy technology fills this gap by classifying the data at the moment it is exchanged, and applying security policies before the transfer is completed – including when the exchange involves an AI assistant or autonomous agent.
Combining this technology with the Kiteworks control plane for secure data exchange, says Kiteworks, governs data in motion and in use through a single policy model that applies equally to people, machines, and systems across the enterprise.
“Bonfy.AI’s cutting-edge technology expands our coverage and capability to deliver the control our customers need in the AI era, and its excellent team will further accelerate the development of our unified Data Control Plane,” suggests Amit Toren, chief business officer at Kiteworks.
This is the eighth Kiteworks acquisition in five years, with each one designed to expand the firm’s data security and compliance platform.
The value of this acquisition includes a governed decision inline at runtime rather than a report after the fact; decisions based on genuine context rather than simple pattern matching; a single policy model for both human and AI workflows; enterprise-wide data exchange control; and provable compliance at the moment of decision. It becomes an extension of Kiteworks rather than a parallel product.
“Everything we build comes back to a single promise to our customers: you stay in control of your private data, everywhere it moves and everywhere it is used,” comments Tim Freestone, chief strategy officer at Kiteworks. “Inline at runtime classification is what makes that promise complete. Knowing where sensitive data lives is part of the equation, but deciding, in the instant data leaves, whether it should leave, and being able to prove that decision to a regulator months later is a big gap we’re closing.”
Bonfy was founded in early 2024 by Gidi Cohen and Danny Kibel. It emerged from stealth in June 2025 with $9.5 million in seed funding. “We built Bonfy.AI around a single idea: risk is created when data moves, not when it sits, and controlling it means reading the full context of an exchange at runtime, before it completes,” said CEO Cohen. “Kiteworks gives that technology a control plane and a reach we could not have built on our own. I’m excited to see it governing data for both people and AI agents at global scale.”

articles.title: Madrid se ha empeñado en levantar un gigantesco parque encima de la M-30: con 16.370 metros cuadrados de jardín, ya está al 70%
articles.text:
Las obras del Parque Ventas se acercan a su fin. Y es que este macroproyecto de 16.370 metros cuadrados que se está construyendo directamente sobre la M-30 ya ha superado el 70 % de su ejecución, según ha informado el Ayuntamiento de Madrid tras la visita a las obras esta semana por el alcalde, José Luis Martínez-Almeida.
Barrios divididos. Durante décadas, la M-30 era lo que ha separado a los distritos de Salamanca y Ciudad Lineal con sus 16 carriles de tráfico. El Parque Ventas pretende borrar esta división cubriendo un tramo de la autopista con una plataforma ajardinada sobre la que los vecinos podrán pasear por encima de la autopista y sin notarla bajo sus pies.
En detalle. El parque en sí se extiende a lo largo de 197 metros y se situará a unos 300 metros al sur del actual puente de Ventas. Según cuentan desde El Economista, el Ayuntamiento eligió esta ubicación específicamente para evitar la demolición de los ramales de conexión de la M-30 con la calle de Alcalá y para esquivar toda la infraestructura subterránea del Metro y el depósito de agua del Canal de Isabel II. Además, que el tramo de la autovía discurra en zanja por debajo del nivel de la calle también ha facilitado las obras desde el punto de vista técnico.
Los trabajos se centran actualmente en acabar con el alcantarillado, el sistema eléctrico, agua potable, riego y telecomunicaciones, mientras que el relleno de tierra sobre la plataforma ya alcanza el 80 %. De las ocho pasarelas peatonales que conectarán el parque con ambos barrios, las cuatro del lado de Salamanca ya están unidas a la plataforma, y los operarios están terminando ahora las cuatro que quedan por el lado de Ciudad Lineal, junto con una ruta ciclista que cruzará a por la pasarela de Ramón de Aguinaga.
En el lado de Salamanca, las obras están prácticamente terminadas, con la mayor parte del mobiliario urbano y los nuevos parterres colocados. En el lado de Ciudad Lineal se está reorganizando el parque de Antonio Pirala, y está previsto que los trabajos de impermeabilización de uno de los aparcamientos para residentes comiencen a finales de este mes.
En cifras. El proyecto cuenta con un presupuesto de 78,9 millones de euros. Una vez finalizado, incluirá 960 árboles nuevos, más de 48.800 arbustos y más de 2.150 metros cuadrados de pradera, junto con equipamiento de calistenia, dos quioscos, fuentes, bancos y una zona de actuaciones al aire libre con gradas bajas. Y ya no solo es el parque, sino que las mejoras a ambos lados de la autovía abarcarán unos 40.300 metros cuadrados adicionales, lo que hace que la superficie total de actuación alcance los 56.600 metros cuadrados.
Un parque infantil temático de osos. Tal y como cuenta el propio Ayuntamiento, una de las particularidades más destacadas del parque es una zona infantil que posee varias estructuras de juegos de madera con forma de osos, que se supone que hace referencia al símbolo de Madrid del Oso y el Madroño.
La instalación incluirá una torre de escalada con redes de cuerda, un tobogán tubular de 4,8 metros de altura y una rampa y tobogán diseñados para niños con diferentes niveles de movilidad.
No exento de polémica. El proyecto no ha estado libre de polémica. Y es que según El Diario, las asociaciones vecinales de ambos distritos, junto con Ecologistas en Acción y la Plataforma por el Derecho a la Ciudad, emitieron un comunicado conjunto oponiéndose a las obras cuando estas comenzaron, alegando el elevado coste del proyecto y su impacto ambiental, incluida la tala de árboles.
El Ayuntamiento tiene como objetivo concluir las obras en la primavera de 2027, por lo que tendremos que esperar un poco para ver el resultado final.

articles.title: Des ambulances pour robots humanoïdes ? Ça existe déjà au Japon pour réparer et remplacer les modèles défaillants
articles.text:
Des ambulances pour robots humanoïdes ? Ça existe déjà au Japon pour réparer et remplacer les modèles défaillants
Au Japon, un véhicule inédit permet de réparer très rapidement les robots humanoïdes en panne et de fournir sans délai un modèle de remplacement temporaire.
Les rues de Tokyo s’apprêtent à accueillir une ambulance futuriste, non pas pour les humains, mais pour les robots humanoïdes. Son but est simple : réparer les modèles en panne avec un véritable atelier ambulant équipé de toutes les pièces nécessaires. En prime, un humanoïde de secours sera prêt à prendre la relève sur le terrain le temps de l’intervention. Après l’ère de l’intelligence artificielle, celle des robots s’amorce à vitesse grand V.
Ambulance pour robots humanoïdes au Japon : l'atelier mobile de GMO Air
Imaginé par l’entreprise GMO Air, spécialisée dans l’IA et la robotique, ce nouveau véhicule conserve le gabarit d’une ambulance, mais avec des gyrophares violets plus discrets et un immense visage de robot sur la carrosserie. À bord, l’habitacle fait office d’atelier, embarquant des ordinateurs, des équipements spécialisés et des pièces mécaniques pour remettre sur pied les robots humanoïdes.
Tout cet arsenal répond ainsi à un impératif clair et grandissant, celui d’éviter les interruptions d’activité quand une machine doit être expédiée loin de son poste pour une réparation majeure. “En tirant les leçons de cette expérience, nous avons eu l’idée de fournir des humanoïdes de remplacement”, ajoute Tomohiro Uchida, directeur général de GMO Air.
	
Quand les humanoïdes seront plus répandus, ce type de service sera nécessaire.
Si la panne ne peut être réparée sur place, l’appareil endommagé part en atelier pendant que son remplaçant prend immédiatement le relais. Comme le précise l’ingénieur Shota Takizawa, “l’ambulance pour humanoïdes transporte l’humanoïde de remplacement jusqu’au site et le substitue à l’humanoïde endommagé”.
L’essor des humanoïdes : un marché de la robotique à 370 milliards de dollars
Pour le moment, un seul véhicule est basé au siège tokyoïte de GMO, mais l’entreprise prévoit déjà d’accroître sa flotte si la demande progresse. Il faut dire que la compétition sur le marché de la robotique est digne de celle de l’IA. Bien que son déploiement n’en soit qu’à ses débuts, tout le monde veut tirer au plus vite son épingle du jeu pour conquérir toujours plus de clients. Le cabinet McKinsey estime d’ailleurs que ce marché pourrait atteindre 370 milliards de dollars d’ici 2040.
Face aux géants chinois et étasuniens, Tokyo compte déjà déployer près de 10 millions de robots d’ici 2040 dans 18 secteurs, de la santé à l’industrie. Pour tenir ce rythme sans paralyser les chaînes de travail, dépanner sur place n’est plus un gadget, mais une obligation.

Crystal Lake is the highly anticipated Friday the 13th prequel series coming to Peacock and Sky. Horror fans around the world, including me, have been counting down the days to this one as we dive into some famous slasher lore.
The series will put the spotlight on Jason's mother, Pam (Linda Cardellini), raising her son alone near Crystal Lake, where she worked. So those curious about Jason's, and indeed his mother's, origins should not miss Crystal Lake when it debuts on October 15.
Ahead of this, I thought it would be fun to revisit the classic Friday the 13th movie franchise and put your knowledge to the test. Since it's among the best horror movies, I'm sure many of you are very familiar with Jason Voorhees and his reign of terror.
With 12 movies in the franchise, this is no easy task, and only true horror fans will get all of these questions right. Are you brave enough to take on the challenge?

Exclusivo: Galaxy S25 Plus cai de preço com cupom do Tecnoblog
Galaxy S25 Plus de 256 GB com câmera de 50 MP e chip Snapdragon Elite sai pela metade do preço no Magalu
O Galaxy S25 Plus (256 GB) está disponível por R$ 4.049,10 no Pix com o cupom TECNOBLOG250 no Magalu. Lançado por R$ 8.499, o smartphone premium da Samsung com tela AMOLED e câmera de 50 MP fica 52% mais barato e se torna uma das melhores ofertas vistas pelo Achados do TB.
O Galaxy S25 Plus possui uma tela AMOLED Dinâmico 2X de 6,7 polegadas, entregando resolução Quad HD e taxa de quadros de 120 Hz. O painel ainda oferece brilho máximo de 2.600 nits e suporte ao recurso HDR10+.
O modelo tem uma câmera tripla traseira com sensor principal de 50 MP, capaz de gravar vídeos em até 8K e cliques com Estabilização Óptica de Imagem (OIS). A câmera frontal de 12 MP é ideal para participar de videochamadas com qualidade de imagem 4K.
Focado em alto desempenho e no Galaxy AI, o Galaxy S25 Plus adota o chip Snapdragon 8 Elite e 12 GB de RAM. Já o armazenamento interno de 256 GB pode ser um pouco limitado para quem deseja baixar muitos aplicativos, mídias e arquivos.
O smartphone topo de linha da Samsung é equipado com uma bateria de 4.900 mAh que, segundo a marca, tem autonomia de até 30 horas de reprodução de vídeo. Ele ainda tem suporte para carregamento rápido que, com um adaptador de 45 W, vai de 0 a 65% em apenas meia hora.
Na parte externa, o aparelho tem estrutura de alumínio e acabamento traseiro em vidro com Gorilla Glass Victus 2. Além disso, o certificado IP68 de resistência à água permite que ele fique submerso por até 1,5 metro por 30 minutos.
Por fim, o Galaxy S25 Plus (R$ 4.029,10 no Pix com o cupom TECNOBLOG250) oferece conexões 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4, Ultra Wideband (UWB) e NFC. O modelo vem de fábrica com o Android 15, mas a Samsung fornecerá sete grandes atualizações do sistema operacional.

articles.title: Celular domina entre gamers da América Latina, aponta pesquisa
articles.text:
O smartphone se consolidou como uma das principais portas de entrada para os games na América Latina. Dados da Pesquisa Game Brasil Latam (PGB Latam), apresentados durante a gamescom latam 2026, mostram que o avanço do mobile acompanha mudanças no perfil e nos hábitos dos jogadores da região.
O levantamento ouviu 7.202 pessoas da Argentina, Chile, Colômbia, México e Peru e também analisou questões como preferência por plataformas, compra de jogos e preocupações relacionadas ao uso de inteligência artificial na indústria.
Geração Z representa quase metade dos jogadores
A Geração Z corresponde a 47,5% dos jogadores latino-americanos identificados pela pesquisa, reforçando a presença de um público que cresceu em contato direto com smartphones e serviços digitais.
Mesmo com a força do celular, outras plataformas continuam relevantes. O levantamento aponta percentuais de 17,5% para PCs e 19,5% para consoles, com destaque para o interesse observado em mercados como Argentina e Peru.
Os dados indicam, portanto, um cenário no qual o crescimento dos jogos mobile não necessariamente substitui outras plataformas, mas amplia as formas de acesso aos games.
Mulheres têm forte presença nos jogos mobile
O recorte por gênero mostra diferenças importantes na escolha das plataformas.
Entre as mulheres entrevistadas, 62,7% apontaram o smartphone como plataforma favorita. O estudo também registrou presença feminina nos computadores, com 40,9% das jogadoras demonstrando preferência pelo PC.
Entre os homens, os consoles aparecem com 61,8% da preferência.
Os resultados ajudam a mostrar como o público gamer latino-americano está distribuído entre diferentes dispositivos e também reforçam a relevância das mulheres no segmento mobile.
IA preocupa jogadores latino-americanos
A pesquisa também perguntou aos participantes sobre o avanço da inteligência artificial no desenvolvimento de jogos.
Entre os entrevistados, 40,6% demonstraram preocupação com possíveis perdas de empregos e precarização do trabalho criativo. Outros 36,2% mencionaram o uso indevido do trabalho de artistas, enquanto 35,8% temem impactos sobre a qualidade e a identidade dos jogos.
Os números mostram que a discussão sobre IA já ultrapassou desenvolvedores e empresas e também começa a fazer parte das preocupações dos próprios consumidores.
Jogadores estão dispostos a esperar por promoções
O preço também influencia o comportamento de compra. Segundo a PGB Latam, 25,8% dos entrevistados afirmam esperar por promoções antes de adquirir novos jogos.
Já 17,5% costumam comprar títulos no lançamento, especialmente quando existem benefícios adicionais envolvidos.
O conjunto dos dados revela um jogador latino-americano cada vez mais difícil de definir por apenas uma plataforma ou comportamento. Embora o smartphone tenha papel central nesse cenário, consoles e computadores continuam disputando espaço em uma comunidade formada por diferentes gerações, gêneros e hábitos de consumo.

articles.title: Spionageangriff auf Trump: T-Mobile stoppt Hacker mit Schere
articles.text:
Wie T-Mobile einen Spionageangriff auf Trump und Vance mit einer Schere verhinderte
Wer an das Verhindern von Cyberattacken denkt, denkt wahrscheinlich oftmals an Software-Lösungen wie eine Firewall. Dass es aber auch ganz analog und pragmatisch geht, beweist eine Geschichte, von der Bloomberg berichtet. Im Herbst 2024 fand eine großangelegte Spionagekampagne mit dem Code-Namen „Salt Typhoon“ statt. Dabei wurden mehr als 200 Ziele in 80 Ländern angegriffen. Am gravierendsten waren davon die USA betroffen.
Wie Salt Typhoon neun US-Telekommunikationskonzerne infiltrierte
Schon vor der Entdeckung soll der Angriff eine Zeit lang unentdeckt gelaufen sein. Dabei haben die Angreifer:innen zunächst neun große US-Telekommunikationsunternehmen gehackt und sich Zugang zu deren Netzwerken und Routern verschafft. Dazu zählten Verizon und AT&T, aber auch T‑Mobile. Anhand von späteren Analysen wurde klar, dass die Angreifer:innen Metadaten von Anrufen und Nachrichten von Millionen Kund:innen abgreifen konnten.
Heute geht man davon aus, dass es sich um eine großangelegte Attacke des chinesischen Ministeriums für Staatssicherheit gehandelt hat, die Daten von US-Politiker:innen sammeln wollten. Dafür priorisierten sie die Region um Washington D.C. herum und sollen sogar Daten von Donald Trump und JD Vance ergattert haben. Verständlicherweise sorgte die Entdeckung schon damals dafür, dass die Telekommunikationsunternehmen mit Hochdruck daran arbeiteten, die Angreifer:innen wieder aus ihren Systemen auszusperren.
Jeff Simon, Chief Information Officer bei T-Mobile, sagte dazu: „Wir haben gejagt, gejagt und gejagt. Jeden Tag habe ich das Team persönlich gefragt, wo die Angreifer sind, ob wir sie gefunden haben. Haben wir überhaupt schon Kontakt zum Feind gehabt?“ Erste Hinweise auf die infizierten Systeme gab es durch einen ungewöhnlichen Router, der im Datenzentrum von T-Mobile in Kalifornien stand. Das Gerät kommunizierte mit einem anderen T-Mobile-Standort, obwohl es abgeschaltet war.
Ein Techniker hat das Gerät sofort abgesteckt und zur genaueren Untersuchung in die Hauptzentrale in Washington gebracht. Dort stellten die Techniker:innen aber fest, dass das Signal gar nicht vom abgeschalteten Router kam. Sie verfolgten das Signal zu einem anderen Telekommunikationsunternehmen in Chicago, dessen Name Simon nicht näher nennt. Die Angreifer:innen hatten den Router in Chicago so manipuliert, dass er im System wie ein T-Mobile-Gerät auftauchte und so mit anderen Geräten des Unternehmens kommunizieren konnte.
So verhinderte T-Mobile weitere Cyberangriffe
Als die Quelle gefunden war, haben sich die Techniker:innen in ein Auto gesetzt, sind zum Datenzentrum des anderen Unternehmens gefahren und haben dort das betroffene Gerät aufgespürt. Einer der Techniker nahm einfach eine Schere in die Hand und schnitt das Kabel des Routers durch. Simon meint, dass sie auch den Router ebenso erst hätten herunterfahren können. Aber dieser Weg war schneller: „Es gibt nichts, was das Durchschneiden eines Kabels ersetzt.“
Der Router wurde mitgenommen und in einer isolierten Testumgebung reaktiviert. Allerdings waren die Angreifer:innen dann nicht mehr zu finden. Laut Simon hatten sie lediglich Zugang zu äußeren Netzwerken, sind aber nie an Kundendaten herangekommen. Heute erinnert das abgeschnittene Kabel in einem Bilderrahmen an den Vorfall. Darüber steht: „Von Grund auf wachsam, sicher durch Handeln. Salt Typhoon 2024.“
Die schlimmsten Security-Patzer
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 20.08.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Hört sich wie eine erfundene US Propagandstory an. Warum wurde das LAN Kabel nicht einfach abgesteckt? Man steht vor dem Router und statt einfach das LAN Kabel herauszuziehen, macht man sich erst auf die Suche nach einer Schere. Das dauert vielfach länger

articles.title: Una copia falsa de 'GTA 6' que circula en internet está infectando con malware a miles de ordenadores
articles.text:
Faltan más de dos meses para que llegue GTA 6 y ya han comenzado a circular decenas de estafas relacionadas con el juego. La más reciente tiene que ver con una supuesta versión filtrada que se distribuye en internet a través de un archivo ISO. Al instalar el supuesto juego, tu ordenador quedará infectado con malware que robará tu información y dejará comprometido tu equipo.
La firma de ciberseguridad Huntress documentó este esquema después de analizar una imagen ISO que circula en foros de videojuegos. El archivo se distribuye como una copia filtrada del juego de Rockstar Games, algo que todavía no existe en ningún formato accesible al público. Los hackers están aprovechando las filtraciones que surgieron días antes de que se proyectara el tráiler de Netflix, haciendo pensar a los usuarios que se trata de esta versión.
Para hacerlo creíble, las ISO pesan más de 100 GB, lo que las hace parecer que se trata de un juego AAA legítimo. Esta cifra es un engaño, ya que la mayor parte de ese peso corresponde a datos basura que no tienen ninguna función real y solo se añadieron para que el archivo alcance el tamaño habitual de uno de estos juegos. El contenido malicioso ocupa una fracción mínima de ese espacio, pero es muy peligroso si lo ejecutas en tu ordenador.
¿Qué hace el malware de GTA 6 en tu PC?
Al montar la imagen y ejecutar el instalador, lo primero que aparecerá será una ventana con el logo de GTA V. Si este error no es suficiente para hacer que te detengas, la siguiente pantalla incluye un mensaje en ruso que advierte que el juego no está licenciado, por lo que si aparece un error de licencia, hay que escribir a un correo para recibir una actualización del crack.
Aquellos que ya hayan pirateado juegos antes, seguramente identificaron todas las "red flags" de este archivo (logo de GTA V, ruso, crack por correo). Pero aquellos que no y simplemente quieren jugar GTA 6 en su PC, dejarán que el instalador copie todos los archivos maliciosos en segundo plano antes de avisar de un error en el proceso de instalación.
El ISO incluye diversas amenazas, entre las que destacan troyanos, infostealers y ransomware. Los primeros, conocidos como RAT, permiten que los hackers puedan controlar tu ordenador a distancia, ver el escritorio, activar la cámara y registrar lo que escribes. En el caso del infostealer, este malware también se roba las contraseñas de Chrome, tus claves de producto de Windows, tokens de Discord y datos de geolocalización del equipo.
La parte más dañina de este paquete es un ransomware que elimina las copias de seguridad de Windows y modifica la configuración de arranque para que no puedas recuperar tu PC. El malware cifra todos los archivos de menos de 200 MB y sobrescribe con datos aleatorios cualquier archivo más pesado. En pocas palabras, toda la información que tenías en el ordenador se perderá para siempre.
Cómo eliminar el virus que instalan las copias falsas de GTA en PC
Los investigadores mencionan que este malware es viejo y se ha usado en otros ataques. Algunos componentes datan de 2023, por lo que si tienes actualizado el Windows Defender, no tendrás que preocuparte. Tanto este como otros antivirus deberían detectarlo antes de que cause daño, siempre y cuando la protección en tiempo real esté activada.
Si por alguna razón caíste en la trampa e instalaste el ISO de GTA 6 pensando en que era legítimo, lo primero que tienes que hacer es desconectar tu PC de internet. Cambia tus contraseñas desde el móvil u otro dispositivo y activa la verificación en dos pasos para tus cuentas principales. Lo malo de este malware es que deberás reinstalar por completo Windows para asegurarte de que no queda ningún rastro en el equipo.

articles.title: PISA 2025 and school rankings: are we asking the right questions about schooling?
articles.text:
KEY TAKEAWAYS
- In France, as in other OECD countries, student performance has seen a steep decline in mathematics and reading.
- The latest Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) shows that this decline affects disadvantaged and advantaged students alike.
- International comparisons are more useful for questioning education systems’ capacity to reform than for identifying a model to copy.
The publication of the latest results from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA 2025) on September 8 prompted the usual flurry of commentary, comparisons and rankings. France has slipped, some countries have improved, while others have proved more resilient. As always, attention quickly turns to where each country stands.
These rankings are useful, but they risk obscuring a more important question: what do we actually make of the years we spend in school?
For much of the 20th century, measuring educational progress seemed relatively straightforward. We counted students, years of schooling and qualifications. There were good reasons for doing so: the expansion and democratisation of education were among the major social transformations of the past century.
But now that the vast majority of children spend many years in school, the question has shifted. It is no longer enough to know how long they remain in education. We need to understand what we make of those years, and what those years enable us to become. This is precisely the purpose of the work we have undertaken with our colleague Nadir Altinok in Edumetrics: Measuring Human Capital for the 21st century. By reconstructing comparable measures of the quality and distribution of learning over the long run, we seek to shift the analysis of human capital away from years of schooling towards the skills actually acquired.
Rankings aside, how far have we come?
The PISA 2025 results bring this question into sharper focus. Across OECD countries, average performance is now at its lowest level since PISA began in all three major domains assessed. Between 2015 and 2025, scores fell by 22 points in mathematics and 28 points in reading.
Twenty per cent of 15-year-olds are now low performers in all three main domains, compared with 16% in 2022.
France scores 483 points in science, almost exactly the OECD average of 482. It performs slightly below the OECD average in reading (456 compared with 461) and mathematics (458 compared with 463). But perhaps what matters more than France’s position is where it’s heading: since 2022, it has lost a further 18 points in reading and 16 points in mathematics.
Whether a country ranks 25th, 27th or 30th ultimately tells us less than knowing where it has come from, which direction it is moving in, and which students are progressing or falling behind.
This is also suggested by a recent report from France’s High Commission for Strategy and Planning on educational attainment. It adds an important qualification to the usual diagnosis. France suffers from substantial educational inequalities, but its difficulties do not concern disadvantaged students alone. They also affect advantaged students and, in some areas, even the highest performers.
There is therefore both a problem of inequality and, at least up to lower secondary school, a problem of relatively low overall attainment, particularly in mathematics and science. Looking only at averages is not enough; neither is looking only at inequalities.
Expanding access does not yet mean democratising learning
France has dramatically expanded access to education. This is a historic achievement that should not be underestimated. But when access becomes almost universal, democratisation must also become qualitative. The question is no longer simply: who gets into school? It becomes: what do students learn there, and who learns what?
Our long-run series shows that, after a period of international convergence in educational performance until around 1990, national trajectories began to diverge again. Since 2000, relatively few countries have experienced a sustained improvement in the quality of learning. PISA 2025 does not, of course, bring this history to an end. It simply adds another observation to it.
This perspective also allows us to look differently at educational inequalities. When potential skills are not developed, it is not only individual trajectories that are affected: part of a society’s collective human capital is unable to ever fully develop.
Our simulations for France suggest that economic growth could have been around 0.5% higher if an effective policy to reduce educational inequalities had been implemented since the late 1970s.
Spending more is not enough
Resources obviously matter. The High Commission highlights several weaknesses in France: relatively modest expenditure on primary education, a comparatively high number of students per teacher by European standards, and growing difficulties in recruiting teachers.
Resources matter, but they do not explain everything. PISA 2025 suggests that the relevance of policies and the way resources are allocated appear to be more closely associated with performance than spending per student alone. This is also one of the lessons of Edumetrics: spending more is not enough; we need to invest better.
Yet between one euro spent on education and learning actually acquired lies an entire world: teachers, students, families, curricula, teaching practices, schools and institutions, and time. Resources do not mechanically produce outcomes. They have to be transformed into capabilities.
This leads to a question we ask less often: students learn, but do education systems themselves know how to learn?
A reform produces intended effects and others that are less predictable. However, too many reforms can defeat the purpose of reform itself. A practice may work in one context and fail in another. Policies need to be adjusted, developed further and sometimes abandoned. Education policy is, therefore, also about a collective ability to observe, experiment, measure, correct and learn.
From this perspective, international comparisons are valuable, not in so much for telling us what to copy but in allowing us to ask better questions.
And then came artificial intelligence
This question takes on a new dimension with artificial intelligence (AI). In a matter of seconds, a student can now obtain a translation, an explanation, a summary, the solution to an exercise or an apparently convincing piece of writing.
One might conclude that some forms of foundational knowledge are becoming less important. Yet PISA highlights that some of the reading skills now in decline are precisely those we need in an information-saturated environment: evaluating information, comparing multiple sources, interpreting evidence and exercising critical judgement.
Human capital in the 21st century can probably no longer be conceived as a stock of knowledge acquired once and for all. It must also encompass a more fundamental capability: learning how to learn. Initial education remains essential because it provides the foundations that subsequently enable people to revise their knowledge, acquire new skills and adapt throughout their lives.
Measure to understand, not to rank
One essential caveat must nevertheless remain: tests are not education, and PISA is not school. No indicator can capture everything a child learns while growing up. Data can inform our decisions; they cannot decide for us what we wish to pass on or what we collectively wish to become.
This is also why the latest PISA findings should probably not be read as evidence of inevitable decline. Some learning journeys are improving. The United Kingdom and Türkiye, for example, have made progress in science.
There is, of course, no single model that can simply be replicated. History never provides recipes; sometimes it offers possibilities. PISA therefore invites us, perhaps, to ask our questions about education in a slightly different order.
We ask how much we spend, how many students succeed, which countries are moving forward and which are falling behind. All these questions are legitimate. But perhaps they come after another one: what does an education system actually manage to transform?
Time into learning, knowledge into skills, skills into the ability to adapt and, perhaps, these individual capabilities into collective possibilities. That is what we should seek to measure instead of reducing education to a handful of numbers, in order to distinguish the illusion of progress from the reality of progress as far as possible.

articles.title: Indian Researchers Look to Neuromorphic Computing - EE Times
articles.text:
Neuromorphic computing mimics biological brains through sparse, event-driven computation, memory-centric architectures, and asynchronous communication. Indian researchers see it as a way to curb AI’s energy use while enabling new hardware designs.
In an exclusive interview with EE Times, Alex P. James, director of the Indian Institute of Information Technology and Management-Kerala (IIITM-K), said, “Today, we have a huge amount of data to process. That is not a sustainable model if energy consumption keeps scaling in proportion to the data we have.”
Researchers often return to one comparison: the human brain. “If you look at the human brain, we still work with around 20 W, and that can be seen as a gold standard for many of the intelligent tasks we associate with neuromorphic systems,” James said.
For decades, semiconductor performance has largely improved by shrinking transistors and increasing processor complexity. This strategy has powered increasingly capable CPUs, GPUs, and AI accelerators but may not be enough to solve AI’s growing energy demands.
Because neuroscience is an evolving field, researchers are exploring multiple architectural approaches rather than converging on one. “We have not yet fully understood the brain,” James said. “We understand its physiology, but we do not have a complete functional understanding of every aspect of it.”
Why spikes matter
One concept that appears throughout neuromorphic research is spiking neural networks (SNNs). Unlike conventional deep neural networks that continuously perform multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) operations, spiking systems communicate only when neurons generate events.
“The brain does not use its entire capacity all the time,” James said. “Many neurons remain inactive during a given task. As a result, a significant amount of energy is saved because not everything is switched on all the time.”
EE Times previously spoke with Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bombay Professor Udayan Ganguly, whose group demonstrated an ultra-low-power neuromorphic neuron by repurposing quantum-tunneling current, a leakage mechanism that conventional chip designers typically seek to suppress.
Unlike digital processors, neuromorphic systems do not rely on a global clock and operate asynchronously, encoding information in the timing and pattern of spikes. The artificial neuron follows a similar biological principle: It receives an input that fills a reservoir until it crosses a threshold, generating a spike before resetting itself. Electronically, it can be implemented with a capacitor, current source, leakage resistor, and threshold circuitry.
Rather than using conventional transistor operation, the IIT Bombay research team turned to quantum-tunneling current. “In the deep off state, quantum-tunneling current flows,” Ganguly said. “We use that quantum-tunneling current as the current source. That leakage current slowly charges the neuron’s capacitor.”
The design was fabricated in standard GlobalFoundries 45-nm CMOS technology, demonstrating that the approach can be implemented using an established manufacturing process.
The team said the resulting neuron consumed about 1,000× less power than comparable implementations and showed about 5× lower process, voltage, and temperature variability than an equivalent low-power design based on sub-threshold operation. The same mechanism, Ganguly said, also improved robustness.
A speech-recognition system built around spiking neurons
To show the concepts could extend beyond individual circuits, Ganguly’s team built a complete neuromorphic speech-recognition system, combining device physics, circuit design, algorithms, and hardware implementation.
The demonstration addressed a challenge that conventional pattern-recognition systems must also solve: remembering information that arrives over time. “The system needs memory to retain the earlier sounds so that when a complete sequence has been received, it can recognize the entire pattern,” Ganguly said.
The team implemented that capability using a liquid-state machine, a form of recurrent SNN that naturally captures temporal information.
“The idea is similar to ripples created when a droplet falls into water,” Ganguly said. “Those ripples gradually fade away, providing a temporary memory of the event.”
Speech signals are converted into spike trains, and the recurrent connections preserve enough information to classify complete words. Unlike many deep-learning models that require multiple processing stages, the liquid-state machine performs recognition using only two layers.
Using a standard benchmark dataset, the system achieved approximately 99% classification accuracy with only about 100 neurons, showing how small spiking networks can perform practical AI tasks. The same network, Ganguly said, can also be adapted for vision and other applications.
The team also fabricated the hardware, demonstrating an end-to-end signal chain.
“GlobalFoundries provided us with a free tape-out through its university program, and we were the first university in India to participate in that program,” Ganguly said.
The complete system consisted of three stages. “The first stage implements the filters and the artificial ear,” Ganguly said. “The second stage is the recurrent neural network. The third stage performs classification.”
The chip’s recurrent neural network contains 36 neurons that generate output spike patterns from spike trains entering the chip over time.
When tested on two-class speech-recognition tasks such as “yes” and “no” or “start” and “stop,” the complete hardware system achieved an error rate of less than 2%.
“We began by looking at the power consumed by data centers,” Ganguly said. “Modern processors generate substantial heat, but we do not observe the human brain heating up in the same way.”
The fabricated neuron operates at approximately 100 kHz, occupies about 40 µm2, consumes 2.70 pW of standby power, and requires roughly 8 fJ per spike, which is “close to that of the human brain,” Ganguly said.
Memory moves to the center of computing
SNNs aren’t the only neuromorphic architecture. James pointed to cellular neural networks, hierarchical temporal memory systems, and other biologically inspired models, each emphasizing different brain-like properties such as robustness and fault tolerance.
Another direction focuses on memory itself rather than neuron models. Researchers at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) Bangalore, led by Professors Sreetosh Goswami and Navakanta Bhat, recently demonstrated a molecular memristor based on a ruthenium compound that delivers 14-bit analog resolution and 4.10-TOPS/W energy efficiency. The device is intended for in-memory computing, where matrix operations are performed directly inside memory arrays rather than repeatedly shuttling data between memory and processors.
James said he believes future AI hardware may rely less on arithmetic units and more on memory itself. He pointed to analog, memory-centric architectures that store programmable conductance values instead of binary states—weights encoded directly, letting MAC operations happen naturally within crossbar arrays.
“A 32-bit multiplication in a digital system may require hundreds of gates,” James said. “The same operation can be performed using only a few memory devices.”
The IISc work follows the same principle. Instead of storing binary values, the molecular memristor stores analog conductance states that represent neural network weights. When input voltages are applied across crossbar arrays, multiplication occurs through Ohm’s law, while the accumulation follows Kirchhoff’s current law, allowing thousands of MAC operations to be executed simultaneously.
Such architectures cut chip area and energy consumption, though they add new ADC, precision, and variability challenges.
Goswami and Bhat said they addressed one of those precision challenges by engineering the switching mechanism at the molecular level. Unlike many resistive memories that rely on stochastic defect formation, the ruthenium-based device switches through a deterministic molecular process that enables linear, symmetric conductance updates across four orders of magnitude.
Sparsity plays a similar role. “In a spiking system, information is represented by ones and zeros,” James said. “If one of the inputs is zero, the multiplication result is zero.” Inactive neurons are simply skipped, consuming little or no energy and lowering computational overhead.
The IISc team is now integrating the devices into a mixed-signal AI inference accelerator under development in a 22-nm TSMC process through a startup incubated at the Centre for Nano Science and Engineering. The prototype will use crossbar arrays for in-memory computation while combining analog computing with digital control logic.
Commercial success depends on applications
Despite decades of research, neuromorphic computing has yet to achieve widespread commercial adoption. James believes the challenge is not simply technical but also about demonstrating clear business value.
“For any technology to move from an idea to the market, you need science, engineering, and business,” he said. “The business aspect is particularly important because it is tied to applications.”
Researchers first need to prove that neuromorphic architecture solves a real-world problem better than conventional hardware. “For each architecture, we need proof-of-concept demonstrations that show a clear advantage in a real application,” James said. Only then can engineering turn those concepts into manufacturable products.
James cautioned that a biologically inspired algorithm doesn’t automatically translate into an efficient chip. Some algorithms may suit analog/mixed-signal hardware; others may be better-suited to in-memory computing or entirely new device technologies. “We are not focused on a single hardware platform,” he said. “We are exploring and identifying the most efficient hardware for implementing these ideas.”
Ultimately, economics has the final say.
An interdisciplinary challenge
Both researchers emphasized that neuromorphic computing extends far beyond semiconductor design, forcing traditionally separate disciplines to work together.
“A computer scientist may not interact closely with an electronics engineer,” James said. “A neuroscientist may not interact with either group. Neuromorphic computing is changing that. You will find biologists, mathematicians, electrical engineers, and computer scientists working together to understand the same problem.
“If this direction continues, I believe we will eventually solve one of the biggest scientific and engineering challenges of our time,” he added.
For Ganguly, the ambition reaches even further.
“If we can build chips with neurons and synapses that communicate natively in the same way as the brain, then damaged parts of the brain could potentially be replaced,” he said. “We could model the human brain and better understand thoughts and emotions.”
He acknowledged that such applications remain decades away: “That is a 20-year vision. It is not something we are doing today, but it is something that could affect all of us in the future.”
For now, neuromorphic computing remains an active research area rather than a GPU replacement. The approaches being explored differ widely. IIT Bombay is developing ultra-low-power spiking neurons using quantum-tunneling current in conventional CMOS technology. IISc Bangalore is engineering molecular memristors for analog in-memory computing. Individual researchers such as IIITM-K’s James are investigating the architectures that determine how those devices should be organized. For India, these projects collectively illustrate that neuromorphic computing is advancing simultaneously at the device, circuit, architecture, and system levels.
As power and scalability limits grow harder to ignore, researchers see brain-inspired computing as one of the more promising paths toward next-generation intelligent machines.

articles.title: The White House says Truth Social is the ‘most powerful and popular social media platform in the world’
articles.text:
The White House claims the Donald Trump-owned Truth Social is the “most powerful and popular social media platform in the world.” The statement, provided to The New York Times by White House spokesperson Davis Ingle, is at odds with the user counts from some of the biggest social media platforms on the web.
The White House says Truth Social is the ‘most powerful and popular social media platform in the world’
YouTube and Facebook are the world’s most popular platforms with billions of active users, while Truth Social traffic has declined.
Data gathered by Search Engine Land shows YouTube is the most popular platform in the world, with 2.65 billion monthly active users. Facebook comes in second with 2.39 billion active users around the globe, followed by TikTok with 2.21 billion and Instagram with 1.99 billion. Truth Social doesn’t make Search Engine Land’s top 10 list, which shows Elon Musk’s X and Meta’s Threads at the bottom with 450 million and 223 million users, respectively. Even those platforms trail Pinterest, which is listed with 579 million global users.
Truth Social’s traffic appears to be declining. As reported by the NYT, data from Similarweb suggests that the number of monthly visitors to Truth Social dipped 36 percent in July compared to the same time last year. From January to July 2025, an average of 28 million people visited Truth Social each month, while this number fell to 25 million during the first seven months of 2026, according to the NYT. Last month, Truth Social launched its $100,000 / month subscription to gain early access to posts from Trump and other prominent users, raising concerns about corruption.
The NYT report details Trump’s posting patterns on Truth Social, which often include AI-generated images, such as one showing his head on Hulk Hogan’s body and another hitting a cut-out of Iran with a hammer brandishing the American flag. Ingle cites President Trump’s “authentic voice” as the reason for the platform’s so-called popularity, adding it’s where “he communicates directly with the American people and the world without the biased media taking him out of context.”

articles.title: Chip Industry Week in Review
articles.text:
News from this week’s SPIE Photomask Technology + Extreme Ultraviolet Lithographyconference:
ASML and TSMC are launching an industry initiative to transition high-NA EUV lithography from current 6-inch photomasks to larger 12-inch masks, which could improve scanner productivity and eliminate some stitching constraints. The companies are targeting a 12-inch mask pilot line by 2031, with production-ready systems by 2033. TSMC plans to begin using high-NA EUV in high-volume manufacturing in 2030.
The eBeam Initiative‘s annual industry survey found 66% of semiconductor experts expect large-format photomasks to be adopted within a decade, while 94% expect mask revenue to grow this year.
imec demonstrated single-exposure high-NA EUV patterning of 22nm-pitch lines/spaces and 28nm-pitch vias using established chemically amplified resist technology, supporting layers envisioned for A14/A10 logic.
Intel Foundry and ASML said high-NA EUV has now processed more than 1 million wafers, including select production layers for Panther Lake, with Intel 18A high-NA layers meeting or exceeding comparable patterns made with conventional EUV.
Samsung formally joined the 12-inch photomask initiative and says it plans to introduce high-NA EUV into DRAM high-volume manufacturing in 2028.
D2S highlighted new PLDC techniques for improving mask uniformity and linearity, including Dynamic Maximum Dose, variable bias correction, and offline processing.
NY Creates joined the industry initiative developing 12-inch photomasks for high-NA EUV.
Arm broadens its AI push
At its Arm Everywhere conference in China, the company announced:
A next-gen edge AI platform, Arm Compute Subsystems for Mobile 2, aimed at agentic AI and cinematic mobile graphics. It features Mali G2-Ultra NX neural accelerator GPU and CPU cluster technology with scalable matrix extension 2.
A physical AI ecosystem program, Arm Total Design for Physical AI, for multiple companies across the technology stack, to boost development of robotics.
Neoverse CSS N4 for AI infrastructure with up to 128 cores per die, supporting LPDDR6, PCIe 7, and delivering up to 2X the performance, complemented by the Arm AGI CPU.
Amkor announced phase 2 of its Arizona advanced packaging and test campus, adding 60,000 square meters of cleanroom space and increasing the planned investment to approximately $12B. Construction is expected to begin in late 2027.
ASML has begun work on a new campus at Brainport Industries Campus North near Eindhoven, creating a second major site to support future manufacturing growth beyond its Veldhoven headquarters.
Memory
SK hynix outlined a strategy spanning HBM, 3D DRAM, HBF, CXL and SSDs, with memory increasingly co-designed at the system level for AI. The company identified 3D memory as a key future technology.
Kepler Computing emerged from stealth with its new high-bandwidth AI memory architecture using 3D stacking and ferroelectric materials. The company, which raised $468M, claims an order of magnitude capacity increase compared to SRAM and HBM, and expects to ramp production next year.
Global DRAM industry revenue jumped ~60% sequentially to nearly $155B in Q2. Market share leaders: Samsung 39%, SK hynix 25% and Micron 23%.
Chinese AI-chip suppliers including Huawei and Cambricon are raising accelerator prices as limited access to HBM drives up costs.
Memory research: USC-led researchers developed a vertically stackable vdW memory selector with >10¹²-cycle endurance, sub-20 ns switching and low device variability, addressing a key challenge in scaling high-density 3D memory. NUS researchers developed an on-chip pulse generator for field-free magnetic switching, cutting write energy by four orders of magnitude and pointing to faster, lower-power magnetic memory.
Analog Devicesagreed to acquireAlif Semiconductor in an all-cash transaction for $1.35B, for its high-efficiency AI-native MCUs and fusion processors optimized for on-device, physical AI.
OpenAI is working with Samsung on next-gen chips, with OpenAI Korea chief Harrison Kim saying the companies have made significant progress in joint production and research, reports Reuters.
Raking it in
Ayar Labs raised $150M and announced Wiwynn made a strategic investment earlier this year for its continued transition to high-volume manufacturing of CPO for AI scale-up.
Xanadu and ASML will collaborate on advanced lithography for photonic quantum chips to improve patterning and reduce optical loss.
The U.S. Department of Commerce finalized $775M in previously announced CHIPS R&D awards for domestic quantum semiconductor development and manufacturing, including $375M for GlobalFoundries and $100M each for Rigetti, D-Wave, PsiQuantum, and Quantinuum.
Market data
Revenue for the world’s top 10 foundries rose more than 11% sequentially to a record ~$53B in Q2, according to TrendForce.
The data-center semiconductor market will reach $1.5T by 2031 as AI drives increasing demand for logic, memory, optical interconnects and power devices, predicts Yole Group. Advanced packaging and HBM capacity are emerging as major bottlenecks, while AI rack power could approach 1 MW by the end of the decade.
Financials
TSMC (August revenue up 53% YoY) and IQE (1st half up 40% YoY).
The U.K. government released an expanded study of the country’s semiconductor sector, identifying 703 companies and estimating that dedicated semiconductor businesses generated £10.6B in revenue in 2025.
SEMI Europe published a position paper outlining nine recommendations for the EU Chips Act 2.0, including broader First-of-a-Kind eligibility, six-month permitting timelines, and measures addressing energy, infrastructure, and manufacturing costs. It also called for balanced funding, so leading-edge projects don’t crowd out pilot lines, mature and specialty technologies, and advanced packaging.
Keysight entered an agreement to support the EU’s Chips JU initiative by making its EDA software and training available to semiconductor startups and small and medium-sized enterprises.
TU Eindhoven and European collaborators fabricated edge AI processors that combine RISC-V processors with specialized AI accelerators and memory-centric and neuromorphic computing.
Americas
Silicon Labs opened a new R&D lab at its Austin headquarters aimed at advanced chip design and testing.
Companies are exploring Argentina‘s remote, cold Patagonia region for data center buildout, per Reuters.
Qolab and SkyWater signed a multi-year foundry agreement to manufacture superconducting quantum devices using SkyWater’s new SC250 platform.
Samsung Electronics and Mistral AI formed a strategic partnership to deploy customized, on-premises AI models across Samsung’s semiconductor operations for defect detection, equipment optimization, and yield improvement. Samsung also led Mistral AI’s Series D funding round and took a strategic equity stake.
Fundings, IPO
Altera is reportedly preparing an IPO that could raise more than $2B. Silver Lake owns 51% of Altera, while Intel retains 49%.
NLM Photonicsexpanded funding to commercialize organic photonics, including an investment from Mitsubishi Chemical.
States That Gave Data Centers Billions in Tax Breaks Are Now Ripping Up the Deals (WSJ)
New Technologies
PDF Solutions debuted Exensio Aurora, its new scalable analytics architecture. The product is designed to handle semiconductor manufacturing data at petabyte scale and securely deploy agentic AI across manufacturing operations and the supply chain.
Taiyo Holdings and imec demonstrated a 3-layer RDL with 700nm wiring and vias on 300mm wafers using Taiyo’s new photosensitive dielectric material. The work advances fine-pitch RDL technology for advanced packaging.
Infineon introduced the TDA235E5 and TDA235E0, a dual-phase smart power stage family designed to meet growing power density requirements of next-generation AI accelerators and vertical power delivery modules. The new offerings will deliver benchmark power density exceeding 2 A/mm².
imec has moved its 96-band hyperspectral linescan sensor into commercial availability for camera and satellite developers. The CMOS-based sensor has a spectral range of 450 to 900nm, improves signal-to-noise ratio by 40% over its predecessor, and integrates its spectral filters directly on-chip.
CoreWeave launched “Physical AI Field Engineering” this week, a new offering built to help manufacturers integrate physical AI into their engineering processes.
Smartphone chips
Apple unveiled new products under new CEO, John Ternus, including its 2nm A20 Pro chip for the iPhone 18 with 50% more memory bandwidth and integrated neural accelerators, as well as the company’s first foldable phone, iPhone Duo.
Powering its new Mate XT 2 trifold smartphone, Huawei launched the first commercial application of its Kirin 9050 Pro chip with LogicFolding architecture, with 42% better performance than its predecessor, per SCMP. (Read a related technical paper: Huawei’s Tao Chip Was Supposed to Melt?)
Connecting data centers
OIF published the implementation agreement for 1600ZR Coherent Interfaces, doubling the capacity of its 800ZR specification.
Meta and Panmnesia proposed an architecture that lets an entire data center operate as one chip by placing CPUs, accelerators, and memory in a single CXL-over-optics-based domain, with a high-fan-out non-blocking switch, a link acceleration unit and a fabric controller to bound latency variability.
Adoptions and certifications
Cadencequalified its EDA tool flow to run natively on AWS Graviton, including front-end design and verification, synthesis, place-and-route, and timing sign-off. Annapurna Labs is now designing future-gen Graviton CPUs using the Cadence flow.
Japan’s NanoBridge Semiconductor adopted Siemens EDA’s FPGA tools for its low-power, harsh-environment FPGAs for aerospace, automotive, and critical infrastructure.
d-Matrix will use NVIDIA’sNVLink Fusion to connect its upcoming Raptor inference processors directly into NVIDIA-based data center systems. Raptor is expected to complete final design this year, with compatible rack-scale systems targeted for 2027.
Redington will distribute Siemens EDA’s Xcelerator portfolio of industrial software across Africa.
Research
Kyocera and Tohoku University developed an isolator-integrated photonics chip that reduces back-reflected light by about 95%, enabling faster, energy-efficient AI data centers.
CEA-Leti, Spintec, and Université Paris-Saclay researchers demonstrated a hybrid nanoelectronic Ising machine — combining hafnium-oxide ReRAM devices with stochastic MTJs — with an intrinsic annealing mechanism that could pave the way for more compact, faster, and energy-efficient hardware accelerators.
Harvard researchers co-designed a layered semiconductor and a metasurface, so every part of the device, including electronic states, optical fields, and geometry, works together toward efficient frequency conversion at a given wavelength, which could help miniaturize photonics and quantum technologies.
Researchers in Japan have demonstrated the first epitaxial growth of single-crystalline polar wurtzite NbAlN on GaN. An optimized NbAlN/GaN heterostructure more than tripled sheet electron density while retaining high room-temperature mobility, suggesting a potential new route to higher-performance GaN power and RF devices.
Security
AI threats
Google published new warnings on agentic AI-enabled cyberthreats this week, sounding alarms for expanded SW supply chain risks, threats to AI IP, and increased LLMjacking efforts.
Independent researchers found that a swarm of OpenAI agents reportedly hacked a German wiki site to create a message board earlier this year, in an incident that appears to have preceded the similar Hugging Face breach in July.
Anthropic published an updated cybersecurity advisory after discovering a fourth instance of a Claude model gaining unauthorized access to a third-party system.
AWS released Deception Benchmark, a new framework designed to test whether AI models can “distinguish real vulnerabilities from code that looks risky but is actually safe.”
A new IAPS report on AI data center security called for new industry security standards, increased cross-company incident intelligence sharing, and security-focused supply chain realignment in the face of emerging AI threats to data centers.
The FBI published its first-ever cyber strategy roadmap, with the document outlining a shift toward more proactive cybercrime disruption efforts.
Cisco updated its Secure Firewall Management Center advisory to confirm active exploitation of a critical authentication-bypass vulnerability that can let unauthenticated remote attackers gain root access.
CERT Polska warned that attackers are actively exploiting a chain of six MikroTik RouterOS vulnerabilities. Two flaws can be combined to take full control of exposed routers through SSH without authentication.
The NSA, FBI, and CISA issued a joint advisory covering cybersecurity threats tied to Chinese AI companies conducting industrial-scale distillation campaigns against US frontier AI models. Chinese companies have “likely extracted billions of tokens across millions of exchanges/requests from U.S. frontier AI models” since 2024, the agencies said.
SK keyfoundry and automotive mixed-signal semiconductor supplier Elmos announced a new long-term wafer supply deal alongside plans to expand the companies’130nm technology collaboration.
Microchip announced a strategic collaboration with Longhorn Automotive to integrate its VS700 ASA-ML chipsets into camera systems for ADAS and in-cabin sensing.
Cadence’s Amol Borkar examines how this technology will improve even further in the future, why the focus isn’t just about faster processors, and why this is so important for edge systems.
Quantum
SkyWater launched SkyWater Quantum Solutions, combining superconducting, quantum photonics, heterogeneous integration, and advanced packaging capabilities to help move quantum technologies into manufacturing.
Fujitsu developed a working prototype of a diamond-spin quantum computer that incorporates tin-vacancy (SnV) centers into photonic ICs, an important step toward a modular architecture.
LUMI AI Factory selected IQM’s staged path to deploy the EU’s first superconducting quantum computer with logical qubits, at IT Center for Science in Finland, as part of a hybrid HPC, AI, and quantum computing platform.
Quantum research
A University of Chicago researcher found that a quantum computer could “use high-powered lasers as ‘optical tweezers’ to capture and control individual atoms of helium,” offering faster tunneling, faster transport, and controllable motional qubits, compared to designs based on lithium.
An MIT researcher tested GPT-5.6 Sol’s ability to run measurements on an uncalibrated six-qubit chip and found that, when the signals were clear, Codex completed a standard sequence of measurements with little researcher intervention.
Workforce, Education
The National Network for Microelectronics Education formed its first Industry Advisory Committee, bringing together leaders from Lam Research, Intel and others to guide U.S. semiconductor workforce strategy. The group will help align education and training programs with industry needs as the sector faces a projected shortfall of 127,000 to 157,000 workers by 2030.
India is providing EDA tools to 13 engineering colleges under its chips to startup (C2S) program.
The U.S. State Department formally launched Foundry School, a training program for engineers, technicians and industry leaders, with instruction spanning semiconductors, factory design, automation, supply chains and manufacturing operations.
Reducing variation in manufacturing, monitoring behavior over time, and targeting specific workloads can have a big impact on power, performance, and area/cost.

articles.title: Victime du succès de GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI ferme les vannes de son forfait le plus cher
articles.text:
La demande pour GPT-6 Astra force OpenAI à fermer temporairement les nouvelles souscriptions à son offre Pro à 200 dollars par mois. Les abonnés actuels conservent leur accès, tandis que les autres formules restent disponibles.
Même à 200 dollars par mois, il faut désormais patienter. Depuis le 10 septembre, OpenAI a suspendu les nouvelles inscriptions et les passages vers sa formule ChatGPT Pro la plus chère. En cause, le succès de GPT-6 Astra, particulièrement gourmand en ressources et déjà capable de mettre les infrastructures du groupe sous tension.
Thibault Sottiaux, responsable produit chez OpenAI, explique que l’entreprise préfère limiter temporairement les arrivées afin de préserver la qualité de service pour les abonnés existants, le temps d’augmenter ses capacités. La mesure est présentée comme provisoire, sans date de réouverture pour l’instant.
Astra demande beaucoup plus aux serveurs
La situation n’est pas totalement surprenante. Plus performant que ses prédécesseurs, GPT-6 Astra a justement été conçu pour prendre davantage de travail en charge sans intervention humaine : programmation, missions longues, production de documents ou de présentations, mais aussi manipulation d’interfaces, remplissage de formulaires et tests de sites web.
OpenAI revendique notamment un score de 72,6% sur OSWorld 2.0, un benchmark consacré aux tâches réalisées sur ordinateur, contre 65,7% pour GPT-5.6 Sol. Des chiffres maison, donc à prendre avec le recul habituel, mais qui donnent une idée du positionnement du modèle : Astra n’est pas seulement là pour répondre plus intelligemment, il doit aussi agir davantage.
Et plus une IA travaille longtemps, utilise des outils et enchaîne les étapes, plus elle mobilise de calcul. Le succès commercial commence donc à rencontrer une limite beaucoup plus matérielle : la capacité de calcul qu’OpenAI peut actuellement consacrer au service.
Les autres forfaits restent accessibles
Signalons par ailleurs que cette suspension ne concerne que l’offre Pro à 200 dollars. La formule Pro à 100 dollars reste accessible, avec les mêmes grandes fonctions, mais des quotas plus serrés. OpenAI annonce environ cinq fois le volume d’usage de Plus, contre vingt fois pour la formule désormais fermée aux nouveaux clients.
Les abonnés déjà inscrits à Pro 200 dollars continuent, eux, de profiter normalement de leur forfait. Plus donne également accès à Astra dans Work et Codex, tandis que GPT-5.6 Sol reste utilisé dans les conversations classiques. Les développeurs peuvent enfin passer par l’API, facturée à la consommation.
Ceux qui refusent d’attendre peuvent aussi regarder ailleurs. Anthropic pousse Claude Pro avec Claude Code et Cowork, tandis que Google AI Pro mise sur Gemini 3.1 Pro, Deep Research et ses intégrations à Gmail ou Docs.
OpenAI n’a clairement pas de problème pour convaincre les utilisateurs d’essayer Astra. Son défi, désormais, est de trouver assez de puissance de calcul pour les laisser s’en servir.
- Chat dans différentes langues, dont le français
- Générer, traduire et obtenir un résumé de texte
- Générer, optimiser et corriger du code

articles.title: Professeur Raoult vs Le Gang des Cerises : quel est ce documentaire HBO qui fait le buzz ?
articles.text:
Si Professeur Raoult vs Le Gang des Cerises agite les réseaux sociaux et squatte toutes les conversations depuis sa mise en ligne ce vendredi 11 septembre 2026, ce n’est pas un hasard.
Si vous avez aperçu ce titre étrange truster le haut des tendances ces derniers jours, sans trop comprendre le rapport entre l’IHU de Marseille et des fruits de saison, voici de quoi remettre les pendules à l’heure.
Six justiciers amateurs contre le géant de la chloroquine dans Professeur Raoult vs Le Gang des Cerises
L’histoire ne se concentre pas uniquement sur le célèbre infectiologue marseillais, interrogé dans le documentaire, mais sur la traque menée dans son ombre. « Le Gang des Cerises », c’est le nom donné à un petit groupe d’inconnus, six chercheurs, soignants ou enseignants, qui se sont improvisés enquêteurs du dimanche en pleine crise sanitaire.
Un détail que la série ne cache pas : le collectif ne s’est jamais appelé « Le Gang des Cerises », c’est le titre choisi par HBO Max. Ces anonymes réunis sur les réseaux sociaux se surnommaient eux-mêmes les « Cerises Trottinettes ». Parmi eux figure la propre fille de Didier Raoult, et la série donne aussi la parole aux anciens ministres de la Santé Agnès Buzyn et Olivier Véran.
Leur objectif à l’époque ? Éplucher minutieusement chaque publication, chaque donnée chiffrée et chaque sortie médiatique de Didier Raoult pour démonter ses théories sur l’hydroxychloroquine.
Formaté en quatre épisodes, le projet nous replonge au cœur de cette guerre des preuves scientifiques. Le récit décortique comment ce collectif de citoyens ordinaires s’est retrouvé à mener la vie dure au médecin le plus puissant de France, sur fond d’emballement médiatique généralisé, de guerres d’ego et de règlements de comptes.
Un véritable thriller du réel
Loin du simple cours de science barbant, le programme est conçu comme un véritable polar judiciaire de la vraie vie. Entre guerre d’ego dans les labos, polémique sur les réseaux sociaux et traque numérique, la série Professeur Raoult vs Le Gang des Cerises dévoile les coulisses d’une bataille qui a totalement échappé à tout contrôle.
Disponible depuis ce vendredi sur la plateforme HBO Max, la série promet déjà de réveiller de sacrés débats de comptoir. Que l’on ait été pro ou anti-Raoult durant le confinement, ce braquage documentaire de trois heures propose une plongée inédite dans l’une des controverses les plus toxiques de l’histoire récente de la santé publique.
Sur le fond, Didier Raoult, lui, a été condamné par l’Ordre des médecins à une interdiction d’exercer pendant deux ans, à compter du 1er février 2025, pour avoir fait la promotion imprudente de la molécule, selon l’Ordre.
